en: May that cheek of Ambikā, kissed by Tryambaka, protect you for a long time— she who is the subject of the *Kirātārjunīya-vyāyoga*.
By the weight of her bold horripilation, the flower-armed god (Kāma) momentarily became one whose weapon was sprouts. || 1 ||
(At the end of the Nāndī) The Stage Manager:
Ho there! Who is present here?
(Entering) The Stage Manager:
My dear sir, what is this you say? You are a devotee of Maheśvara; therefore, let my lord recite other *nāndī* verses dedicated to Maheśa, infused with the sentiment of horror (*ghora-rasa*).
Sūtradhāra—(Laughing) Noble sir! What is this? Sthāpaka—
Let the venerable one read first.
Sūtra:
By whom [the sun] was made to serve as the staff for the umbrella of his body, which was darkened by the mass of hair standing erect;...

May that trident of the Blessed One, who is adorned with the crescent moon, be for your welfare— that weapon by obtaining which even Ambikā, though a woman, brought about the destruction of the demons; and upon seeing which, the thunderbolt in the hand of Indra, despite his fierce prowess, became as if painted in a picture.
Therefore, tell me now: what is this? The Stage Manager:

Noble sir, this Trailokyavarman, the lord of Kālañjara, who is permeated by the singular impression of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*), commands that the play named *Kirātārjunīya*, a *vyāyoga* composed by Kavipaṭmatasarāja, be performed. For that reason, I have recited four other introductory verses (*nāndī*) consisting of the heroic sentiment.
Sūtra—
(With pride) It is fitting:
she is dark-complexioned, blessed with every limb, cherished at the tips of her lotus-like hands, and lovely as she moves about.
In the mind of King Trailokyavarmā, it is the creeper-like sword that manifests joy, not his beloved.
(Reflecting with joy) The poet’s skill in composition, the proficiency of the actors, and the sacred life-story of Bhargava and Arjuna—
this commission, which is the cause of happiness both in this world and the next, has today been granted by the lord of men.
Mārpa! At what time, then, has the performance been scheduled?
Sthāpaka:
Noble sir, is it not this very moment, delightful with the beginning of the twilight, that is the time for the commencement of the play?
For here,

having taken up the cause of Arjuna, this Moon shall reach the quarter of Indra; and soon, opening the mountain-lord who is the cause of his rising, he will manifest the joy of the world and the destruction of the darkness of his adversaries.
(Not out of turn) Excellent, crest-jewel of the Śaiṣṭhas! Excellent! Let this [instruction] you have received bear fruit through right hearing. Sūtra—

(Listening with joy) My son! This follower of Arjuna, who is performing austerities on Mount Himavat, has been brought by Dvaipāyana; this one who possesses the prophetic insight of the Siddhas speaks. Therefore, come, let us two accomplish what must be done next.
(Thus they both exit. The Prelude ends.
(Then Arjuna and the Siddha-seer enter.)
Siddhārādeśa:
O long-lived one! Why do you appear as if dejected, even though the complete collection of conditions for the accomplishment of all your desired goals is present?
Arjuna:
(With anger and egoism) What peace can there be for my despondency?

I am a Pārtha of no purpose; this bow is stringless; and these arrows are now merely spreading about. So long as the King does not experience the festive joy of his eyes through the dances of the headless trunks of the Kaurava forces upon the battlefield... (6)
Siddhā:

Long-lived one! Why do you distress yourself thus? Your enemies, though appearing like figures in a magician's trick, are in fact non-existent. Even now, the son of the Sun (Yudhiṣṭhira) alone remains king. For this reason, sovereignty—which causes the union of your foes with Yama—is of even greater manifest utility to you.
By that [wealth] bestowed by the dice-game, which is appropriate for a true kṣatriya, whom does the son of the Sun (Yudhiṣṭhira) not cause to flourish? ||7||

Moreover, I do not consider it even appropriate for you—whose soul is accompanied by Vāsudeva and who are skilled in the science of the bright bow—to undertake the audacity of enduring such exceedingly harsh ascetic hardships.
Arjuna:
Friend Siddhādeśa! I have set out upon this penance at the command of my preceptor. Yet, it is the very conduct of the sages that fills me with longing. May your honor listen.
When the sun of great valor has risen, appearing like a mountain for the emergence of my staff-like arms and casting a dark shadow upon the destruction wrought by cruel enemies,
may I, becoming a sage devoted to the love of performing sacrifices with the fuel of the bodies of arrogant warriors ignited by the fire of my wrath, become one who seeks only this— I pray.
Moreover,
this skill in mental prowess and proficiency in weapons is the very path for those who bear arms;
yet I consider even that application of mantras in the practice of discharging missiles to be nothing but a shameful act of sorcery.

Siddhā—(Looking ahead with joy) Noble sir! By good fortune you prosper; your asceticism has indeed borne fruit. Behold, behold her who surpasses the most harsh radiance of the sun with her lovely peripheral jewels.
A procession of celestial chariots, making the snowy mountain appear like a mountain of gold, approaches you from the sky.

Arjuna—(With derision): Oh, how clever is this Priyavrata! Indeed, he is greatly delighted when the enemy chariots, intent on fulfilling their desires for battle, actually come within the range of his vision.
Siddhā—

"Let the illustrious one mock me! But I know that it is only those who have accumulated a mass of merit through the performance of difficult austerities whom celestial damsels such as Ghṛtācī, Rambhā, Tilottamā, and Urvaśī approach in their aerial chariots.
Arjuna:
(Laughing with disdain) "Does my friend seek to tempt me?"
When those long-lived ones come together to seize me or my enemy in battle, and see the celestial chariot of the gods and the kinnaras, then I shall be filled with joy. (11)
(Nepathya) Behold the emaciation of this sage, who, though his body is covered by waves of loveliness, maintains such extreme thinness that even his face appears parched! 12.
Behold the state of the sage, who, though his body was covered by waves of perspiration as he endured emaciation, nevertheless became a vessel for the messengers of self-restraint and discipline.

Arjuna (listening): What? Are celestial chariots descending from the sky so close by! (With distress) Alas! For me, who have endured the humiliation of external enemies, this defeat by the enemy of the body—the one whose weapon is deceit—has arrived; it is unbearable and impossible to remedy. Indeed, these Apsarases are the great weapon of the flower-armed god. (Reflecting) Which fire of a curse, directed at women, is now prevailing over the activity of arrows and wasting away the entire store of my ascetic merit?
Therefore, O celestial nymphs, what means is there for you to act as actresses in this great drama of the fresh sentiment of love centered upon the Inner Self? 12.

Thus it stands. (Aloud) Friend Siddhādeśa! For one who is devoted to penance as the fruit of the grace of the Moon-crested Lord, beholding a celestial nymph is not fitting. Therefore, I shall spread this canopy above, [using] the mass of lotus petals here. (He does so.
Siddhā—

(Looking all around, with wonder) O noble Savyasācin! Many great treasures have been experienced by me in the abode of Kubera; yet this treasure of the bowman, which consists of slaying a youth, has never before been experienced by me. Indeed, such a feat cannot be accomplished by an archer who possesses but a single bow, two arms, and a limited number of arrows.
(Offstage) Has the lord of birds descended into the netherworld? Are the serpents fleeing, terrified by the slayer of Vritra, their surging waves of hissing sounds resounding?

Is Śiva dancing even during the day because he is independent? Or has it arisen from the smoke of the fire of the eye on his forehead, which is fanned by the waters of the Gaṅgā flowing from his crest? || 13 ||

(Again, behind the scenes) Ah! What is this perverse reasoning? Indeed, the rows of iron arrows are clearly quivering, and the celestial chariots are turning back. Let it not be that this is some great assembly of Asuras who have come to insult us. Therefore, for the Apsarases, approaching the company of sages is surely unwholesome at this time. Following Purandara alone is our refuge. He himself will do whatever is necessary to match this marvel. Siddhā—
(Reflecting) O Pārtha! The celestial chariots have indeed been turned back by the companions of Indra. Arjuna—(To himself, with joy):

By good fortune, the encounter with the Apsarases, which had become an obstacle, has been averted by the mere intimidation of the arrow-shield. And yet, a single opening has been made for the purpose of beholding the solar orb, the means for my ascetic penance.
Siddhā:
(With amazement) Oh, what dexterity of hand you possess! Behold!

With dense nets of arrows, having pierced the other [side] and leaving openings for the clear manifestation of the sun's orb, this [forest] appears like a house being plundered by clever thieves from above who have breached its walls.
Arjuna:
Friend Siddhādeśa, direct those two Kirātas of yours so that no one may approach here unobserved.
Siddhā (looking toward the tiring-room): Friend Śārdūla! Friend Kaṇṭhīrava!
Both—
(entering) Let the noble sir command us.
Siddhā—
"Good sirs! Stay attentive hereafter; let no one unknown enter here.
The Kirātas:
Indeed, he shall come together with his son. (Exiting and re-entering) Noble sir! A certain great sage has arrived, accompanied by a pair of disciples."
Arjuna:
(Respectfully) Let the great lady approach.
Lord, please command the two Kirātas. (Thus he departs.)
(Then enters Mahendra, dressed as a sage, as previously described.
Mahendra:
(...... ...... the sight [of her]. (With remorse) My other eyes, concealed by this change of disguise, have been utterly deceived. (Pitifully) Or rather, it has turned out well.

Although my multitude of eyes has been rendered useless by the tasting of the nectar of beholding my son’s lotus-face, it is nevertheless those very eyes that have triumphed over sin; for, upon seeing this wretched state of his which brings forth such fierce agony, they found no burning pain from the hot tears of sorrow welling forth from them.
Arjuna—(Approaching Mahendra disguised as a sage, with joy): Friend, you whose prophecy has been fulfilled! Oh, the greatness of the great sage!
Even though he is a lord of ascetics, this compassionate being immediately assumes a non-ascetic form.
Ah, even though it is subject to the process of gradual decay, my soul feels affection for this [body] as if it were a parent.
Therefore, let us rise. (Having risen accordingly) The fierce Dhṛtarāṣṭra, with his middle finger raised, addresses him with fear.
Mahendra:
O kings, you are the vessels for what is to be spoken.
Siddhā:— (Approaching) Please take your seats. (Everyone sits down as is appropriate.)
Mahendra:

O illustrious one! I do not know by what means of assistance I may serve you, for I am tossed about by the oscillation of the *tyad* (demon) and *pada* (foot/step). For instance, my mind, though accustomed to the path of the great tradition (*mahāsṛti*), has now become agitated and deluded.
Those great sages have been seen, and those wandering mendicants have been observed;
yet neither the splendor of Indra has been beheld,
nor has penance been witnessed that is adorned with the ornaments of a water-pot, a staff, a deer-skin, and a rosary of seeds.

I bring this [offering] so that you may cross over the four-fold moat of worldly existence; desiring liberation from fear, I approach you with these waters. O Prāṇa, I purify myself through austerities.
If you possess the power for liberation, then abandon this cruel practice; O serpent-like one, cast off your sleep and consider your mind to be pure. 18.
Arjuna:—
(Casting off his pride with a smile) This one, having bathed in the news of my victory, seizes me by the throat.
With his hands, which are like the banks of a river broken by a flood, he strikes me with the blows of his clenched fists.
If I could obtain liberation from the king’s noose through some stratagem,
then even the mention of food and drink would be a source of distress for me, who am touched by such weakness;
therefore, let the commencement of the practice of austerities be undertaken here at the feet of the gurus.

Mahendra—(To himself, with apprehension): How is it that my child has addressed me as "Father"? Surely I have not been discovered by him through this super-sensory knowledge born of his ascetic penance? Very well, I too shall speak with uncertainty. (Aloud): My child! Why is your mind still stained by delusion? Abandon, abandon this wicked resolve! Look, look! It is certainly not the case that those enemies who have not been slain by you must die; nor is it the case that you, having slain your enemies, must die.

"A mouse does not die merely because it has been swallowed by a cat; nor do mice fail to die from the danger of being swallowed by cats who have been deceived. Thus, this wicked deed is a laughable matter for those whose downfall is brought about by common fate. Therefore, let His Honor Mahodaya himself enjoy [the fruit of] it.
Arjuna: (With remorse) Father! You have never experienced the touch of defeat. What can be said? I shall inform His Honor. Your word is not to be transgressed; do not speak thus again and again.
Having pierced the body of the enemy—who was arrogant with pride in battle—with a sharp iron arrow, he attained that very liberation which is reached by his own feathered shaft;
may that liberation alone be the source of our joy. I bow to that [liberation] produced from the union of action and knowledge, which is difficult to attain. 20.

Mahendra—(To himself, with joy) Oh! how my dear son is singularly devoted to the sentiment of heroism! Oh! how steadfast is his enmity! By good fortune, the removal of the earth's burden is already accomplished. For indeed:
he is a fire that consumes the clouds of the three cities, fanned by the wind that is the enemy of Mura.
He will also burn up all the lineages of the twice-born, even those who are gurus.
"Therefore, I shall now manifest myself to comfort my child. (She does so accordingly.
Arjuna:—
(Looking with wonder and a smile) How is it that this thousand-rayed one has become a festival for my eyes? Therefore, I now bow to him with special devotion. (Approaching, he prostrates at his feet.
Mahendra—(Raising him up and smelling his head) My child!

May that Supreme Lord, who at the beginning of time emitted the waters from his eyes, who subsequently became the four-faced god Brahmā, and who in due course became the Lord Śiva, the slayer of demons, and who repeatedly created the oceans—
that Supreme Lord, whose activity is as exalted as that at the end of a kalpa, may he strike down our enemies with his thunderbolt, shattering both the universe and those two [oceans] simultaneously.
Arjuna:
(With humility) Blessed One! Since you are the sovereign of the host of gods, even before the blessed Bharga, this is merely a command and not a request.
Mahendra:
Child! Child! Do not speak thus.
That which the minds of those who tremble on their path to attain, turn away from out of shame; that for the presentation of whose gifts the skill of even those expert in policy falters;
and before whom even the three-eyed Lord Śiva bows when entreated—only the one Śaṅkara can accomplish those things by the mere play of a sidelong glance.
Sishudra:
O Lord, Thousand-Eyed One! Pārtha has indeed become one whose desires are fulfilled by the direct vision of You. For how could fear arise for those Pāṇḍavas from one who is blind?
The thousand-eyed one [Indra] always utters their praise at every turn.
Mahendra:
O best of the gods! Do not speak thus.
Having attained oneness with the Supreme Person (Śrī Puruṣottama), he brought about the destruction of the fierce power of Andhaka.
By the grace of Śiva, this son of Pṛthā shall become possessed of auspicious power through the majesty of Śiva. || 25 ||
"Therefore, let my child take leave of me.
Arjuna:
(With compassion and humility) "O Father, Indra!"

O Goddess, scorched by the summer heat of ill-conduct and its attendant misfortunes, the swan of my mind desires to abandon this lake of your body, which is filled with the forest of lotuses that are eyes moist with love. (26)
Mahendra:
Child! Child! Do not despair. I shall see you again when the moon-crested Lord has been propitiated and all the Kauravas have been struck down by the weapon of Candraśekhara. (He vanishes.
Arjuna:—
Friend Siddhādeśa! Come, let us worship the Lord Bharga after having worshipped the divine Bhāgīrathī. (Behind the scenes) A great calamity! A great calamity!
Making a gurgling sound, with broad cheeks and a snout that seems to burst open as it draws in a great mass of air, and possessing thick,
massive forelegs, this boar— his mind intent on devouring the ascetics on the banks of the Gaṅgā— rushes forward with speed like the wrathful Kali, cruel in his intent.
This formidable female snake, darting at every step into the hollows of the trees along the path, acts like a spade upon the thick clusters of tubers, like an axe upon the tips of the trunks,
and like a battle-axe upon the branches and crests of the trees.
What cannot be accomplished by one who is devoted to fierce and cruel valor? || 28 ||
Arjuna:
(Turning his gaze with apprehension and looking about) Why is this harsh clamor heard as if it were right at my ear, yet no one comes within the range of my vision?
Siddhā—
But where are those two Kirātas? Have they not indeed been slain? (In distress) The two Kirātas—

O noble sirs! Save us, save us! Indeed, some demon of terrifying form, a death-dealing enemy, has entered here—his path made uneven by the bodies of excellent warriors falling from the vast mass of entrails torn out and struck by his iron-tipped beak; his fangs joined with a stream of blood, as if tearing apart all the worlds with his horrific roars.
Arjuna:
(Laughing with feigned composure) Noble sirs! Do not fear, do not fear!
Siddhā:
O illustrious wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow! Prepare yourself, prepare yourself! This boar has indeed come within the range of your vision.
Arjuna:—
(Gazing steadily with wonder and reflection:
Is this a young elephant of the waters, bold beyond the surface of the water, its trunk like a lotus-root for cutting off the prey of [other] tusks?
Or is it the Primordial Boar himself in person, who, even in his withdrawal, displays such intense proficiency in his own power, having formerly lifted up the surface of the earth? (29)

(Offstage) Alas, alas! Though this lord of sages has set out upon asceticism, which is renowned as the sole refuge for those seeking peace, how is it that he encounters this blow from the fangs of a fierce and cruel tiger? O Śaṅkara! Save him, save him! Why do you remain indifferent? Why do you thus proclaim your own name in vain?
Arjuna:—
(Hearing this, fixing his gaze sorrowfully upon the sky, and sighing:
"O evil fate! May you be pleased that Pārtha has attained such a state of wretchedness!
Alas, the sages now fear for me because of my digging into the earth."
(Again behind the scenes: O Lord of Sages!
That Blessed One, who bears the crescent moon upon his crest, is indeed worthy of service; yet even for him, there is the influence of compassion brought about by the power of destiny.
In this forest, it is this very Hara, bow in hand, who has become a Kirāta for the sake of pacifying the afflictions of the sages. (31)
Therefore, let this very Arjuna be entreated and appointed to save the life of this sage.
Arjuna—(listening): Alas! Yet another most dreadful situation has arisen, that this Kirāta seeks my protection.
"Success, O Pārtha! You alone shall first strike down the boar.
Arjuna—(aiming at the Gāṇḍīva bow, with compassion and tears):

O Gāṇḍīva! During that momentary Tandava-dance of hundreds of Tāḍakavanghas in the tumult of battle, I shall now, for the purpose of splitting his chest, even while stringing you, deprive you of your string. 32.
(Thus he draws the bow; acting out the drawing of an arrow from the quiver:
Why do the arrows not emerge? Are they held fast by long-standing attachment, or are they ashamed of this improper act? (Having drawn them with some effort and sighing:
O arrows, it is well that you have remained in the quiver with your tips turned downward.
Now, alas! Pārtha aims at your ear-rings.
(Thus he draws his bow.
(Offstage) Noble sir! Do not fear, do not fear! This is indeed our master who, with a single arrow, is striking down the wicked Bhūtākāra. Only the great sage remains.
Arjuna—

(Hearing this, with agitation) How could this Kirāta become my superior? (Thus, acting with speed, he makes a sound as if discharging an arrow. Siddhā—(Disregarding him, with wonder) Noble sir! Your arrow has already passed behind him! Look! Look!
Touched by the glance of someone, no, no, he moves within with faltering speed; his fall is inferred by the piercing of his vital parts through the weight of his shrill cries.
This sudden onset of someone is like the flood of the great wind at the time of cosmic dissolution.
A fierce iron arrow instantly shatters the slender body of one who wears a frown.
Arjuna—(with embarrassment):

"How is it that even though I am the one who has aimed, this arrow has fallen as if it were mine, since it fell upon the boar when struck down by the Kirāta's shaft? Very well; before anyone else notices, I shall retrieve my own arrow."

(Approaching and observing the earth-dweller with wonder) Ah! Never before have I seen a boar of such vast proportions. Is this some illusory being, perhaps one who has received favor from the Kauravas, or is it simply a wild boar nourished by its own roaming and feeding? Very well, I shall first test my own arrow. (She does so. Siddhā—

(Examining closely) Noble sir! I perceive a second wound on this very limb. Therefore, having recognized it by its cause, take up your own arrow. Perhaps, due to the force of the blow, your arrow, having exited through a wound made on the opposite side, might have gone elsewhere. Arjuna: O Siddha-deśaka! This indeed is my arrow; I shall not speak falsely out of boastfulness.
Siddhā:
"It is not merely a Kirāta, then; this is some great being, for it is not known where his son or grandson has gone.
Arjuna: [listens].
(With reflection) Surely it cannot be that the Kirāta has gone away taking his own arrow?
Siddhā—Then wait for a moment! Is someone perhaps rushing toward us here?

Puruṣa:—(Entering and looking around) What! Is this that sage? (Approaching with agitation) O Lord of Sages! Are you not being tormented anywhere by this wicked hunter, who has rendered me unconscious by the pain of the arrow-wounds from his Kirāta-arrow?
(Arjuna looks on with a smile of contempt.)
Kaṇṭhīrava:

(With reproach) Hey, you jackal! Why do you speak such improper words? This wicked dog was killed by the lion himself as he was approaching him face-to-face. Do you not see the arrow smeared with blood in his paw?
Gomāyuka:
(To himself) How wonderful! How wonderful! This is some unprecedented sage, adorned with a bow. (Aloud, as if recognizing him) Ah, Lord of Heroic Sages! That very voice of our master!
Arjuna:
Friend Siddhādeśa! Alas, alas! What misery!
"By a turn of fate, my bird has today met with this cruel double stain: first, it was snatched away by a hunter;
and now, alas! that hunter, while killing a vile insect, cries out 'Bhama!'—oh, what a tragedy! (35)

O cowherd—O you wretch! Your asceticism, joined with the mere fruit of bodily emaciation, has resulted in such ignorance and such greed for another's property. This hunter has indeed been released by our master, who is intent on your protection, despite this most unbearable offense. Now you have escaped from the jaws of death. Speak, O elephant with flapping ears, whatever seems fit! Our master will certainly not break the pillar of his own reputation.
Kaṇṭhīrava:
(With a taunt) Hey, you tiger! This is a disgrace to us that a jackal howls fearfully before us!
Jackal:
(With a mocking laugh) Hey, you lion! Hey, you tiger! What is not within your reach? What is beyond the range of our arrows and spears? (As if with significance) Ah, this is no boar!
Fie! Fie upon him who, beholding such a Kirāta cakravartin who surpasses the playful ease [of others], does not even recognize himself!
Arjuna: (With contempt)
The Śabaras and Kirātas, for whom meat is their sole refuge for life, repeatedly search the forest lands for it;
yet, alas, what extraordinary excellence is this of theirs in the slaughter of boars, deer, roe-deer, rhinoceroses, antelopes, and wild sheep! 36.
Gomā—(Circling seven times) Noble sir! Whisper it; remain right here, concealed by the great forest, so that the Lord of the Vāhinīs does not hear you.
Arjuna: —
(With reproach) If he hears it, then what?
Siddhārthaka: He will come.
Arjuna:
Siddhā, will Padyā arrive?
Siddhā: Yes.
Pārtha! Fearing that he might perish by the rain of your arrows, this jackal, devoted to his master, is apprehensive.
Jackal:
Indeed, you are not a snake; you are a leader of sages, since you speak thus.
(Arjuna recites aloud, "Flesh repeatedly on the forest grounds," etc.
(A clamor behind the scenes) Siddhā—
(Listening and assuming a gesture of reflection: O Pārtha! I perceive that the army of Kirātas has set out immediately upon hearing your words. Ahuhu!
By the sounds of their feet falling [upon the ground] with thighs throbbing from the forceful placement of their steps, and by the multitude of sharp twanging sounds produced by the hard bowstrings;
With the accompaniment of thundering roars from their throats, powerful with the pride of their advancing [elephants],
the Kirātas quickly take refuge even in the abode of the gods out of fear.
(As if in distress) How will that now come to pass?
Alas! This is no mere beast, a boar; he is indeed a true beast who, beholding such a feat—one that surpasses even the power of Kiraṭārjunīya—does not recognize himself.
Arjuna:—
(With contempt and derision) Friend Siddhādeśa!
If there were a mass of noise like that of locusts due to the forceful leaps of your majesty, what doubt would there be regarding the fire’s circle of flames being fierce?
Yet, in an instant, does not the foul sound arising from the consumption of his limbs—variegated by a thick, rising stench—become defiling? 38.
Jackal:
(With agitation) O Sage, I have been caught! What shall I do? That Kirāta, full of daring, has now arrived!
(Arjuna, laughing at the thought, "Now he shall flee," takes steps forward.)
Harakirāta: (Entering) Jackal... the entire sky is filled with jackals! Where is that sage?
Jackal: [He is here.]
(With a laugh) My lord! This is indeed that very same lord of sages.
Harakirāta—(to himself, observing) Oh, the majesty of the warrior’s splendor!
For thus it is: one hand holds a crystal rosary, while the other hand firmly grasps a bow;
for Dharma is being tormented by the harshness of this degenerate age.
What refuge has a true kṣatriya ever followed? || 39 ||

Arjuna—(Beholding the Kirāta, to himself with wonder): Ah, this is no mere Kirāta; I perceive him as if possessed by a deity. (Reflecting): Could it be that this Kirāta, having come here to a mountain peak from the company of sages, has performed some service to the Three-eyed Lord [Śiva] within the range of his vision?
Indeed, the power of valor and enthusiasm is dependent upon accumulation; it cannot exist, nor can there be greatness, without the Moon-crested Lord. 40.
Kirāta:
Jackal! Was even he unable to endure the excellence of our prowess?
Jackal: Yes.
"What then?
Harakirāta—(pointing with a gesture toward Pārtha)—"Ho there! Draw back, draw back!"

O Sage! That which is difficult to attain even through austerities that are hard to perform and expanded across the three worlds—that destruction of karma, the state of Nirvana, I shall grant to you today. 41.
Arjuna:
(With derision) O you who feed on raw flesh by wandering through the forest until the dawn!
You drink the clear water of the mountain stream incessantly, as if it were a flow of melting frost.
Shame on you, shame on you, Kirāta! Why do you set foot upon the path of the Kṣatriyas?
You have no regard for their lives or their love; indeed, this [deed] is not worthy of one such as you. || 42 ||

Harakirāta—(To himself, with apprehension) Ah! On one side is Pārtha, and on the other, a vast army of Kirātas. Therefore, I shall protect his life by another means. (Aloud) O hero among sages! I did not tell you that I was accompanied by a multitude of Kirātas. I am merely restraining these for now. Ho there, you impetuous Kirātas! Is this the duty of a hero—that you, who are outside the count, should attack this lone hero among sages? So retreat, retreat! Arjuna—
(Mockingly: O hero of the Kirātas! You have indeed reaped the fruit of your enmity;
for, while my arrows—having fasted through their engagement in penance—are now present at the commencement of a wondrous battle, what can you do with such a pittance? (43)
Siddhā—(Seventh turn of the whirlwind) Pārtha! Pārtha! Why do these lowest of scoundrels, disregarding the commands of their own masters, rain down such a torrent of arrows upon you?
(Arjuna mimes the discharge of arrows.)
Siddhā—(With a sigh of admiration): O crest-jewel of heroes! Behold, behold! The fruit of the majesty of your own arrow’s velocity!

Having drawn the creeper-like bowstring to the very edge of the ear with force, those enemies, whose quarters were set ablaze by it and who had begun their terrible cries, have been released [by you].
But having turned back midway by the force of your speed, you have engaged in hostilities here with those very half-arrows discharged by you, against the multitudes of the Kirāta army.

Harakirāta:—(Turning and looking, to himself) How is it that we have been bypassed by the Kirātas! Pārtha has indeed provided his own protection. (Aloud) By good fortune, the Kirātas have been made to release their weapons; the clamor has ceased. Kaṇṭhīrava:—
(With derision) Let it be; they have already been subdued by the Kirātas themselves. Now their clamor is occurring right in the city of Kāntanagara.
(Hara’s Kirāta looks on with agitation.
Arjuna (with derision):
"Do not fear, O illustrious one; these volleys of arrows have been warded off by me.
O hero among sages, this sharp edge of my bow has been given to you by Hara in his guise as a Kirāta. May your lordship discharge your own arrows with impetuosity against me.
Arjuna:
(With reproach and pride) Ho there, hunter!
We are born of the lineage of Śakuntas; we certainly do not discharge arrows everywhere. What talk can there be with those like you, whose minds are unacquainted with battle?
Why does my bow draw you toward me? It is out of a desire to witness its prowess; behold then the skill of splitting mountain rocks, lest your life depart! 45.
Furthermore, the manifestation of this twofold compassion—arising from both my state as a sage and my being abroad—overwhelms me.
Harakirāta:
(With derision) What more can be said? You yourself have witnessed the power of your bow’s majesty, since you, unable to accomplish your own tasks, were reduced to the life of an ascetic.
Arjuna—
(With anger) O lowest of all,
you most wicked of liars! O Kirāta, with the effortless discharge of but a single arrow, I shall bring you under the power of Death!
Great shame has overcome the wielder of the Pināka bow, the foremost archer who stands at the head [of all]. || 46 ||
Harakirāta: (With a joyful laugh) Oh, what a stroke of fortune for me! For when you are pierced by an arrow in the heart, both you and your preceptor will be slain. (He discharges an arrow.
Kaṇṭhīrava:
(Seizing the falling arrow that had been held within him. "Hey there! Do you not hear yourself? Do you not recognize the Lord of Men? Harakīrti:
(With anger) "Hey there, Sahula! Why do you not restrain this cruel one? I am not averse to Nārāyaṇa; therefore, he is boasting thus, so I shall now do the same to him!"
Śārdūlakaṇṭhīravau— (With reproach) Come, come here, you two...
Harakirāta—

(To himself) How is it that Pārtha, acting with contempt, does not display his prowess before me? This great jewel must not be given away to one whose true nature is unknown. Therefore, assuming the form of Duryodhana, I shall test his prowess. (He acts out the form of Duryodhana.
Siddhā—(Entering with astonishment) Noble Pārtha! Look, look! He has become someone else entirely.

Arjuna—(To himself, with indignation): Ah! How is it that this wicked wretch, the disgrace of the Kuru lineage, has arrived? Could it be that Duryodhana, having learned some method of illusion from some Rākṣasa or other, has come to see me under the disguise of a Kirāta’s garb? What is appropriate here? Or rather, I shall transgress even that boundary established by the Great King; I will certainly not now let him go when he is within my reach for slaughter. (Looking at him with derision and mockery): Ho there, you stain upon the Kuru race, Duryodhana! You alone know what is fitting for yourself!
That form consisting of sin which was assumed as the Kirāta; || 47 ||
Hara-duryodhana:
(With reproach) O wretched Pāṇḍava! Where has that expertise of yours with the Gāṇḍīva bow gone? Now you desire the kingdom out of a sense of asceticism!
Arjuna:—
(With reproach) Ho there, you intoxicated Kaurava! I am alone and weakened; quickly bring those unbearable akṣauhiṇīs of the lords of the earth.

Surrounded by allies such as Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, the King of Aṅga, and Śakuni, and having caused my... [obstructed], establish yourself firmly upon the kingdom acquired through improper means. || 48 ||
Or rather: "I am alone here, and you are alone here. Take up your bow!
There is but one teacher at Kurukshetra; the training ground is not divided, nor are our lineages or birthplaces.
Today, O hero, display the strength of your arms and your mastery of the bow; even though we are equals, I grant you victory. (49)
Haraduryodhana:
(With reproach) Release these matted locks... [tya...]
"...form a firm seal with the ring of your brow-leaf;
for Duryodhana, the world’s sole hero, will never prepare his bow for the sake of ascetics. (50)
Arjuna—(With anger) Ah, Kirāta! How can you doubt me so?
That very wielder of the trident, Giriśa, the ascetic, is the creator of the worlds.
With my arm embraced by that fierce state, I shall cause a burning.
Hara-duryodhana:
O you beloved of Draupadī! You wretch, cast away this vain hope in me! At that time, you did not even protect the kingdom earned by your father; how is it that you are not ashamed now to boast so?
O son of Hari! Blessed indeed are those men born of grass, who, with wings fashioned from blades of grass, have traveled as far as the ocean.
For those whose great worldly existence has been produced, [their state] overcomes the deer, just as the passion of the Bodiless One (Kāma) overcomes them. 52.
Arjuna—
(Smiling mockingly) O Suyodhana! Our boasting in your presence is indeed a cause for shame,
since it was by you that the challenge was issued while we were looking on.
"Having seized our kingdom, Duryodhana has taken it away!
(With indignation) "Ah, Phalguna! You mock me! At that time you were aided by gambling; now, with the clash of battle, make the Gāṇḍīva bow either alive or lifeless! (He strikes his bowstring.)
Arjuna:
Not at all, not at all! At the very moment of birth, you were howling like a jackal; it was I who gave you this distinct form.
How is it that you, having attained such audacity, speak thus? I suspect you are something other than Duryodhana for the sake of this battle. ||53||
Haraduryodhana:—(To himself) Ah! Indeed, I have been discovered. Very well then. (Aloud, laughing with feigned gravity) O Pārtha! O Pārtha! This is indeed the truth:
that Duryodhana has been appointed to another office within Yudhiṣṭhira’s own treasury of personal possessions.
While Duryodhana was exiling the sons of Pāṇḍu to the edge of the forest, I became quite another person indeed.
"Then show your proficiency in discharging volleys of arrows!
Arjuna:

(With disdain) Ah, Suyodhana! You are smooth in the science of archery, and you are agile in the art of the mace. Therefore, take up the mace—or, in its absence, the bow. I too shall act accordingly. Come, you who are skilled in combat...!
(Both act accordingly.
Kaṇṭhīrava:
(With curiosity) Sahūlaka! Look, look! Both great heroes have joined together in this battle with the *kodaṇḍa* staff.
Śārdūla—(With pride and wonder): O Lion!
Behold, behold the lightness of hand of both! Oh, what a battle of power! They appear as if they were stationed within a cage fashioned by Kodaṇḍa himself.
Siddhā—
Ah! Look, look!
The son of Madhu [is striking] the Kauravya on the head with his bow...
(He speaks directly, with agitation.)
Alas! Here, in this autumn season, from the moon—which is as lovely as a young crescent—blood has been obtained.
(With joy) Ho there! Behold, behold! This sage of the rays, the Lord of Light, is expanding with bliss, scattering an imperishable flood of radiance. || 55 ||
(All look on with joy and wonder; Arjuna, beholding Śaṅkara, falls prostrate on the ground with his eight limbs touching it, crying out in agitation, "Salutations to you! Salutations to you!
Śaṅkara—(With joy and playfulness): My child, my child Dhanañjaya! Rise, rise! Speak! Speak!
Arjuna—(Rising suddenly and placing his joined palms to his head) O Blessed One, whose crest is adorned with the moon of nectar-like rays! Salutations to you, salutations to you!
By the ripening of my own good deeds, I behold you directly—even though I am but a thief; indeed, there is no one capable of grasping the full extent of your forms.
O Lord! Why, having committed such a manifold deception, have you, who act improperly even for a moment, cheated me, your servant? (56)
Śaṅkara:

(Laughing with delight) Dear Pārtha! This great weapon must not be given to one whose manly valor has not been proven; this was merely a means to test your resolve. Now, take up this great weapon. (Having given the great weapon, he places his hand upon Arjuna’s head.
Siddhā:
How wondrous! How wondrous!
Having emerged from Śaṅkara as a certain light that delights the eyes, a form of Arjuna now traverses the quarters of the sky, illuminating them.
Arjuna:
(With joy) O God of gods, Preceptor of the three worlds! What fee for my teacher may I offer you—you who consist of the playful activity of creating, protecting, and dissolving the three universes?

By what rite, O Bharga, shall I gratify you, the white one who grants all desires? Nevertheless, I shall repeatedly accomplish the preparation for your adornment with a profusion of severed heads of noble heroes, crushed in the height of fierce battle, hanging down as ornaments. 58.
Śaṅkara:
(With joy) Our bestowal of the great weapon has borne fruit, since the dear child displays such great enthusiasm immediately upon its manifestation.
Blessed is Dhanañjaya! Your father is Devarāja (Indra), and Dharma is your elder brother—the beloved friend of Puṃrupottama (Viṣṇu).
Having slain the most excellent of great heroes, you shall cast off this earth, my body, which is now heavy with its burden, becoming light once more. (59)
Arjuna:
(With humility, to Viśvāvasu) My feet, overcome by the sentiment of compassion, command me—even though it is improper—to make my body light; let this be the authority.
Śaṅkara:—
(With a smile) Dear Kāpīdhvaja! Tell me, what further favor can I do for you? Arjuna:
(With humility and satisfaction) Blessed Lord, Master of the World! What more than this could I possibly ask of you? O Lord, the splendor of the weapons has already been bestowed upon me by you.
I believe that by his splendors the darkness of the Kuru lineage was cast away this very day;
today the son of the Sun, possessing full glory and filling the entire world with cities of joy, has become manifest.
Nevertheless, let this be:
may the rain-god Parjanya bestow desired rain, being filled with the waters of compassion; and may the rulers of the earth, devoted and acting through righteous means, protect the world.

May the non-duality of Śaṅkara abide in the minds of the great, destroying the darkness of delusion; may the lords of poets incessantly gladden the three worlds with the drinking-fountains of the nectar of their speech. || 61 ||
Thus ends the one-act play (*vyāyoga*) titled *Śrīkirātārjunīya*, composed by the poet Vatsarāja:
"O gambler! I shall give you embraces won by you at dice."

May that Hara protect you, who was thus addressed by Śivā: "This longing of yours is such that its limit is a hundred days and nights"; he who is occupied with the joining of tens of millions of openings and closings of his two luminous eyes, which perform the functions of night and day.
Moreover,

with hundreds of sidelong glances, those who are preeminent in cleverness, smiling, secretly restrain their friends as they move the pieces on the chessboard, feigning defeat while actually overstepping the proper positions.
Triumphant are the games of the moon-crested Lord, who, in the act of gambling where the wager was a neck-embrace, deceived the Goddess through a course of profound guile.
(At the end of the *nāndī*):

The Stage Manager—(joyfully) Ah! Today, indeed, I have been commanded by the discerning audience gathered for the great festival of the pilgrimage to Nīlakaṇṭha to perform the *bhāṇa* titled *Karpūracaritā*, composed by Vatsarāja, the poet and minister of the Great King Śrī Paramardideva, Lord of Kālañjara. For this work, which is to be enacted by a single actor, my younger brother is well-trained; my own role is limited solely to the auspicious rites of the preliminary stage (*pūrvaraṅga*).

(Looking around, with joy) Ah! This very dawn has arrived, naturally beautiful and suited for dramatic representation. For now, the end of the night has been reached by the couple who have concluded their festive vigil of playful assistance during their amorous conflict, as signaled by the tinkling anklets of the palace women moving from door to door upon leaving the royal residence.
Even at dawn, not even the slightest opportunity for sleep is granted to the Lord of Love.
Moreover,
having immediately snatched away the splendor of the rival leader, the dull-witted Candra—
Having left that wanton woman far behind during the night, the rogue approaches the courtesan at dawn.

(Listening toward the sky) Mārpa! What are you saying? Ah! Why is this improper being discussed? Where is the venerable Sun, whose rays are capable of destroying the pride of both gods and demons? And where is the world of rogues, who deceive the entire universe with their magic? (Reflecting) Enough, enough of this loud chatter! Have you not heard:
"One should speak only after observing during the day; at night, one must never, never speak at all"?
They wander about like great rogues, just as Vararuci did at the banyan tree.
"What do you say? Why do you threaten me? I have no fear of a rogue!
(From behind the scenes) "Ah, you wretched, false Gāriṣṭa! Stop, stop!"

The Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu) dwells in the lap of the Lord of Rivers (the Ocean), having firmly embraced Lakṣmī; the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) occupies Mount Kailāsa, taking possession of his treasury of treasures;

and Śakra has placed the Kalpa-trees and other riches upon the peaks of Meru. Thus do the inhabitants of heaven maintain their fear of those who have seized their wealth—what humans, then, are so fortunate?
Sūtra—(Having praised him): Ah! This rogue named Karpūraka approaches here in a rage. Therefore, it is not proper to remain here. (He exits.)
Prologue (Then Karpūraka enters.
Karpūraka:
(With anger) Moreover, you wretch! How was your tongue not torn out by your own throat for defiling my *māyā-vidyā*, which is the wish-fulfilling cow for the world of mortals? Look, look!
How did the leader of the Raghus bring about the destruction of Vālin, and how did Indra [reduce] Agnidyumna to ashes?
How could she, whose hands were occupied with crushing the *damanaka* flowers, not be afraid, if her concealment were merely a physical covering? 7.
Or rather, enough of my insistence on resolving this talk with scoundrels. Therefore, I shall now go to the gambling hall itself to demonstrate the means for winning wealth;
for: "To one who is devoid of the sport of dice and who turns his back upon courtesans..."
Even wealth that is manifest and currently existing is like wealth seen in a dream.

(To the air) Friend Candanaka! Stay, stay! Wait for me as well! What do you say? "Your face has not been seen for seven or eight days because of your absence from the gambling table"? (Smiling) Enough of pointing out faults to one who is destitute of wealth; for stinginess regarding wealth is censured when it involves a breach of established custom. Do you still say this? "It does not seem right to you at all that [the King] has given his heart to Vilasavati"? (Laughing) I am recognized by my friend! It is exactly so.
Day after day, though they have been experienced, they remain like unprecedented wonders.
The fair-browed women, whose speech is sweet with passionlessness and who sport with love, cause his inner self to dwell upon them; thus, with his meditative concentration fixed upon them,
he remains slack in his conduct regarding other duties.

(Standing thus, he recites. (Listening to the air) This is what my friend says: "I am indeed very eager to hear those playful sports by which even you, who delude the entire world, were deluded. (With a bashful smile) I shall tell it, provided my friend does not consider me too forward. Once, when we had been separated by a lovers' quarrel, she—having cast off sleep due to the weight of her longing—recited a verse while secretly leaning against the slope of the palace roof. That verse remains as if engraved upon my mind.
O Agvai, there is no use for other messengers here; bring her in a dream. Do not be so cruel as to leave her in sleeplessness.
(Sitting down, he likewise mimes dejection.

(Again, to the air: What are you saying? Why do you hold this lute upon your lap? It has been cherished in her embrace all along, and it delights me. She indeed plays the lute for the Blessed Goddess Bhavānī; even before her rivals, she sings songs marked with my name with such artifice. (He shows the lute. What did you say? "Sing that very song yourself. Let my friend listen.
O Blessed Rudrāṇī! May there never be separation from camphor—your dear friend who delights in pleasure, as beautiful as the moon, and the bringer of bliss. 10.

(Thus she sings variously upon the lute. Acting out meditation, then beating her breast and shaking her hand: What do you say? Why do you close your eyes and strike your heart, shaking your hand? (With tears) Friend! Having made your friend an object of your affection through a clever imitation of me so vividly, why do you now act thus?

Then, beginning with a dispute over the ghee while together with her, the slender-limbed girl, having repeatedly won by means of firm embraces as the wager, was delighted and said: "I must see her once more, even while my body is concealed. (11)

Peace! Or rather, this recollection of him is itself death. (Reflecting for a moment, looking upward, and shedding tears) (To the air) What do you say? Why have you suddenly become one whose face is clouded by the spray from the flapping of your wings?

Friend! I seem to behold before me today that very pinnacle of the palace, where I was personally favored by her out of affection—she who was overcome with remorse for her physical form of love and who had offered herself like moonlight. For first, reclining upon a crystal slab veiled by a mass of camphor powder, she addressed the moon in this way while making me hear it through her friends:
"Surely here within the orb of the cool-rayed moon resides Hara, inferred by the smoke of his dark mark."
Bring him to me in a dream; O Sleep, do not be merciless.
Otherwise, how could this flood of its rays spread such a mass of flames? || 12 ||

Then, remaining right there as if I had not heard a word, I was myself made to rise by her with her shame dispelled; she was won over. While the circle of friends laughed at our mutual slapping of hands, the talk of pride was cast aside, and this man here, with palms joined, accepted his own insignificance. O fortunate one, the series of thorns of offenses committed against me by you have been removed from my heart.
All those [lights] were eclipsed by the light of the stone that kisses the orb of the moon. || 13 ||
(Looking toward the dressing room, with apprehension, to the air:

But why does my dear friend have a smiling face? Surely you are not mocking me? What do you say? If such a bond of mutual affection has been formed between us, like a god of love whose arrows have been made of flowers, then why have you come here as her messenger, having accepted the gift, only to abandon me like a snake that has seized its prey? I am broken by this laughter! Friend, let not a stranger be thus mocked. Have you not heard the stories of those who act as intermediaries in matters of duty?
For those who are unshakable by the waves of pride and who possess skill in their duties, even humiliation may sometimes be desirable, as it results in auspicious consequences. (14)

The perfection of the fruit itself will surely propitiate you. (Listening to the air) What do you say? My curiosity is indeed great; therefore, tell me in detail your own story. Let my friend listen. I went to the Manodyāna garden to the side of Mañjīraka, who was engaged in a drinking party. (Acting out laughter) That is what you said. But why do you remain laughing at the very beginning? Friend! I am overcome with laughter by the recollection of those gestures. What do you say? Then reveal that very thing before me.
Why do I not tell my friend?
His matted hair is crooked like a villain, always clinging to the region of his ears; his beard is thin like a soldier who has repeatedly encountered the touch of iron.

In his hand is a scholarly treatise that performs hundreds of revolutions like a bold dancer; in his mouth is speech that obstructs all others like a disease, and furthermore, a ball of betel-leaf. (15)

Moreover, the loud recitation of verses is inauspicious for the ears; singing by oneself is likewise; and the art of drumming upon the chest with trembling hands is like the playing of a mṛdaṅga drum.
"Again and again, my gaze falls upon her limbs marked by the impressions of fingernails" (thus he demonstrates the gesture accordingly).
"Who indeed would be able to commit such wicked deeds against her? || 16 ||
And he was addressed by me with some flattering words regarding his companions, the footmen standing nearby, as he moved with a slight tremor.
(With humility) Noble Mañjīraka! I have been sent to you by my mother Kalāvatī, and she said:

"Son Mañjīraka, Vilāsavatī is yours; what am I compared to her in her favor? My heart trembles at the thought that if she perishes through the fire of separation from you, you alone shall be my son, defiled by a stain. For now:

O fortunate one! Your body-creeper is as frail as a digit of the moon in the cold of frost; even the mere effort of sustaining its life-journey is difficult. Yet, in separation from you, the five-arrowed god of love pities her who is thus distressed by the conflict of longing. (17)
Then he said, "Such is indeed the heart of my mother, but what can be said of Vilāsavatī, whose mind is attached to Karpūraka? Thereupon I replied, "It is not so, it is not so.
Then he addressed me: "Good sir, because you have arrived recently, you are ignorant of this;
I am at variance with her, and I must perform a vow."
"My limbs ache today; I have a command from the King at Nāṭava today"—
thus, as her mind was intent on refusing him, a certain manifestation of her great distaste unfolded through a sequence of ever-new pretexts and clever arguments.
Moreover,
while I have begun a conversation, she praises her circle of friends;
she utters another word with a meaningful gesture, and repeatedly displays a partiality for censuring someone else as a pretext against me.
With her face contorted by my fragments of consciousness, she resorts to silence;
she feigns sleep, and yet again, she manifests the ancient offenses.
"What was spoken? "Why did you not clearly see the camphor-painting in Vilāsavatī’s pleasure-chamber, wherein this verse is inscribed:
'The anklet on my foot has long been silenced;
alas, it has now become the vessel for the fortune of contact with all her limbs'? (20)

Out of affection for the similarity of their names, she even sprinkles camphor over all her limbs during the winter season. (Listening to the ear) What do you say? "Oh, how fortunate we are that our own good fortune has been heard from the mouth of our rival! (Acting out bashfulness) Dear friend! Listen to the whole of it. Then, having heard those words and covering my ears, I said: "The noble one speaks thus because he is quarrelsome; even in a dream, this cannot be believed! For now—"
With her heart fixed on you,
she who follows no other path desires the destruction of your body, which is unlike that of any other, for the sake of all her kinsmen.

"What did you say? Did he understand this speech of yours in a contrary sense? (Gesticulating with a frown) "How could he have understood it? By the very presentation of these words, he was satisfied and accepted a gift of betel, sandalwood, new garments, and so forth. And I was addressed by him with satisfaction: 'Good man Nipuṇaka! Go, go; by means of that signet ring of ours as recognition, you shall receive a reward of one thousand dīnāras from my house. We too shall have almost arrived.
(Gesticulating as if listening toward the tiring-room, with satisfaction, to the air)"

Candanaka! Listen, listen! Such an act is met with such a consequence; indeed, for this very kind of deed, this very kind of fruit is appropriate. If this wretched Mañjīraka has stolen the property of the courtesan Candrasenā, then why does he wander openly through the streets, adorned as he is with your own Chinese silk garments? Now that he is locked up in the royal prison, what remedy can there be?

Even my accumulation of wealth has been entirely stolen away by someone under the false pretense of a ring adorned with gems. What do you say? Did you, having robbed the courtesan Candrasenā of that Chinese silk garment, give it as a gift to Mañjīraka?
(With joy) Friend! Indeed, so it is! (Again, to the air) That is what you say, sir.

Excellent, friend, excellent! I have received half the fruit of my friendship with you, in that you have rescued Sarvasena from Candrasenā. Indeed, I was made her own slave by that Hāradatta, whose heart was given away to her; however, it must be said that the full fruit [of our friendship] will be realized when Hāradatta is cast into some difficulty by you. Friend! Wait for a little while longer; even that will be as good as accomplished. (Again, to the air) This is what Your Honor says.
"This is indeed a cause for supreme joy; therefore, relate it in detail, how Candrasenā has been won over by you.

Listen to me, my friend: I presented that necklace belonging to Hāradatta to her and said, 'My lady, congratulations on your good fortune! Lord Hāradatta has won the game of dice; by means of Hāradatta, the entire wealth of the gambling hall has been won. I have indeed been sent to congratulate you. Then she [asked], 'Is this a playful engagement with jewels in a pool of nectar?'"
"Does spring bring forth a rain of nectar?
Or have I arrived at the royal capital of the God of Love?"—thus did the deer-eyed woman think as she fastened her necklace upon her heart. (21)

And on that day, there was a great festival even at the arrival of the necklace, just as if it were the arrival of Hāradatta himself. And I was addressed by my mother Māyāvatī: "Child, child! Today our entire retinue is indeed intoxicated with wine. This whole property of ours belongs to you alone; therefore, you must remain vigilant. Then I replied:
"There is no doubt in this matter; I shall remain most vigilant."

Then, while that house was filled with my own attendants who were intoxicated, I departed, taking away all my property at will as if I were masterless. (Again, to the air) Friend Candanaka! Why are you so angry?
Why was this message sent to my rival Hāradatta?
Be gracious, be gracious! No, no, this was not resolved by me acting as his servant; listen, listen! (With a sneer) You yourself surely know it then:
with nothing but a tattered old cloth for wealth, its knot loosened, and his upper garment—a double-folded shawl—draped over his shoulder...
I became exceedingly gracious toward my lord, whose lips were white with chalk used for writing while in a fit of anger, and who was exhaling smoke [from his breath]. 22.
Having performed such actions, I went to the temple of Māṇibhadra. Did you say this? But what does Māṇibhadra have to do with you, gambler?
Friend, do not speak thus.
He is a manifestation of the Enemy of Cities (Śiva), intent on crushing his adversaries.
May Maṇibhadra always dispel our misfortunes. || 23 ||
And by me, afflicted with poverty, the Blessed Maṇibhadra was censured; they exhaust my wealth through a succession of demands for offerings and gifts,
and they tighten even this already firm noose.
For the gods are always intent upon deceiving the world. || 24 ||

"Therefore, return to me the offerings for worship previously presented. Māṇibhadra! You have seen my devotion; now let my lack of devotion also be seen. Having spoken these harsh words, and while I was still speaking half a sentence—"and when I too had ceased [speaking]"—he sighed deeply and hotly and acted out his distress.
(Again, to the air: "Friend Candanaka! What are you saying? Why are you yourself so distressed?"
Friend, even a most terrible battle is nothing compared to such a state; for it was the very cause of my passions that the time preceding night unfolded—
that heart-stealing wave of sweet wine’s fragrance.
That naturally charming melody of the youths, which had risen up, became for me like the words of the gatekeeper of the city of Yama standing close at hand. (25)

Then a certain man, approaching with joy, addressed the venerable Māṇibhadra: "Venerable Māṇibhadra! Homage to you! All this is your power, that my master Hāradata, who is dear to the Goddess of Fortune at dice, has been granted to me. Therefore, accept this offering of worship. Moreover, if my younger brother Nipuṇaka, who is living abroad in another land, should return, then I, Caturaka, shall satisfy you with his entire fortune."
Having heard this, and having resolved that "I must act so as to provide some consolation for our grief," Caturaka emerged and approached.

Then Caturaka entered the tavern, which possessed the beauty of a dark-blue curtain formed by the swarm of bees attracted by the fragrance of the wine. Then, standing not far from its courtyard, I began a performance of feigned sorrow with a piteous voice, saying: "Ah! Truly, something well-said has been uttered by someone whose heart is full of noble sentiment."
In every land there are wives, and in every land there are kinsmen;
yet I do not see that land where one has a brother born of the same womb.
Alas, alas! Oh, the stubbornness of my wretched life, that it does not depart even at the separation from such a younger brother, so handsome and so clever!
Then, he—his heart melting with excessive compassion stirred by my sweet words—approached me in agitation and said:
"Good sir, you are not my younger brother, nor are you my kinsman."
Then I, Sakra, silently grasped his two feet. Thereupon, he seized me by the throat with a cry that caused the stars to tremble, born from the weight of the sorrow of separation from his brother.
Then I said:
"Release me, release me, noble sir! I am Ravu, not your real brother; it is I who am causing you this very suffering."
(To the air) You laugh in this manner!

Oh, how true is the skill in deceitful speech even of one who is fond of his own dear ones! Friend Candanaka, what is the use of words? Behold my skill in action itself; listen first to what follows. Then, with a grand festival of great authority, the Caturaka addressed the vintner:

"You are indeed my mother in Dharma. Grant me another favor: I shall celebrate a great festival. My younger brother Nipuṇaka, who has been away on a long journey, has returned. I shall give you this necklace sent by Hāradatta, which I received from Candrasenā; I will give it to you when I receive that [other one] from her. Then, having untied it from the knot of my worn-out garment, I brought out a piece of gold for him and said:

"Noble Caturaka! Take this. Indeed, it is by your power alone that I have acquired much wealth. Why, moreover, do you speak thus, as if you were a thief who has stolen it? Then he said, "Child! This is indeed appropriate, for you are my younger brother. Thereupon I replied, "Noble sir! What is this wealth? I, however, must acquire much more through the favor of another! Then, taking that [wealth], he took the king's wine, Madirā. What do you say?

But why have you, out of place, cast away your wealth? Do not fear, my friend; gold, the vessel for the welfare of the world, does not change through heating, cutting, or rubbing—unlike that which is otherwise.
[That other] gains its own existence from a dense web of deceit, characterized by the striking of breaths upon the ground where gold is buried.
Then Caturaka,
his collection of vital faculties rendered powerless by excessive indulgence in liquor,
fell down as if seized by a violent derangement of the humors (sannipāta) due to deep sleep.

And I, intent on nothing more than kissing the *capaka* fruit and not overcome by the wine, took the necklace from her lap and departed. (Acting as if hearing a clamor toward the tiring-room, looking forward and smiling) (Crying out): Virodhaka! Why are you running about so distractedly?
Your intellect is intent on the highest peace and its perfected accomplishment; we perceive not even a trace of fear in you.
If you are somehow subject to negligence, then here is my sword, the destroyer of enemy clans, at your disposal.
(Miming the act of listening) What do you say?

"I have no fear at all; indeed, I have been sent to congratulate Candanaka. This Hāradatta, the brother-in-law of the King, has been seized by the king's men and is being banished. It is said that his servant Catura deceived Soḍhaka by giving him false ornaments. Furthermore, the clever Candraśekhara, who was deceived by the gift of a necklace [as a token], plundered all of his property."
That very Kalāvatī, the daughter of the courtesan Kuṭṭanī and your rival, has renounced her lifelong vow of enmity before the assembly of courtesans led by Vilāsavatī.
(With joy) Friend Virodhaka! Live long! Live long!
You who have destroyed the crocodiles born from the ocean of nectar.
The literary assembly has become one where the talk of the wicked is cut off;
today it has become like a sandalwood creeper separated from its serpent, or like a courtesan who has become free from a quarrelsome woman.

Tell me, how did this come to pass? (Gesticulating as if listening) Is that what you say? Indeed, I told her first: "Listen, Kalāvatī! This daughter of yours has set her heart upon Jyotīraka-Karpūra; she will uproot all your wealth and hand it over to him. Therefore, you must remain vigilant. Furthermore, I have secured Vāsavadattā in the same manner.

"Just as this Keira has become estranged from you because of her partiality for Kappūra, she will uproot all your wealth and depart for some other place. Therefore, she must be driven out by you tonight. Consequently, during the first watch of the night, while Kalāvatī was digging up the treasury, she was quarreled with and silenced by Vilāsavatī, who seized her by the hair.
(With joy, looking toward the sky) O worthy Candanaka! Look, look at the greatness of the grace of the blessed Māṇibhadra! In just two or three days, we have accomplished our purpose.

(Once again, making a gesture of listening toward the sky, with wonder) Thus a voice from the sky is heard: "Dear Karpūraka! I am not so pleased by your devotion as I was on that day by your reproaches full of resentment. What further favor shall I do for you? (Bowing toward the sky with wonder and joy) O Blessed One, be gracious, be gracious; forgive my ill-mannered conduct. Here I bow again and again.
My enemies have been cast into an ocean of calamity, and my treasuries are filled to the brim with gold.
The obstacle has been stilled; I pray for the name of the bliss of a woman—what purpose, then, does one who has accomplished his goal have [in seeking it]? || 31 ||
Nevertheless, let this be:

may the world always rejoice with its desires fulfilled, maintaining intense devotion toward Him whose crest-jewel is the crescent moon; may the clouds, their hearts moistened with compassion, rain down water at will, and may the lords of men shower gold.
This *bhāṇa* entitled *Karpūracaritābhidhāna* is completed. It is the work of the great poet Vatsarāja.
O Daughter of the Lord of Mountains, whose face is like a smiling lotus, with eyes slightly closed, you have attained intense joy!
May the deceptive display of Śāmbhavī, who has cultivated the mudrās of meditation through internal states consisting of pride and delusion, bestow delight upon you. || 1 ||
Moreover,
my Kaustubha gem, which is like a mere fragment of stone, throbs within my chest; by whom can the departure of those beautiful women be prevented?
"You are Kuvalayābha; you have been crushed by her side-glances"—may Murāri, who was rendered speechless by these words of Lakṣmī, protect us. || 2 ||
(At the end of the *nāndī*:

The Stage Manager—(with joy)—By good fortune, the time for performance has arrived as suddenly as a long-cherished desire and delights me! For I have been commanded by the discerning audience who have gathered here for the festival of Lord Cakrasvāmin at Kālañjara: "Today, at moonrise, before the Lord Cakrasvāmin, the *īhāmṛga* composed by the poet Vatsarāja, concerning the two [heroes] Rukmiṇī and Hari, must be performed. (With eagerness) But why does my retinue behave so confidently?
The Stage Manager—(entering)—Sir! Hurry, hurry! The time for the performance is passing by. Let the noble sir look:
[the moon] has been drawn away by the noose of passion of the doe of the Eastern Mountain.
"Let this deer fall; let him not escape me, for he is bewildered.
He thuds his hooves like a leather water-skin; surely this is the moon, the one marked by the deer, approaching the center of the stage of the sky with rapid steps. (3)
Sūtradhāra—(Laughing) Oh, how great is the skill of my attendants in attributing their own faults to the very head! You yourselves are full of confidence; it is you yourselves who are urging me away.
Sthāpaka—

(With a smile) May your honor forgive me, may you forgive me! That actor named Duḥśīla, who is the object of your favor, having set his heart upon a certain maiden who was both difficult to obtain and indifferent to him, delayed for this long time despite being repeatedly warned and forbidden.
(Looking toward the backstage)
O Lord of the herd! Make some beautiful female elephant delightful to you;
this delusion of hope for union with Abhramu is causing me great anguish.
(To the air) My good man, go and cause this verse to be heard by that ill-behaved actor and by that Śiśupāla.
(Behind the scenes)
"Make Śiśupāla hear it, not Śaibya!
Let this man, acting without reflection, become a vessel for calamities.
Sūtra:

Mārpa! This Akūra, having heard the arrangement for the marriage of Rukmiṇī and Śiśupāla, speaks with the sprouts of impetuous anger suddenly bursting forth. Therefore, come, let us two accomplish what must be done next!
(Exeunt both). [End of Act One]
(Then enters Akrūra.

Akrūra—(With anger and astonishment) Oh! the childishness of Śiśupāla! He desires to forcibly settle Rukmiṇī—the royal swan upon the lake of love for the enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha—within the desert expanse of his own mind. Indeed, the account of Rukmiṇī was related to me by the wise female ascetic.
Hearing of her marriage to Kṛṣṇa, that fawn-eyed girl, her limbs swelling with the thrill of horripilation,
considers this marriage to be another, as if it were a dream-marriage.

Thus was it reported by Rukmiṇī’s sister, Revatī: "Indeed, those two who were sent by Rukmiṇī have arrived with Sugupta to examine Kṛṣṇa. And that female ascetic Succhidri, who is the preceptor for the instruction in the Gaurī-mantra of Rukmiṇī, is one whose command is not to be transgressed. Both of them have gone forth having made a vow for the marriage of Rukmiṇī and Kṛṣṇa; yet fate is the ultimate authority. Or rather, let Śiśupāla choose Rukmiṇī;
enough of this despondency on my part at a time of joy."
This is indeed a great triumph for the Yadus that the King of Cedi commits such offenses;

yet the fire of Murāri’s wrath, which alone is equal to the submarine fire (Ratnakarpa), does not subside, for this cannot be otherwise. Moreover, even today the evil report—that Kṛṣṇa has taken another bride, Rukmiṇī’s sister—does not cease to burn like a foul wind.
Varta: Oh! A great despondency has come upon Janārdana. For it was told to me by his attendant who was nearby:
"What more can be said? Even when the enemy of the demons (Kṛṣṇa) had merely accepted her into his hearing, Rukmiṇī gave him such a festival of joy."
She seemed as if gazed upon, as if brought close by the proximity of fire, and as if cheered by words of sarcastic flattery. || 7 ||

Therefore, I shall approach that very deity and kindle the fire of his wrath with the terrible news of the wicked conduct of the Lord of the Cedis. (Walking about and looking ahead) Ah! I have already reached the assembly hall. (Observing with joy) Why, here are both Rāma and Kṛṣṇa! Oh, how world-renowned is the affection between these two kinsmen! For instance: some bear Rāma, whose form is reflected in emerald [seats], while others clearly carry Kṛṣṇa, fashioned from crystal.
Is it that even the charming pillars of their palace, sharing in that innate and auspicious brotherly affection, have been made partners in this [beauty]? (8)
How is it that these two—the doorkeeper and the attendant—are here? What is this? (Taking a few steps) Why do these two appear as if possessed by anger?
For indeed, their cheeks are armored with drops of perspiration, and their gaze is red.
His body is suffused with a coppery glow, and his two lower lips are trembling;
such is the condition of the slayer of Bala even in a state of intoxication, yet it does not occur in one who merely chants the names of the enemies of the gods without the heightening of wrath.
Therefore, I shall approach them. (He approaches.
Pratī—(With humility):
O divine Rāma and Kṛṣṇa! Akrūra bows down before you both.
(Akrūra bows.
Kṛṣṇa:—
(With feigned indifference) A seat!
(The doorkeeper brings forward a seat.
Akrūra—
(with courtesy and agitation) Why do I perceive as if there were some dejection on the part of your honors here?
Kṛṣṇa:
(With disdain) Nothing at all.
Rāma:—
(Sitting down with a sigh) O Akrūra! Is Kṛṣṇa truly a mere child? Listen to me:
He who indeed lifted Govardhana, the king of mountains, as if it were a blade of grass—that very Kṛṣṇa, that hero, Rukmī considers no more than a straw. (10)
Akrūra—
(With astonishment) My heart does not believe that this man is the one who bears the Śārṅga bow in his hand.
Kṛṣṇa—
(With a smile tinged with pride) Chamberlain! Report what has transpired. Chamberlain:
When I announced, "Your Majesty, let it be known that King Kṛṣṇadeva is arriving here," a certain bard standing outside spoke with great agitation.
O kings, listen to the speech of the gods regarding the enjoyments available on this earth; abandon your vain pride!
For those who have fallen within the range of the arrows of the God of Love, even the radiance of the moon becomes like that of a fire.
May the title of "God" belong to you in the abode of the gods. || 11 ||
Moreover,
what reckless person embraces a forest fire? Who would play with a black cobra as if in sport?
To whom in this world of living beings are the vital breaths not dear? Who would provoke a wound for the sake of battle? (12)
Akrūra—
(With agitation) What was said by Rāma then? The Messenger—
"What was said by the dark hero Pralambāri when he arrived here just now?
Akrūra—
(with eagerness)— "What was said?"
Pratī said:
"Having been told this, bring that hero, the ornament of the battlefield;
he shall simultaneously bestow upon you Rukmiṇī, a gift that brings supreme bliss."
With my sword as my wealth, I shall act upon the field of battle.
Akrūra said:
"Well spoken by Kṛṣṇadeva! As for me, however, I do not believe that Rukmi is acting with enmity toward Murāri.
The goat repeatedly leaps about, its joy overflowing as it contends with the lion of intense pride."
Who knows what kind of despondency one experiences upon seeing a lion rendered silent and paralyzed by fear? (14)
But the panegyrists are indeed worthy of praise. Why do they not say this? "O Kṛṣṇadeva, crest-jewel of heroes!
Even though the mountain of Vaikuṇṭha was shaken by the gentle swaying of your eyebrows, that supreme preceptor of Rukmiṇī trembles exceedingly. (15)

I have heard of Śiśupāla’s insolence; yet it is not proper to inform him of this until Priyavrata has arrived. (Looking offstage) Ho there! Who is present? Announce that Priyavrata has arrived from the city of Kauśāmbī.
(The doorkeeper approaches suddenly and enters with Priyaṃvada.
Priyaṃvada:
(Approaching suddenly) Here is Priyaṃvada, bowing.
Akūra—
(Sitting down) Please, inform me.
(Priyaṃvada sits down and remains.)
Akūra—(To himself) His very facial expression reveals the failure of his purpose. Nevertheless, I shall ask him again. (Aloud) Priyaṃvada, inform him!
(Priyaṃvada remains silent as before.)
Akṛira:
O Priyaṃvada! Why do you not inform me? Priyaṃvada: [speaks].
"If it is appropriate to make a request, then why do I not request it? Who will give me a second tongue for having made such a request?
Rāma:
(With agitation) Why do you not report exactly what has occurred? Is there some fault of yours here?
Priyamvada—(Frightened) Even so, I shall not inform him; let this letter itself inform him. (She hands over the letter.
Akura—
(He causes her to recite:
"Your breasts attained full development through milk;
you wandered in the depths of the forest together with those young calves."
If someone like you, alas, were to choose the king’s daughter as his bride, then what cause for anger? Does not even an infant desire the moon? || 16 ||
Priyamvada:
But this letter was sent by Śiśupāla to Rukmiṇī. Rukmin, saying "I shall show this to Keśava," handed it over into my hands.
(Thus she offers the second letter.)
Akūra—
(He recites:
"From childhood, he has long attained full growth in the house of the cowherds."

Therefore, let the majesty of our sword, which is filled with the essence of treachery against you, be considered by you as truly unimpeded—even if the Sun-god himself, along with Vaikuṇṭha, were firmly fixed within its heart. || 17 ||

This is not surprising in the case of Śiśupāla, who is by nature ill-disposed; however, this reversal of character in Rukmin is indeed strange. (With astonishment) Priyaṃvada! Have you not heard of his possession by a malevolent spirit? Is that not his perverse fondness for—
(Aside) Friend, how is it that you are skilled in other matters?
Akrūra: Was this letter not given [to you] at the time of drinking wine?
Priyaṃvada: No, indeed not!
Akūra:—
No other than Kṛṣṇa was conceived in her mind, though through the power of delusion she thought otherwise.
Priyam—
(with longing) Is he not the beloved Kṛṣṇa, the younger brother of Balabhadra, the son of Vasudeva, and the delight of the Yadu clan?
Akrūra:
Surely Time, when enraged, soon shatters even the virtuous intellect. 18.
Rāma— (With agitation) While the king does not carry himself anywhere with the impetuous vigor of a true hero, my plow shall ply in this parched, desert land.
May the plowshare of Saṅkarṣaṇa now successfully reap the harvest from the body of the King of Cedi, which has been a heap of accumulated happiness. 19.
Kṛṣṇa—(to himself, with joy): O mind, be at peace; your desire approaches you.
That beloved one, though difficult to attain, has today become easily accessible;
that tormenting routine of household life has been abandoned, and now Nandaka himself has suddenly become a messenger.
Rāma—
(brandishing his sword with joy and agitation):
At my own will, during the sport of drinking honey-wine, I have established my soul in happiness.
My own attendants there have been made happy, while you alone have been deceived.
O sword! Now drink your fill from the abundant stream of sweet, flowing blood of these well-struck Rukmiṇas; I shall wipe away my own stain.
Akrūra—(With laughter and anger) O crest-jewel of heroes, Rāma! Even at the marriage of Śiśupāla and Kṛṣṇa, Rukmin was an ally of yours.
Rāma—

(With agitation) Oh, Akrūra! You have spoken as one who is not cruel. If the enemy of Kaṃsa marries that supreme jewel of a maiden, the Lord of Cedi will finally sport with the host of celestial nymphs after a long time.

If I bring this [victory] to fruition on the field of battle with my arms upraised in valor, then my name shall indeed become "Kāmapāla" (Protector of Desires) through its unrestrained virtues. || 22 ||
Doorkeeper: Let the drum for the expedition to victory in battle be sounded! Doorkeeper:
As the Lord commands.
Kṛṣṇa:—(With humility) O son of Rohiṇī! What is this sudden and terrible agitation, this reproach against Rudra who is enraged at the end of an aeon? This is most improper.
For it is the lion who, in the forest region, bestows a quart-measure of pearls from the frontal globes of rutting elephants he has slain.
Alas, how is it that shame does not arise in him when he wishes to give a slap to the fickle young of a sparrow? 23.
Rāma:
Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Stay! This is no time for delay.
[This is] a task devised by mean, petty insects who are ignorant of the vows of the warrior class.
For those who consider harsh speech to be impure and take it as cruel to my ears,
the Ordainer of the mind will bring about their end; they shall be crushed in the mortar by pestles,
their very bones bursting with the sound of the grinding.
Kṛṣṇa—(With agitation) Ah! Is the earth not black that you are thus distressed? On my account, this unbearable pain of hearing the harsh, cruel words of my arrogant enemies has become heavy upon me.
If I am dark-complexioned, alas! then I shall delight your ears with the intense amorous dalliances of that woman.
Rāma—(Affectionately) Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇā! Not so!
You are no fool in the mastery of sacred scriptures and weapons.
Nevertheless, O Keśava, you are a fool! I will not make you my ally for the purpose of crushing Rukmiṇī’s pride, nor will I make you my warrior. || 26 ||
Akrūra—
(With joy) May the Yādavas rejoice, if Rāma and Kṛṣṇa have thus made their vow for the destruction of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons!
Rāma—
