(With agitation) Akrūra! Listen to my difficult resolve, which I cannot endure delaying in the slaughter of my enemies:
until Keśava and Rukmiṇī bow their feet before the jackals, who shall be fed with the sacrificial offering of the wine of the blood of my Dāśārha foes.
Let this Hala consider wine—which possesses qualities dearer even than life and which creates the bliss of non-duality—to be like the poison *hālāhala*. || 27 ||
Akūra:
Alas! A most difficult vow has been undertaken by Rāma.
Kṛṣṇa:—
Ah! Alas, what misery! What calamity has been undertaken by the noble one so untimely? O Akrūra! Let the festival of departure take place this very morning. Akrūra:
So be it. For now the sun is eager to set toward the west. (Looking offstage)
O Sun, staying within the palace atop the other ocean, pass these few remaining watches with your eyes—the rays—closed.
Be gracious; when you have risen again, you, lovely with fresh beauty, shall delight the world.
Rāma—(Hearing this, with joy) Oh! What auspicious news!
Kṛṣṇa—
Having heard this, I have been awakened. Therefore, come; let us spend this night, which is as difficult to pass as a city gate-bar, at home.
(Thus they all exit. End of the First Act.
Priyaṃvada:

(Looking ahead) How is it that this attendant of Her Majesty Queen Rēvatī, Adhavadīva, is walking this way? I shall learn the news regarding the pleasure-garden from him. (Approaching) Noble Dīpaka! Priyaṃvada salutes you.
Dīpaka:
May you become a recipient of the grace of the Enemy of the Daityas. Friend—Noble Devarata! Has Baladeva awakened?
Dīpaka: When did Valadeva fall asleep?
Priyam:
(With agitation and wonder) Oh! What is this state of possession by a great hero? Then, did he remain awake for the entire night?
The lamp illuminates the elephants, the best of tigers, and the horses yoked to their saddles; O warriors, stay awake today, for this is the arena of valor! Alas, where have the elephants vanished?
They are repeatedly made resonant by these cruel cries, uttered in the manner of those who are dreaming of their own defeat.
Balarāma indulged in a sleep that was deep and rare due to the great obstacles caused by his rising anger.
Priyam—
Where again has he been sent?
Dīpaka— I have been dispatched by Baladeva to the presence of Devakīnandana to begin the journey.
Priyamvada:

But I have been sent by Kṛṣṇa to bring Kāmandakī’s son! Kṛṣṇa is staying in the Sahakāra grove accompanied by Uddhava, Akrūra, and Sañjaya. So come, noble sir; let us go together to the forest of Balabhadra. Dīpaka: Priyamvada: But I have been sent by Kṛṣṇa to bring Kāmandakī’s son! Kṛṣṇa is staying in the Sahakāra grove accompanied by Uddhava, Akrūra, and Sañjaya. So come, noble sir; let us go together to the forest of Balabhadra.
Dīpaka:
Krodhana: Pralambārī, I shall therefore accomplish what has been commanded. You too, fulfill your own duty.
(Exeunt both) The Interlude (Viprakambhaka).
(Then Kṛṣṇa enters the assembly hall as described.
Kṛṣṇa— (To himself, with longing and anger) Ah!

At the time of the marriage ceremony with Rukmiṇī, my two arms— charming in their amorous play against the intoxicated enemy Madana, and now trembling with both passion and anger— were made to oscillate between the clasping of her hand and the drawing of the sword.
Moreover, oh! the power of passion!
By the mere mention of her name, that lovely-eyed beloved has become present.
Having seized even my heart, he makes me his servant;
for even this flash of the aesthetic delight in the playful crushing of merciless combat occurs solely in accordance with his will, as if out of a desire to crush those who harbor enmity.
So, this much for now. (Aloud, with anger) O ministers! What is being said about you?
By those very atoms, as soft as lotus petals, were these mountains shattered before his [Indra’s] thunderbolt!
By those ten enemies, with their harsh, sharp-edged axes of bitter words, not a single trace of distinction was left upon the breasts of those [women].
Sātyaki—(With contempt) Ah, Janārdana! I address you:
those who possess a conduct loathsome to the virtuous, and those who have been struck down by the wielder of the thunderbolt—[they are all here].

Those who have transgressed the grasp of pride and for whom Yama is a source of torment—what account can be made of such men in the syllables of the Purāṇas? Only lamentation is appropriate; for who would hesitate in the matter of inflicting punishment suited to their wicked conduct?
Kṛṣṇa—
(With joy) Why then delay now?
Uddhava—
(To himself) O Kṛṣṇā! Why this anxiety?
Will those enemies, their pride swollen by the prospect of battle, not surely flee, abandoning the festival of war, upon encountering me in combat?
Now that they have come within the range of your vision, will this Śārṅga bow remain fruitless for you? (6)

Atrikūra:—(With humility) O son of Devakī! Is the journey to be directed toward the city of the King of Cedi, or rather to Kauṇḍinapura? Let there be a great surge of enthusiasm for Your Majesty amidst this darkness of doubt. (The Lamp-bearer enters.)
Dīpaka:—(With confidence and humility) My Lord! I have been sent by Rāma to arrange for the departure to Kauṇḍinapura.
(Kṛṣṇa looks at Akrūra’s face with a smile.)
Atrikūra:
"My good Dīpaka, go and inform Lord Balarāma to come here. This is already settled. Kṛṣṇa: [He departs.]
I have already dispatched Mairpavada there for me.
Priyam—(entering) My Lord! Here is the heroic Rāma, who has returned after the conclusion of the night spent in the tumultuous, rattling wakefulness of battle.
(Then Rāma enters.
Kṛṣṇa:
(With agitation) A seat, a seat for your honor!
(Priyaṃvadā brings them near. Rāma, having observed everyone's expectations, sits down.
Kṛṣṇa—(Observing Rāma, to himself, with joy:)
The lord of the city of Tripura was utterly destroyed; Rukmiṇī was won by Rukmin, and he too, having cast off the burden of battle, was made a mere vessel of impotence.
Having realized that what was desired was thus effectively accomplished, her heart is deeply delighted.
Having seen this body of the enemy of the serpent [Śeṣa], which is expansive and adorned with the ornaments of great vigor... || 7 ||
Uddhava:
(With joy and wonder, to himself) Oh! How the heroes surpass all others! For instance:
When a more powerful force is encountered, even if its violence is directed against us,
tranquility suddenly flees from the heart like one seized by the throat.
Rāma—(With anger and disdain) O ministers! Why do you still deliberate?
Or rather—
Is it to be praised that some incomparable power of counsel flashes forth from your wise ministers, which instantly uproots the long-nourished sprout of the warrior-dharma,
stupefying the mind of the subduer of demons and paralyzing the fire of his wrath?
It causes the flow of tears from the pair of eyes of the wives of arrogant kings to cease. || 9 ||
Uddhava:
(With a mocking laugh) O Rāma! Let your wrath be directed toward the host of enemies alone. The departure has already been decided upon here. Priyaṃvada! Let the astrologers be summoned.
Rāma:
(With a sneer) What is the use of this vain elaboration?
All the planets are favorable due to the auspiciousness of Nandaka’s fist-grasp;
the exertion of the astrologers through their extensive calculations of planetary movements is in vain.
Moreover,
having hurled my pestle into the sky and whirled that circle of planets, I shall arrange them exactly as you have described;
through the overturning of their high and low positions, it will surely bring about the fulfillment of your desire.
Uddhava:
(With humility) O Pralambāri! You have descended as an incarnation to relieve the world from its heat; therefore, do not speak thus.
The desires of the powerful are fulfilled by their own strength.
However, the established order of the world must not be transgressed;
for while the Lord of the Mountain is capable of destroying with a mere glance, he brandishes his trident only for the sake of cutting down the wicked. 12.

Rāma—(With enthusiasm) O son of Aṅgiras, crest-jewel of the omniscient! I myself shall bring success to your counsel. Summon the astrologers; let the auspicious hour for the wedding be determined. Let the enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha remain right here, his arm adorned with the marriage bracelet, awaiting the day of the wedding.
With that hero, Rukmiṇa himself, I shall suddenly bring that Rukmiṇī right here. || 13 ||
Uddhava: O Rāma! Do not say this, do not say this!
In this pavilion where the rows of jewel-encrusted banners flutter and sway in the gusts of wind, meeting together—
In that arena of the sport of battle, filled with the sound of clanging kettle-drums,
Hari will first perform the wedding of the Goddess of Victory before his elders, the lords of the earth, and afterwards he will perform the marriage of Bhīṣmaka’s daughter.
Kṛṣṇa—(With agitation and derision) This is indeed fitting for the elder brother, Baladeva. For instance:
the destruction of Ariṣṭa, the crushing of the deceptive Hayakeśin, and so forth.
He who [easily] performed the slaying of Aṇūra and even the crushing of the Lord of Mathurā—
how could that compassionate one, whose arms were honed on such minor occasions, employ me in battle against that fierce man marked by the palm-tree? (15)
Rāma—
(With joy and agitation) O ministers!
This fire of wrath has arisen within the cottage of the mind of the enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Let this very place remain as a sacrificial fire for the destruction of the auspicious rites of departure, fueled by the fuel-sticks of evil intellect. (16)
O slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha! Arise; having saluted our parents, let us prepare for the expedition of victory.
(Then enter Vasudeva, Devakī, and the female door-keeper. Door-keeper: *Note: The text provided ends with "pratī," which is the abbreviation for *pratihārī* (female door-keeper).*

"Come this way, come this way, O Lord! Come this way, come this way, O Goddess! Rāma—(Looking on with joy): "O Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Look, look! My parents have arrived simply by being remembered. Therefore, by this auspicious omen, I perceive that even the fulfillment of your heart's desire is swiftly approaching. So let us both rise and go to our parents. (Rising, they both prostrate themselves in a dramatic gesture.)
Vasudeva—(Smelling both on the head): O Rāma and Kṛṣṇa! I know not what I may hope for from you both; may you two become the vessels for all our desires. Devakī—
"O undecaying ones, O unconquerable ones! Oh, how great are my sons!
(Uddhava and the others rise from their meditation and prostrate themselves. The female doorkeeper and Priyamvadā bring forth seats. All sit down as is appropriate.
Kṛṣṇa:
(To himself, with joy and a choked throat: Beholding this mother, my innate affection wells up and awakens an indescribable rapture;
indeed, even that affection of Yaśodā, accumulated through many previous births, seems almost to be surpassed by it.
Rāma:
(With humility) What do my elders command?
(Vasudeva looks toward the face of Devakī.)
Devakī:
O Rāma! We shall go to Koṇḍinapura for the sake of Kṛṣṇa’s marriage. Let it be so; my sister’s son, protected by the god of love and adorned in red garments, is a vessel of supreme happiness.
Rāma: [Listens]
(With a meaningful smile) O Kṛṣṇa! Please accept the command of your parents.
Kṛṣṇa—(Placing his joined palms to his head) May your honors consider this command already accomplished.
Uddhava:

(Aside) Oh Satyaki! Oh Akrūra! Let them bind [the gifts] in bundles while eating, according to the command of the goddess Devakī. Oh Rāma! Go to the city of Kauśāmbī for Kṛṣṇa’s wedding. Let my sister’s son be there—(he smiles, acting out the thought as he speaks thus).
Akrūra and Sātyaki: Let it be, let it be! Enough with this explanation.
Devakī:
(With a smile) Oh, Vijayā! Go and bring Śiśupāla’s messenger.
Pratīhārī:
As the Queen commands. (Having exited, she re-enters with him.)
Devakī—(With joy) Sandhānaka! Approach Kṛṣṇa with reverence.
Sandhānaka—
Victory, victory to Kṛṣṇa together with Rāma!
O Kṛṣṇa, accept from the king this jewel-necklace, which is complete with auspicious marks, deeply beloved, and exceedingly difficult for others to obtain. 18.
(Thus she offers a necklace of rubies; Kṛṣṇa accepts it with a gesture.
Devakī:
Vijayā, bring a seat for him.
Sātyaki—(Aside) O Uddhava, crest-jewel of ministers! O Akrūra! By this employment of words and by the bringing of the jewel-garland, Rukmiṇī has come into the possession of Hari.
Uddhava and Akrūra—
(With joyful excitement) Excellent, excellent! It is even so.
(Looking offstage) Alas, this [plot] has been set in motion for the sake of Kṛṣṇa! What is this?
Out of delusion, you touch Mālatī with the palm of your hand; shame on you, shame! You are being heedless in vain. People say that improper conduct is the gateway to the onset of calamity. (19)
Uddhava:
(With joy) Ah! This noble report informs Śiśupāla’s messenger, provided only that he understands it.
Rāma:—
(With agitation) Priyaṃvada! Find out who this is and whose he intends to steal!
Priyaṃvada:

(Going out and re-entering, offering the Mālatī garland to Kṛṣṇa) Kṛṣṇa! Take it, take it! This very Mālatī garland was being brought for you by a florist when it was seized by someone. Then that florist, threatened with a severe beating, fled.
(Rāma, smiling with intent, looks toward Uddhava and the others.
Kṛṣṇa— (to himself, joyfully:)

Possessing some indescribable abundance of bliss— the very essence of the flower-arrowed god of love— she arrived at my lotus-like hand like Rukmiṇī herself, and not merely as a garland of *mālatī* flowers.
Uddhava:
(With joy) O Lord Kṛṣṇa! This garland of *mālatī* flowers, brought here at the very moment the wedding procession begins, is an auspicious omen; let this imperishable wreath be worn immediately.
(Kṛṣṇa acts with joy.
Vasudeva:
O Saṅghāraka! When, again, will there be the festival of the wedding?
Sandhānaka:
"I say that the wedding will take place right here, this very day.
Uddhava: [listens]...
(With intent) Sandhānaka speaks the truth.
Rāma—(With a meaningful smile) Oh Kṛṣṇa! Why do you still hesitate? The wedding of Rukmiṇī is indeed in Vaiśākha.
Kṛṣṇa:
Sandhānaka, inform the Lord of the Cedis that we have indeed arrived at Kauṇḍinapura, now that the time for the wedding is near. Akrūra: [Listens.]
Having instructed the treasurers and granted them rewards, he dispatched Sandhānaka.
Sandhānaka:
Oh, dear Kṛṣṇa! How indeed can I go there, having abandoned Queen Devakī? I shall vomit [this thought] up.
Devakī: Sandhānaka! Having heard that Rāma and Kaṇha have become the chosen brides, my paternal aunt will be pleased; what need is there for me?
Sandhā: —
Therefore, your daughter-in-law will surely come right here to pay her respects to you.
Sātyakī: Who would disagree with this? This is indeed the house of the bride.
Vayadeva: We ourselves shall dismiss Sandhānaka, having granted him his reward; you gentlemen, prepare yourselves for the morning march. Vijaye! Show the way.
Pratī—
This way, this way, Your Majesty; this way, this way, Your Ladyship.
(Exeunt both behind the curtain.)
The splendor of rut suddenly arose from that elephant,
foretelling in the assembly the defeat of the host of enemies; meanwhile,
the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) was hastening for the expedition of his enemy’s foe (Kṛṣṇa).
How indeed will one whose mind is distracted obtain the fruit of this? || 21 ||
Rāma—(Hearing this, with joy and aloud): O elephant-driver! Well done, well done! By good fortune, my elephant’s rut has begun. Do not despair; there will be fruit from this.
No, no, it is not merely a bridal procession; this is something delicate.
On the battlefield, there will arise in the hereafter those causes of horripilation:
the harsh sounds of blows from elephant tusks that crush the bones of the broad chests of enemy kings, who were his equals in valor.
"O Kṛṣṇa! Therefore, let us all go to our respective homes and prepare for our departure.
(Thus they all exit.
The Second Act.
(Then Subuddhi enters.
Subuddhi—(Sighing long and hot): Alas! The state of being a maiden is fraught with great hardship. For instance:
The heart is dependent on love, the body is dependent on the elders alone, and death is dependent on fate; how then do daughters of noble families not despair? (1)

Alas! What a duality of my own poor intellect! For I, a doe wandering at will in the garden of my own soul, longing for the sprout of love for a mere mortal, have cast myself into the snare of delusion. Therefore, now that Rukmiṇī’s life is at its end, my own life is stained with blemish; stained is the power of Bhavānī’s mantra-instruction. And this very arrival of Kṛṣṇa here under the pretext of the bridegroom’s procession is a bolt against Rukmiṇī’s life-breaths.
Like the autumn moon, he delights her heart and incessantly consumes the life of Rukmiṇī.
The arrival of the dark clouds is cool, while the harsh heat of Śiśupāla is cruel.

(Stepping aside twice; standing still and feeling startled) Ah! Where indeed have I set out? (With embarrassment) How is it that my footsteps, as I am departing for Rukmiṇī’s residence, have turned elsewhere? (Looking around) Very well, I shall go by this very path. For this is indeed the path for the affectionate nurse Suvatsalā to reach Rukmiṇī’s house; perhaps she will meet me here to share in my distress. (Then Suvatsalā enters) Suvatsalā:—
"Revered Subuddhi! But why do you move about with such rapid steps? Wait for me!
Subuddhi—(Turning around and looking) How is it that Suvatsalā is coming up from behind? (Standing up) Come, child! Come!
Suvā:
I have met him! Move now, move now, O Blessed One! But where shall we go?
Sucuddhi:—
(Sighing deeply) Where else could she go?

Suvratā—Has the lady set out for Rukmiṇī’s residence? (With tears) O lady! Your noble conduct and my own devotion have both come to naught... the hope for life has become as unstable as one riding upon a swing.
Sucuddhiḥ:
Even in following [him] in death, my state of being well-disposed has been proven false, but not your state of being well-affectionate.
Suvā:

O Blessed One! That even the power of your mantra fails when thwarted by destiny—that is the misfortune of Rukmiṇī. Yet my heart does not believe that Kṛṣṇa will ever disregard Rukmiṇī. Even the Blessed One knows this from Kṛṣṇa’s own circle:
as soon as the name of Rukmiṇī entered Hari’s heart like a mantra syllable, at that very moment he was carried away by other wives.
"Then the power of the Blessed One’s mantra will become effective even through the agency of Nandana. Sucetā—O dear one!
Come, let us first comfort our child.
Suvatsalā: Noble lady!

A portrait of Kṛṣṇa has been sent into the hand of my friend Makarandikā for her consolation. Therefore, please come, noble lady. Let us go to Kṛṣṇa’s camp and, having ascertained everything unobserved, quickly return, Rukmiṇī.
Sughuḍḍhi: [Agrees.]
O Suvatsalā! If you are still so full of enthusiasm even now, then take this painting featuring Lakṣmaṇā, by which Kṛṣṇa may be enticed.
Suvatsalā:
Then, by this path, let us go quickly to the painter with the portrait.
(Thus they exit. Interlude.
(Then enter Rukmiṇī and Makarandikā, their hands busily occupied with black lotuses.)

Rukmiṇī—(Sighing with regret) Surely in another birth I must have worshipped the Moon-crested Lord in a manner contrary to his nature, since even by the mere sight of this handsome youth, fate torments me so. Friend Makarandikā! The venerable Subuddhi and Suvatsalā have failed; for at that time, not a single cowherd girl among those sixteen thousand was entreated by them to obtain the affection of Kṛṣṇa.

(Reflecting) Or rather, this is the wretchedness of me, cursed by fate; for gifts once given cannot be taken back. Therefore, I shall manifest this very same [token] as something unrecognizable and indistinguishable. (She does so.
Makarandikā—(To herself, with apprehension) The princess is greatly distressed. Where then has that merciless, blessed Sucetā, who was so kind to us, disappeared?

(Then enter Subuddhi and Suvatsalā. Subuddhi—(Observing Rukmiṇī; aside) Oh, Suvatsalā! Rukmiṇī’s mind is so absorbed in a portrait of Kṛṣṇa that she does not see us. Come, let us distract Makarandikā with a sign and remain quietly behind her. (They do so.)
(With astonishment and wonder) Oh! How firm is Rukmiṇī’s resolve!
For indeed, her foot is now placed—momentarily upon the waves of the fragrance of her sighs, momentarily upon her play-lotus, and momentarily upon her ear-lotus.
This woman with tremulous eyes, her mind completely absorbed in the painting of Murāri, does not perceive the incessant, heavy humming of the bees.

Rukmiṇī—(Gazing at the painting with longing) Blessed are those cowherd girls who, warmed by the fire of love, sport in this river of beauty that is this fortunate youth. (Looking closely, sighing long and hot, and weeping with a faltering voice) Whence could such a person be for those like us? (Leaving the sentence half-uttered, with tears and a sobbing voice) O heart, have mercy and desist! Why do you torment yourself with this love so difficult to attain?
The doe of the hunter laughs at her passion for the deer marked by the god of love. || 5 ||
Sucitti: (Rising in agitation and lifting Rukmiṇī’s chin) My child Rukmiṇī! Why does your elder relative distress you so much with these tears?
Rukmiṇī:
(To herself, with embarrassment) How is it that the Blessed Lady was right here! (Aloud) Blessed Lady! It is you who have deceived me; my elders alone are cruel to me.
Subuddhi:

(With enthusiasm) Let him be whoever he may be, and let things be as they are. But since he, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, has taken her hand with his own—O dear, most affectionate mother! Why do you not announce this to your child?

Suvatsalā—(Stepping forward) Child Rukmiṇī! Has the Blessed One ever been a speaker of falsehood? An auspicious moment was honored; you were taken by Hari with his own hand as if in a painting. Now Hari will sustain you, having taken you by your own hand as is fitting. Rukmiṇī—
(To herself, with joy) O heart, take heart, take heart! It seems as if my beloved is standing right before you.
Subuddhi:

(With a smile) Why does the dear girl not believe it? Therefore, he has already grasped you by the hand—even while depicted in this very painting of Śauri. (She causes Yārṇi to grasp the cloth-painting of Kṛṣṇa.)
(Offstage, a drum resounds.
Suvatsalā and Makarandikā—(with pride) Oh! A good omen, a good omen!
Subuddhi:

This is certainly no mere auspicious omen. Now Govinda himself shall enter the city by this very path on the palace roof, followed by Śiśupāla and the others. We have just seen the great king Bhīṣmaka approaching to welcome him, accompanied by his sons, headed by the great prince Rucipraba.
(Looking offstage)
"O citizens! O daughters of the city! The Great King commands you: prepare yourselves for the auspicious festivities. Illustrious kings are entering the city.

Makarandikā—(With eagerness) "Venerable Subuddhi! Here, you have had Kṛṣṇa’s marriage performed through this painting. But as for that, I am curious to see both of them together in one place through the portrait of the princess. Therefore, please paint the princess beside Kṛṣṇa on this canvas."
Suvuddhi:
(Laughing) Who can restrain the impetuosity of one so full of curiosity? Moreover, this desire of yours is already close to fulfillment through direct perception.
(Makarandikā, acting it out, draws a portrait on a canvas and places it in her hand.)
(A confused clamor behind the scenes) Sūtradhāra:
"O Noble Lady! The lords of the earth are now close at hand, facing the entry into the city, since this deep sound of kettledrums is being heard from nearby."
Makara—(With eagerness) Noble daughter! Come then; let us ascend to the roof-terrace, the crest of the palace, and look out from between the windows.
Rukmiṇī—
(To himself, with joy) Well done, Mārāṇḍī! Well done! (Aloud, with modesty) As the lady says.
Subuddhi—Let this be done. (Rising, they all do so.)
Makara—(looking through the lattice of the window) Look, look! The kings are entering.
(Everyone looks.)
Makara—
(Looking with joy and wonder) Dear friend! Whose body is this that shines so brightly, with chowries waving about it?
It was as if the face of the mountain were embraced by rows of swans.
Suva—(Observing) Look, look!
There comes that slayer of Madhu, who enchants the minds of twenty thousand cows, mounted upon his chariot.
Rukmiṇī—

(Looking with eagerness) O eyes! That virtuous one, whose multitude of virtues you have been praising for some time—now that your thirst to behold him has grown because of your envy, look upon him now at will! Seize the fruit of your birth for just a moment! Who knows what the blessed Lord Pradyumna will do before us? (Then enters Kṛṣṇa on a chariot atop the palace roof, along with Priyaṃvada.
Makara:

(With eagerness) By good fortune, I behold the fresh mango sprouts hanging from the window. (With recognition) This is that Priyaṃvadā who, having come here on that occasion, departed after her business was accomplished.

Śakuṇṭalā—(Reflecting with sorrow, to herself) Indeed, indeed, my lord, I have no desire to look at the mango tree through this window. Therefore, let it be. (Aloud) O Mādhavikā! You look through the other window. Let the dear Rupinī look here as she pleases.
Makaranda: So be it. (As Makaranda steps aside from Madayantikā, the painted cloth falls from her palm.
Priyamvadaka—)
"Kṛṣṇa, take this; something has been hidden within your lotus-like hand, O you who are marked by the lotus!
Kṛṣṇa:
(Taking it and examining it) What is this? It is a portrait of my own form, featuring the likeness of Rukmiṇī! Priyaṃvada, look, look!
Priyamvada—(Examining the painted canvas) My Lord! This Rukmiṇī has been depicted here beside your portrait.
What do you say? Here is an opportunity for my lotus-hand to rest upon the hand of Hari.
This is your leaf; take this lotus and kill her. || 7 ||
(Seeing the palace, recognizing it with joy and excitement) Kṛṣṇa! This is Rukmiṇī’s palace. Surely this has fallen from Rukmiṇī’s hand.
Kṛṣṇa:

(With longing, casting his eyes upward toward the top of the palace; seeing Rukmiṇī with her face leaning out of the window, and recognizing her with joy and longing) This is surely Rukmiṇī’s; the painting corresponds [to the reality]. (Pointing it out)
The face of the fair-toothed maiden, with its cheeks possessing the luster of gold and its dark curling locks hanging down, bears a mark fashioned by saffron;
with its radiant splendors, it resembles the moon’s orb shining forth from a cave on the mountain of sunrise. 8.
(Rukmiṇī draws her face close to his.
Kṛṣṇa:— (Sighing deeply and hotly with regret:)
Having fasted during the cool season like the autumn moon,
he quickly dispatched his eye as a cakora bird;
alas, destiny is by nature merciless!
The covering is torn away by the cloud. || 9 ||
Rukmiṇī—
(To herself, with remorse) O shameless one, you are even more heartless than our elders, since at the mere sight of him you have obstructed the happiness of my beloved Subuddhi.
Subuddhi—
Child Rukmiṇī! Why have you withdrawn?
Rukmiṇī—(With a look of bashfulness) Having taken a portrait that fell from the hand of Mārkaṇḍeya, someone has looked up at me. (With a faltering voice) Someone has looked up at me.
Subuddhi:

(Looking out the window with a smile, then stepping back apprehensively) It seems that all opportunities have now vanished; King Bhīṣmaka has arrived from Kṛṣṇapura. (Then enters Bhīṣmaka, mounted on a chariot.)
Bhīṣmaka— (Observing Kṛṣṇa, to himself with regret):
This beauty, this heroism, this character, and this youth!
Rukmī pursued Kṛṣṇa and forcibly abducted Rukmiṇī.
(Offstage, with a cry of distress) The young prince, alas, forcibly seizes the female swan from the pigeon!
But she, her limbs languid with passion, seeks refuge with speed in the male swan alone. 11.

Bhīṣmaka:—(To himself) Ah! This well-spoken utterance, mocking the lap of a young prince, has awakened me. But how could such a thing possibly come to pass? Or rather, the course of destiny is difficult to discern.
(Looking toward the stage direction)
O bards! Recite, recite auspicious benedictions for the sake of the kings!
Bard—(with pride and joy)
Bearing the majesty of a pillar-like arm that humbles the prideful gestures of the lords of heaven and earth,
with fierce arrows placed in his hand and haughty heroes cast down at his lotus feet;
he whose wheel-edge is ever-unfolding and who has shattered the pride of the celestial damsels.
May Mukunda, the king who has crushed the hosts of great Daityas with his teeth, protect you both.
Moreover,

Hari triumphs, having been fashioned by those atoms of the thunderbolt with the desire to crush kings who are averse to discipline; or rather, he was filled by the Creator with dense masses of the excellence of his own majesty.
Dark as a water-laden cloud, he was capable of captivating the heart of Śyāmā. || 13 ||
Subuddhi—(Hearing this, to himself) Enough with the word "mind. Let it be capable of seizing Śyāmā.
Bhīṣmaka—

(To himself, with apprehension) Ah! This bard recites as if with some underlying purpose. Kings are somewhat prone to sudden anger. Therefore, I shall first lead Kṛṣṇa away and settle him elsewhere. (Aloud) O Lord Kṛṣṇa! By honoring this street with your presence, you will grace the encampment. O charioteer! Drive the chariot; I shall follow as your attendant. Kṛṣṇa: (With humility) As it pleases your honor! Dāruka, drive the chariot.
(Thus he exits.
Bhīṣmaka:—(Pausing) How is it that Śiśupāla’s chariot is so slow? Why does Rukmin approach right before Śiśupāla? Therefore, I shall follow Kṛṣṇa alone. (Thus he exits.)
(Then Śiśupāla and Rukmin enter.
Rukmin—(Looking toward his side with a sudden start) Oh, bard! Why do you not recite [the praises] of the great lord of the earth, the King of Cedi?
The bard— (with pride, in a loud voice)— that [form], which was like a strange and extraordinary transformation produced at the moment of birth...
Even though he now dwells apart from his abode and is equal to any other man,
Virūpākṣa— possessing many arms and the destroyer of Smara— is victorious as the son of Damaghoṣa, worshipped by kings in battle.
Sucīṣmā—
(listening with eagerness) Let us all look at Śiśupāla through the window together.
(They do so.)
Suvatsalā:
Venerable sir! Who was it that was present at the time of his birth?
Subuddhi:—

Thus it is heard: this one was born with four arms and three eyes; having entered the lap of Kṛṣṇa, he became two-armed and two-eyed. At that time, those skilled in divine portents predicted, "Kṛṣṇa will indeed be his end-maker.
Rukmiṇī—(fearfully) My lord, is this some kind of demon?
Subuddhi: Just so.
Rukmiṇī:—
"Venerable one! My heart trembles; therefore, I shall not remain here. (Thus, trembling, she steps back.
Subuddhi:
(With affection) Child Rukmiṇī! Why do you tremble thus in such distress? Whence comes fear for one who is the beloved of the enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha?
Rukmiṇī—(tearfully) O Bhānumatī! I am truly distressed. I do not know what will happen here; how will my life be sustained?
Subuddhi—

(Lifting Rukmiṇī’s chin) Child! Take heart, take heart! Your heart’s desire is on the verge of fulfillment. Am I a hypocrite? Am I untruthful? The success of the incantation is swift. Is Mukunda slow in his affection for you, or lacking in power? Yet, even in such a dire crisis, you have been cast down by your ill-behaved brother Rukmin.
Śiśupāla — (To himself, with longing and remorse, looking all around) Alas! Our curiosity for the city’s festivities has resulted in a vain sin. For instance:
In this city, the deer-eyed women are indeed like fires as soon as they are seen;
yet that curved moon of Rukmiṇī has not been seen anywhere.
She makes the rows of white mansions appear like a sky devoid of the moon.
It averts my pain, just as the eye of a cakora bird [averts its own]. || 15 ||
Aha! Even me—the one who has reduced many heroic enemies to powder in the crush of battle—the flower-weaponed god (Kāma) makes his servant! Or rather, Rukmiṇī is an ocean of beauty;
her excellence extends even to valor.
By whose power the flower-armed god, having utterly overwhelmed me, the lord of the Cedis, brings me under his control. || 16 ||
(Offstage) Lady Subuddhi!

I have been commanded by Her Majesty thus: "Indeed, having informed the venerable Subuddhi, you must quickly bring the dear Rukmiṇī to the temple for the purpose of worshipping Indrāṇī, as required by the customary rites preceding the wedding. Therefore, let her ladyship come here, taking Rukmiṇī with her.
Subuddhi—
(Having heard this) Child Rukmiṇī! Come, come; let us depart.
Rukmiṇī—(With tears) Blessed One!
Grant me permission for my death-like departure. By your power, having attained the path to heaven, I shall now ascend right there.
Subuddhi:
It is indeed fitting for the wife of Indra’s younger brother; staying here, she will constantly worship her sister-in-law, Indrāṇī.
Rukmin: [He continues.]

(To himself) How is it that the Queen’s chamberlain is summoning Rukmiṇī for the worship of Indrāṇī? Therefore, I shall quickly lead Śiśupāla to the camp at once. (Aloud) O Lord of the Cedis! Hurry, hurry! The time for the second marriage ceremony is drawing near. Śiśupāla—(With impatience) Charioteer! Speed up, speed up the chariot!
(Sārayi does so.
Śiśupāla—(indicating the throbbing of his left eye, to himself with distress) Ah! What is this? (Directing his gaze toward the sky)
At the moment of attaining grace, that beloved one is gone;
alas! my left eye throbs—what can this mean? Or have I become steeped in a dense state of intoxication?
That Rukmiṇī became the cause of that auspicious omen. || 17 ||
Rukmin:
Charioteer! Hurry, hurry!
(He exits.)
Rukmiṇī—
(Sighing) May the Blessed One’s affection for me restrain my life-breath from departing for even a moment.
Subuddhi—
"O child, beloved of Kṛṣṇa, you are forbidden by Kṛṣṇa’s command; do not speak such inauspicious things again. Come now, for your desires are fulfilled.
(Thus they all exit.
The third act.

(Then enters Sātyaki mounted on a chariot, along with his charioteer. Sātyaki (with joy and wonder): Ah! What a confusion of states for Rukmiṇī at that time! For, having finally obtained Kṛṣṇa—the object of her long-cherished desire—with her mind agitated by impetuous longing, she was overcome by a surging trepidation due to the act of his forceful abduction.
Wandering from peak to peak with eyes wide open, free from fear due to her close association with the very wise Suvatsalā, she once again approached the chariot of the gods. || 1 ||

I too have done well, in that Kṛṣṇadeva—though seized by a firm resolve amidst the tumult of battle—was sent forward after being entreated with prostrations. For Rukmiṇī, whose mind is as delicate as a flower and who has witnessed the suffering caused by the slaughter of her kinsmen, I know not how she might fare.

And here are the royal attendants who move within the maidens’ inner apartments, those dwarfs, hunchbacks, and others, as well as the Brahmins who have arrived with great joy for the rite of worshipping Pulomajā.
I have long since avoided those whose valor is based on falsehood by smiling at them from afar; my sword is not yet satiated with the manner of crushing even a few warriors.
Therefore, I shall now approach Baladeva and the others, who are preoccupied with warding off the host of enemies led by Rukmin, Śiśupāla, Pralamba, and Sāraṇa. Charioteer! Hurry, hurry the chariot!
Charioteer:
(Acting accordingly and looking ahead) Long-lived Yuyudhāna! Why is this Baladeva seen returning from that direction, accompanied by his forces?
Sātyaki—(Reflecting with apprehension) Ah! What is this? Has he, having slain Rukmin, Śiśupāla, and the others, now rushed forward to destroy the city? I shall approach and restrain him.
(Then Baladeva enters.)
Sātyaki—(With a bow) O Rāma, supreme king of heroes! Why is this being undertaken? Now that Śiśupāla and the others have been slain, enough with the destruction of the city of the innocent Bhīṣmaka!
Valabhadra—
"Sātyaki! By whom have they been slain, and into whose range of vision have they come?
Sātyaki—(with apprehension):
"O Balarāma! Those who possess the pride of heroes do not flee. Surely—"
"Driven by anger, they are pursuing Kṛṣṇa. Therefore, enough with delay! Come, let us approach this Kṛṣṇa who has fled toward that direction. (They do so.
Valadeva—(looking ahead with joy)—Sātyaki! Your suspicion has borne fruit; those wicked ones have been seen.
Sātyaki—
(with agitation) Those who were seen by Baladeva have now been seen by Kāla.
Valadeva—

(With indignation) Alas! They are indeed close at hand, yet they turn their backs. How shall I pierce them with my arrows? Sātyaki—Wait! Wait! I shall bring them face to face with me. (Loudly, with anger)
"O you, O you! Is Death being bypassed by words consisting of mere empty threats? Who told you that a long life comes from abandoning the battle?
If you do not remember that true hero, then consider your own lineage as that of eunuchs."
Do you not see that the sword, which is easily propitiated and held in the palm of your hand? || 3 ||

Balabhadra:—(With a reproachful taunt) Ho, ho, you fool Śiśupāla! Why do you flee, agitated by fear, transgressing the conduct of the stainless Kṣatriya lineage? Look, look at the descendant of Śūra! Stand firm with steady feet; shame on this cowardice!
"Either enjoy the happiness of worldly existence after conquering your enemies, or shatter the orb of the sun!

Standing before you with head bowed in prostration, this servant of yours, whose sins have been washed away, entreats you for the earth while grasping your hand. Thus does one born of a great lineage beg of you.
Moreover,
O Rukmī, Andhaka, and Nṛpa, this is the supreme course for you:
these kinsmen have come to you for protection.
Having attained unity with us in this festival of battle, let the application of the pride of your powerful arms be brought to an end.

Sātyaki—(Looking ahead, with joy and excitement) O Śaladeva! By good fortune you are prospering; for Rukmin and Śiśupāla have turned back, drawn by the noose of your words. (Then enter Rukmin and Śiśupāla.)

Śiśupāla: (With derisive laughter) Oh Yaladeya! What is this "brotherly affection" you speak of, that you invite premature death upon Kṛṣṇa and then cast it back upon yourself? Rukmī: (Proudly) Oh Lord of Cedi! Do not speak thus. It is precisely our own strength that leads to the death of Kṛṣṇa; this very sequence of death is a mark of good governance, a duty that must certainly be maintained.
Balabhadra—
(With anger) Ah, Śiśupāla! Why do you speak to me with such mildness at this time of famine in battle, when my majesty rises like the morning sun?
"You have arrived as the supreme prey for the sword of Madhumathana;
therefore, I shall swiftly bestow upon him even my own arrows.
Is it not known what fruit is truly appropriate for affection toward one's kin?"

Rukmiṇī—(Reflecting on his pride in strength, to himself) Ah, the plow is his great weapon! Therefore, let it be so for now. (Aloud, with a contemptuous laugh) O Balabhadra! You are a fool. Why do you exert yourself upon this path trodden by slaves?
You might as well attempt to drag a soft river as you do the daughter of the Sun.
You have the strength of an unbridled bull to sever this dangling [snare],
yet this ground is full of pits, treacherous, and as hard as iron; thus, even with this exertion, O Bearer of the Plow, this plowshare is rendered useless.
Moreover, O Valabhadra! While you are merely moving the plough like a bullock, what fame is gained by us from breaking it? (8)
Śiśupāla:
Rukmin! Welcome, welcome to us! Listen to the drum! Immediately upon hearing the drum of our own battle, Kṛṣṇa has turned back. Sāmī: [He turns his head.]
(Recognizing the sound of Kṛṣṇa’s drum, with joy) This is welcome, this is welcome to us! May our hope for victory in battle be fulfilled at least in part now!
Valabhadra: Sātyaki, what has been done by Kṛṣṇa?
Sātyaki:
Having heard the drum of battle, how indeed could Kṛṣṇa remain indifferent? No, no; a lion does not hesitate upon hearing the roar of an elephant.
(Then enter Kṛṣṇa, Ramiṇī, Subuddhi, and Muvatsalā.)
Kṛṣṇa:

(With reproach) O Dāruka! You are excessively timid and falsely encouraged, since your hand—which once grasped the reins of the chariot horses with a cruel fist even from the hands of a miserable beggar—now falters.
Do not let your body, which was once adorned with armlets, grow weary.
May the loathsome paleness of ill-repute not arise for Kṛṣṇa, whose natural splendor is black, by the haste with which the arrows of his adversaries pull at our horses.
Dāruka—
(With fear and humility) Here I release the reins of the chariot; let Your Majesty now behold that the battlefield has, in an instant, become a place of safety for Your Highness.
As she approached his presence, she was like the Goddess of Victory herself, with whom she had entered into a contest.

Rukmiṇī—(Aside with sorrow) Blessed one! I have seen the power of your mantra through its accomplishment of grace. Therefore, now show me the accomplishment of the body; for it is indeed fitting that I be restrained by death as the cause of the end of my circle of kinsmen.
Suvṛddhi—
Child Rukmiṇī! Take heart, take heart! There is no power of incantation here on my part;
it is your own abundance of beauty and fortune that unfolds in this way.
Do not despair; all that is to come shall have a happy conclusion.
Dāruka:
My Lord, your chariot has arrived, seeking your adversary. Prepare your bow, O Kṛṣṇa!

(Grasping the jewel and looking at Rukmiṇī) My beloved, why are you so agitated? This man, who is destined to be the vessel for a succession of blessings from the lineage of Bandhumatī, shall pacify your distress.
(Rukmiṇī, sighing, stands with her face cast down in modesty.
Kṛṣṇa:—
(Looking elsewhere) What! Is this Śiśupāla pursuing Baladeva’s chariot? (With reproach) Ah! Stop, stop!
Do not, O fool, King of Cedi, leap into the fire of the churning-stick!
Do not provoke the son of Rohiṇī!
When he has mounted even a slight degree of anger toward him, Kāla’s supreme residence is in that city. 12.

Śiśupāla:—(Turning the chariot around, with anger) Ho, ho, Kṛṣṇa! Move aside, move aside! You are not worthy of such noble exertion as that of one like me. For instance, [you have been occupied] with the task of performing the worship of the feet of Indrāṇī’s daughter.

O Hari! When you came to the sacrifice and seized him who had approached you with trust, what dharma was practiced by you then? Was it the vow of a kṣatriya, or perhaps the practice of stealing from one's own kin, or some worldly convention? || 13 ||
Kṛṣṇa: (Laughing with feigned contempt) It is fitting, it is fitting!
[To speak of] Sundarī, in whom the dawning of supreme love has proceeded from the moment Caitanya first appeared.

O Śiśupāla, you who are worthy of praise, you are shamelessly uttering these reproaches against me; for I am merely observing a maiden of beautiful limbs and great fortune, who has already formed a firm alliance with me through the employment of her charms for the purpose of casting off her body.
Thus, you are indeed praiseworthy for speaking such insults.
Śiśupāla:

(With contemptuous derision) O hero Kṛṣṇa! It is exactly so. We are insufficient merely by our exertion in offering reproaches; you alone are the preeminent leader among those possessed of valor. For indeed, you are fortunate by virtue of your very lineage of achievements: you have conquered the serpent Vyāla, subdued the donkey Khara, crushed the bull Dhenuka, and slain the horse Aśva.
Who is capable of praising this pair of your heroic strides, which are most excellent, since Kaṃsa was struck down by you and Pūtanā as well? (15)
Sātyaki:
Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Let the Lord of the Cedis speak, let him speak! His hundred offenses must be endured.
Śiśupāla:—
(With anger) Begone! I am not protected from a hundred offenses. Look, look!

What indeed was that hundredfold offense committed today? It was a single offense, surpassing hundreds of thousands of terrible crimes, that I shall now rend asunder and offer to the jackals in battle—that hero who stole away Kṛṣṇa under the pretext of another woman.
Valabhadra:
(With anger) O Śiśupāla! It is your face alone—skilled in uttering those harsh words while you are blind to what is being seen and useless for the work of battle—that is so arrogant toward our limbs.
As for that pair of arms, they have become useless; as for that eye, it has set.

For those virtuous souls, there is not even the slightest acquaintance with ill-repute. These two faults—the great sin of defiling Damaghoṣa’s lineage and this failure to obtain the joy of victory in battle—now belong only to them. || 17 ||

Therefore, enough of this excessive noise from the multitude of innocent kings who have come like crocodiles to a pool; come, you two—Śiśupāla and Rukmin—to the earth which is being trampled in battle.

Rukmin—(Aside) O Lord of Cedi! These two, Baladeva and Govinda, are poorly trained in the sport of open combat. So be it for now. (Whispering into his ear, then aloud with anger) Ah! What need is there for Rāma alone? Come, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa! Let us go to the field of battle. (They do so.)
(Offstage) Oh,
how wonderful! This rain of iron arrows is falling from the sky as if it were without an agent at all!
Even at the very height of its youth, this darkness has risen like the sun, possessing the hue of the neck of Kārttikeya’s elephant.
(Again, behind the scenes: Behold, those two noisy chariots have gone somewhere, leaving the vehicles empty;
it is strange that this army continues to fight even more vigorously despite being leaderless.
Kṛṣṇa:

(Hearing this, to himself) Surely Rukmiṇī and Śiśupāla, stationed on the ground, are displaying their cruel proficiency in illusory warfare. Therefore, mounting my vehicle drawn by serpents, I shall strike them down from the sky. (Aloud) Blessed Sughuḍḍhā! Noble Suvatsalā! You two must cherish Rukmiṇī until I have averted this calamity.
(Rukmiṇī stands with her face cast down, bashful and distressed.)
"O you who are most wise and most affectionate... may the hero be victorious!
(Kṛṣṇa mimes the act of meditation.
Akrūra—
(Looking upward with wonder) Is this the Golden Mountain that has taken wings?
Or is it the Fire, dense with spreading, fierce, and matted flames?
Is this indeed that same god, the sovereign lord of all splendors, who comes here to destroy these exceedingly dense darknesses? (20)
Valabhadra—(with agitation) Surely this is a stratagem of those who hate the wicked; therefore, I shall cut him down right here in the sky with a sharpened arrow. (He strings his bow.
Kṛṣṇa—
[Śaṃdhapram]: Noble Baladeva! Stay, stay! Here is Tārkṣya, whom I have called to mind; he is approaching. Having mounted him, I shall seize the two adversaries who move through the sky.
(Then Tārkṣya enters.
Tārkṣya:
(With a step forward) May the Delighter of Devakī favor me by granting his command! If you are eager to conquer the nether world, I shall forcibly agitate the oceans with the wind from my wings.
If you are longing for them, then I shall bring those [gods]—
Induśekhara (Śiva), Viriñca (Brahmā), Purandara (Indra), and the others.
Kṛṣṇa—(With pride and a smile) Come now; first, I shall search for those two opponents, those great illusory chariot-warriors who range the battlefield of the sky.
Tārkṣya—
"Do as you wish. (Having thus placed Kṛṣṇa upon his hip, he mimes ascending into the sky; everyone gazes on in wonder.
Akrūra:
"Aha! Behold, behold!"
Warding off the sharp streams of weapons,
this king of birds acts as a shimmering sunshade;
above him, the enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha appears like a glistening sapphire dome.

Valabhadra—(Looking with agitation) Ah! Has Viṣṇu himself mounted his chariot, that it speeds so swiftly? Is the sky difficult to traverse for arrows and missiles? (Laughing loudly) Is the mace of Yaladeva sluggish in ascending to the heights of the heavens? (He brandishes the mace.
Sātyaki—
Vrātyadeva! Listen, listen for a moment! Something is indeed being heard.
(All act out the gesture of listening.
(Behind the scenes:)
O Tārkṣya! Do not release them, nor crush them with a violent grip; hold these two as you would your own sons out of compassion, for their limbs must remain unbroken.
Hand it over to the heroes of your own group and depart. || 23 ||
Valabhadra:
How were Durvṛtta and Muktta slain by Murāri? Akrūra: [He replied:]...
Rāma! This victory at the feet of Samaravija is exceedingly great.
Sātyaki—Listen further; something else is being heard.
(All perform the gesture of hearing.
(Offstage:
O Rukmī, brother of Rukmiṇī, and you, O Lord of the Cedis, both are my kinsmen.
Even though you two are ill-behaved and of wicked character, you are both to be cherished by me.

Subuddhi:—(Hearing this, with joy) Child Rukmiṇī! By good fortune, you have now been doubly blessed: that the enemy of the Daityas, who is dearer than life itself, has been found by you; and that he was not consumed by the fire of your anger, which was extinguished by the flood of the rasa of compassion.
(Rukmiṇī takes him by the hand with joy.)
Balabhadra:
(Looking ahead with joy) How is it that Dāmodara approaches on foot alone, having commanded Vainateya to escort away his enemies?
He is being praised by rows of bees acting as bards, who have gathered from the celestial *mandāra* garlands cast down by the joyful gods.
Having attained the fortune of victory yet remaining unprovoked toward the destruction of his enemies, Śauri—whose very form is the embodiment of valor and compassion—triumphs, he triumphs! (25)
(Then enters Vāsudeva as described).
Vāsudeva—(With a feigned smile): Noble Rāma! Those two heroes, having been reconciled by me, have been dispatched for the purpose of crushing [the enemy] in an unbearable battle.

Valabhadra—(With a meaningful gesture: It is only thus that one is joined with a superior; therefore, our desired ends have now been accomplished. May you ascend the chariot for the journey to Dvārakā. (Kṛṣṇa approaches and acts out descending from the chariot.)
Dāruka:— (With a salutation) May the Lord be victorious!
Subuddhi:—
O hero Kṛṣṇa! Even blessings do not suffice for that which has been accomplished by you; therefore, a mere salutation to you is most appropriate. Kṛṣṇa:
(With humility) Blessed lady! It is your grace alone that unfolds in this manner.
The affectionate one:
Victory, victory to the Lord!
(Rukmiṇī stands with her face bowed down.)
Kṛṣṇa—(With great agitation and remorse):
O moon-faced one! O passionate lady! Why do you still maintain this dejection toward the lords of your enemies, even though their lives have been spared?
O tremulous-eyed one! Because I was cowardly, O beloved, even this dear enjoyment of the passion of amorous play in battle was abandoned by me. (26)
(Rukmiṇī stands with her face cast down, filled with longing and bashfulness.
Subuddhi: (With eyes wide with wonder) O Lord Kṛṣṇa! Behold, behold!
This loveliness belongs not to the cruel rays of the sun.
No, no; even a mass of lightning would be so transitory as this. [It is] exceedingly delicate... how is it that such a strange light appears in the sky nearby? (27)
Kṛṣṇa:— (Looking with wonder and suspicion) Could this be some illusion...?
(Offstage)

O blessed Succharddha! Quickly, quickly! I have swiftly rendered your service as my disciple fruitful. And you, O Kṛṣṇa, are like the very pinnacle of supreme affection for my beloved Nīlakaṇṭha. So, what can I do for you? Speak! Nevertheless, what further boon shall be most pleasing to you? (All bow with joy and wonder. Kṛṣṇa:
This favor is attainable from the Goddess alone even through ten million meritorious deeds.
What is to be accomplished by that which is already established? For me, there is something even greater than that. || 28 ||
Nevertheless, let this be: let the clouds rain down water more lustrous than nectar; let the lords of poets rain down excellent verses superior to ambrosia;
and let the Brahmins properly offer oblations into the sacrificial fire.
And may the kings bestow immeasurable wealth upon those who seek it. || 29 ||
Thus ends the fourth act in the *Śrīrukmiṇīharaṇa*.
Thus concludes the *Indumṛga*, composed by the great poet Śrīvatsarāja.
Victorious is the head of the moon-crested Lord, encircled by the waters of the celestial river;
upon which a flower, when sown, immediately becomes a wish-fulfilling tree.
With its tawny, towering sparks that make the sky appear as if filled with fire-tongues, and carrying clouds that seem like mountains being lifted up by the lords of the gods,
the fire of Bāṇa— which causes the destruction of the city of the Enemy of Tripura— causes the mass of waters of the Mandākinī to roar as it boils while it performs its silent recitation (japa).
Obscuring the faces with smoke, flooding the eyes with tears,
and spreading [the fire] with a vast circle of flames as the gods were overwhelmed by the intensity of their anguish—
even at the height of their supreme joy— this fire of Śiva’s arrow triumphs as it consumes Tripura, performing actions befitting grief.
(At the end of the benediction) Director—
(looking all around):
Pāripārśvaka: ... [you] are being addressed by your honor.
Sūtradhāra:—
Mārpa! Why do you mock me? That very god is at fault here. For instance, the earth sometimes reaches a state of exhaustion through incessant successions of gifts;
yet it bears a joy as if it were filled with them once again.
The king, the supreme giver, [honored him] with repeated offerings. || 4 ||
Pāri:

May you receive it, may you receive it! I am not a vessel for the impurity of stinginess; rather, I am grieved that my lord does not begin to give what is appropriate to his wealth. For prosperity, even when abundant and well-guarded, falls away from one who is devoid of charity.
A cow that has become barren becomes a source of extreme distress for the householder. || 5 ||
Sūtra:
(Casting aside his pride) Mārpa! Wait for an auspicious occasion such as an eclipse of the sun or moon. You fool! Behold my great acts of charity!
Pāri:

O noble one! Why this delay? For it is proclaimed that even among those who pride themselves on the strength of Tripura, there are Daityas such as Kaiṭabha’s sons who desire the slaughter of Gaurī even while she is in the midst of the ocean; and though armless, that Rāhu repeatedly strikes the sun and the moon; and when the host of gods was shattered by the humiliations of Tripura, I know that in some days Vali too will emerge from the depths of Pātāla here, powerful and with his bonds destroyed. 6. O noble one! What is the delay? For it is proclaimed that even among those who pride themselves on the strength of Tripura, there are Daityas such as Kaiṭabha’s sons who desire the slaughter of Gaurī even while she is in the midst of the ocean; and though armless, that Rāhu repeatedly strikes the sun and the moon; and when the host of gods was shattered by the humiliations of Tripura, I know that in some days Vali too will emerge from the depths of Pātāla here, powerful and with his bonds destroyed. 6. O noble one! What is the delay? For it is proclaimed that even among those who pride themselves on the strength of Trip
(Nepathya, with derision):
This is fitting, this is fitting for you! For actors, by means of the perverse cravings of ill-conceived roles, cause the creepers of discord to grow and destroy the weak with their own excesses.
Pāri—
(With fear) Noble sir! Who is this who is angry without cause?
Sūtra—(Recognizing him by his voice) This is the great sage Nārada, the son of Viriñci.
Pāri—(Having recovered his composure): Oh! How great is the sage’s disposition toward tranquility!
Sūtra—
(Withdrawing) This is simply his nature. Do you not know this? For instance:

The resonance of the *sāman* chants, though it delights the ears with its arrangement of pleasant musical scales, does not nourish such a sweet dream as the quarrel of the sage Nārada, which abounds in mutual, cruel, and harsh speech sharpened by intense anger. (7)
Therefore, he who is eager to behold the battle and is himself wrathful must be saluted from afar. Come, let us both perform our own duty, which is the next task to be accomplished.
(Exeunt. Prologue.)
(Then Nārada enters.
Nārada—(Looking all around with excitement) Why is there no one here? Oh, what audacity on the part of this actor, who is so glib with false speech! For instance:
While those who were parched by the swelling fever of fear meditated upon the sport of the trident in the darkness, there occurred the treading of the discus of Murāri.
When was there even a trace of valor among the Daityas? || 8 ||
Or rather, why is this actor blamed, who even counts Rāhu among the ranks of heroes?
(Offstage) Ah! You are a Brahmin! What shall I do? Speak as you please, for my tongue is unrestrained.
The enemy of the Dānavas, though alive, does not abandon his fortress on the Golden Peak because of the fortresses of the waters of the ocean;
and he who has the moon as his crest (Śiva) occupies the cemetery as his fortress.
This indeed accords with the glorious reputation of the gods as great warriors.

Nārada—(Looking upward by following the movement of the notes, to himself) How is it that this Rāhu is moving about? Very well; who is this wretch? (Then Rāhu enters by means of a celestial chariot. Rāhu recites the verse beginning with "kanakaśikhari...")
Nārada:
(With feigned indignation) O hero Rāhu! The speech of the gods regarding great warriors is indeed laughable. For instance:
the Lord of the Gods has his prowess paralyzed by Jambha; the Sun is dull-witted and devoid of splendor.

He too remains there, the god with the thunderbolt for a weapon and hips as firm as an elephant’s trunk; yet even that Kṛṣṇa is repeatedly tormented by Dānavas such as Madhu and Mura. Only you, O Rāhu, being a man of refined taste, truly know the state of valor and lack thereof.
(Rāhu, as if apprehensive, stops him with a nod of his head.
Nārada—(Laughing) O son of Siṃhikā! Stop him with a gesture of the hand.
O Nārada, shameless one, why do you laugh so joyfully at Bhāmā’s distress? Alas! You are mocking her who has been rendered helpless.
You do not possess a thousand faces to laugh at the rays of the sun, which have been eclipsed by me.
Therefore, listen to the words of me who desires your welfare:
"Speak softly, O Nārada! Why do you not abandon this brahminical fickleness expressed through your false pride? Alas! Let not the Dānavas become angry with you."
O Sage, now that the gods have suddenly departed, where indeed could you employ your destructive power, which is characterized by mutual conflict and sported with in anger? (12)
Nārada:
(With a laugh) O son of Siṃhikā! For this very reason, I too do not uproot the Dānavas by provoking the gods. For it is thus: when the Dānavas have been uprooted from their very roots...
Among the gods who delight in the happiness of freedom from enmity,
how could Nārada possibly have any curiosity for the spectacle of the intense tumult of battle?

Rāhu—(With derision) Oh! What great curiosity for battle this great sage possesses! Therefore, I shall fulfill your longing to witness the combat, even though you have no desire for any other kind of gift. Wretched as he is, the moon, having come within my grasp on the full-moon night, was left without refuge; yet now, having sought the shelter of the sun, he shall likewise be seen.
Therefore, behold for yourself this very day how I shall make this [Rāhu], who has long been a tormentor of the world, a mere morsel with his cruel rays spreading forth. 14.
(Thus he exits in anger.

Nārada—(With astonishment) Oh, how fierce is the power of the Dānava-khaṇḍa! Therefore, having worshipped the blessed Bhāgīrathī, I shall follow [the Lord] to play the lute for him who wields the axe in his hand. I shall provoke that very God to wrath against the Dānavas. (Looking upward) Even the host of gods will now be serving Śiva.
(Thus he exits. Interlude.
(Then enters Maheśa, being worshipped by a multitude of gods.)
Maheśa—(To himself, with apprehension) Ah! Why do I see the very marks of the nectar-eating gods obliterated? Very well, I shall ask. (Aloud) O Preceptor of the Gods! What is this?
The thousand eyes of Śakra bear the seal of the life-force of the moon, which is pale as frost.
The noose of Varuṇa, falling under the sway of indolence, portends the destruction of happiness;
the fire of Yama, its vigor dormant, brings about a second blackness upon the mind;
and the guardians of the world, visibly agitated, clearly declare the cruel, ultimate limit of suffering. (15)

Bṛhaspati—(ironically) Does the venerable omniscient one wish to make us chatter for his amusement, like Nārada? Let the Lord himself know. Nārada: Close your eyes; Rāhu, the devourer of the sun and moon, is approaching.
Let this elephant-hide, the carpet of enmity, be spread out in secret.
"O Śambhu, cast this spear, which is the very essence of war's transgression, far away somewhere; let you remain merely as an ascetic, for the Dānavas are formidable in battle. (16)
Maheśa:—
(With composure) I am always surrounded by all the Daityas in this assembly.
"Tell me, tell me, Nārada! Who is this whose form is suddenly bent?
Let the Pināka bow—its roar from the twanging of its bowstring rivalling the thunder of the clouds at the dissolution of the world—render the realm of heaven free from fear. (17)

Indra—(to himself, with joy): By good fortune, Hara’s mind has become steeped in the sentiment of wrath (*raudrarasa*). Well done, Nārada! Well done! For you have reached the further shore of the ocean of calamity.
Nārada—(looking to the side) O thousand-eyed one, you who are like a blunt axe! Why do you not inform him?
Indra—

(Sighing with distress) Oh, Great Sage! To whom may I, who am an object of ridicule, address my request? For indeed, hardness has departed from the thunderbolt and taken up residence in my heart along with terror;
it is now shattered and distressed by the rising pride of wicked demons.
I do not possess even a fraction of an eye, though my body has a thousand eyes;
surely my fame has been stolen by my enemies who behold this wondrous spectacle.
Maheśa—(With great enthusiasm): O Subduer of Jambha! Why do you weary yourself thus? How small are the grasses of the Dānava clans to the forest fire of your thunderbolt?
Indra—
(With humble courtesy) Why this addiction to speech filled with pride?
This thunderbolt has been hurled, but it is not by you, O Lord; it is by your power.
While you stand firm in your magnanimity of mind, who among the Dānavas is capable of breaking your staff-like arms in combat? (19)
Maheśa—(With distress) Alas, O Puruhūta! What is this that you have uttered? Even in his own dreams, the Lord would never be indifferent toward the affairs of the gods;
to whom would a trident not cause pain in the head?
Or rather, whose bow does it not destroy?
And whose life-breath would this axe not take, were it to deliver Indra’s command? (20)
Yama:

(With indignation) Ah! What? Do the immortals think that the sport of crushing the Daityas in battle will distract the Lord Ugra? O God of gods! Fearing the power of the boon granted by you, we have become powerless in that matter. Therefore, now, O Giriśa, let your weapons rest upon your lotus-like hands.
"Do not be afraid of the fatigue of battle; indeed, there is no servant of yours.
Let this staff of mine roam freely upon the field of combat, intent on breaking the limbs of the Danavas with its exceedingly fierce efforts that cause their bones to shatter and resound. (21)
Hutāśa:
(Looking toward the sky with anger) O flames, all of you, who are agitated by the tumult of the time of universal dissolution!
Be bold toward me, for I am instantly eager for the flavor of battle!
Once that forest of the asura host has been consumed by me, let the wrath of the other gods be like an oblation poured into ashes.
Nārada—(Laughing with joy) O Vāyu! Behold, behold the heroic energy of your own friend! Vāyu—
O friend Nārada! I alone am the wind that shall uproot the very foundation of the multitude of demon-trees from long ago.
Then the executioner of the dead burns them, while Tanūnapāt heats them and Ravi dries them.

Nārada—(With joy) By good fortune, may you prosper, may you prosper through your righteous deeds! When the gods are thus arrogant in their power, where is there life for the Dānavas who are submerged in the waters?
Varuṇa—

(With his body trembling with rage) These irrepressible enemies of the gods, rendered helpless by the cruel noose around their necks— (pointing to himself) this unrestrained Lord of Waters will forcibly lead them to the depths of Pātāla. Therefore, let the gods, devoid of the passion for battle and shorn of their pride, abandon their broken vows.
O Sage, act in such a way that they do not become angry; I entreat you thus.
Nārada:
Friend Kuvera! You are the giver of wealth; therefore, now become the giver of death to your enemies.
Kuvera: [Listens.]
O friend Nārada! Whether due to the expansion of my arm-stumps or out of affection for the Three-eyed Lord, the Dānavas who long for battle do not encounter me at all.
For me, whose soul has been distressed for many days by the great exertion of battle, this festival of war is now at hand before the powerful Śambhu for the sake of Hari. 25.
Nārada—(With joy) Ah! By good fortune, I have now become one who has fulfilled his purpose; henceforth, there is no need for anyone else’s eyes.
The Nairṛtas—
(Angrily, to himself) How is it that this boy does not even count me by the mere calculation of commoners? Therefore, let it be thus—
(Aloud) In the matter of tearing asunder those who commit treason against the gods, I alone am the foremost.
O Nārada! Does the dignity of such a person not diminish through disregard for you?
Your fickleness in these playful quarrels is merely a matter of curiosity;
how is it, O Brahmin, that you, being so timid, do not know that your arrow is firm? (26)

Nārada—(To himself) Fortunately, he has indeed joined our side. Let him be angry, let him be angry; it is exceedingly pleasing, most pleasing to me. (Aloud, with humility) O night-stalker! Who else is there who is a leader among heroes like you?
The supreme sword, the foremost of weapons, sports in your hand;

yet why must you, who are capable of uprooting even the gods, be entreated? By whom was this cosmic order commanded that it repeatedly brings about the destruction of this world for the sake of the enemies of the gods? 27.
Nandī—(longingly) O Lord of the Gods! Truly, this service rendered by such a distinguished Dānava as myself makes you favor me. For instance:
"Is this earth, whose sun has set, to be transgressed?"
Was it perhaps by some other means that he alone, the foremost of men, [was spared],
while those many cowards, having suddenly assembled, repeatedly initiated that calamitous conflict? (28)
"Therefore, tell me, who is this crest-jewel of heroes? Bṛhaspati said:
"O son of Śilāda! Is it necessary to explain that he is to be known as the comet named Tripura, which roams the firmament and portends the destruction of the three worlds?"

Difficult to behold, their waters discolored by the mass of spreading flames of abundant fire, the faces of the quarters covered by a multitude of crackling sparks—these arrows of Śiva swing upon the head of Gaṇeśa, who is armored by the waters of the Gaṅgā; yet that wicked deity of the gods does not hear the whizzing sounds they make.

And this one who moves through the atmosphere does not merely destroy the atmosphere; even the earth is thoroughly scorched by him. Even that lord of the netherworld, the king of serpents, has been shattered by him.
(Then the Earth enters.
Earth:
(With agitation, fixing his gaze upon the sky) Blessed One, Lotus-Born! May I address you? Oh, what a wicked transgression of yours!
The eight families of serpents are common to you, as are those guardians of the quarters and that king of serpents himself.
Having supported me thus in detail, why do you now abandon me with such cruel punishments? || 30 ||

Therefore, I shall not approach you. I will go for refuge to that very Candrashekhara; he alone will protect you as well. (Walking about, acting out a stumble, with distress) Alas! I have stumbled quite badly. So, who is my support? That king of serpents is far away.
(Entering in male attire, Śeṣa) Śeṣa:—
O Blessed Sustainer of Beings! Support me, O Achyuta!

Pṛthivī—(Looking) What? Has Nārāyaṇa arrived! O King of Men! I am ashamed, even here, O you who are like adamant! O Achyuta! Have you forgotten my hooded circle, which, while supporting you as you reeled from the downpour of the rain of Duḥśāsana’s blows, served as a difficult-to-bear, throbbing, and quivering cushion?
Śeṣa:

O Blessed One! "I am fortunate indeed that the Goddess Earth herself, the support of all things, honors me in this way. Therefore, please take hold of me. Here is the Blessed Lord, the husband of Bhavānī, seated nearby, being worshipped by a host of gods led by Purandara. Come, let us approach him.
(Umā and [Śiva] approach.)
Earth:
O Blessed One, cause of protection from the destruction of all the worlds! Homage to you, homage to you!
Śeṣa:
(With humility) O you whose bull-bannered vehicle has undertaken all the duties of the world through the distribution of the eight [forms]! Homage to you, homage to you!
Maheśa—(With agitation) Ah! What is this?
O Earth! You have arrived before us in person, your face clouded with tears, moving unsteadily,
your broad braid disheveled by the flow of perspiration,
bringing exhaustion to our minds.
Therefore, tell me, what is this? O Blessed Earth, honored by all the world, this is a great calamity! O Sovereign, you are like a peahen of unprecedented form, embraced by manifold delights.
Standing upon the earth, you nourish even the worlds above with the offerings of *havya* and *kavya*.
Pṛthvī—(With humility) Blessed One! Why this self-exaltation? Indeed, I am but the manifestation of your own form. Maheśa—
(Looking at the remainder:
O Lord of Serpents! Though you do not bite us, you torment our minds with the multitude of wounds from your flickering hoods that have been severed. 33.
Śeṣa: (With agitation) O God of gods! I am subject to your command; it is not that I am incapable.
With a thousand hoods, emitting a spreading and vast hissing—

Is it not a mass of widespread flames spreading through the sky? Yet, by the extinction of this lamp, neither my feet nor my body are capable of performing the task of extinguishing the demon Tripura. || 34 ||

Nārada: (With joy and wonder) Excellent, excellent! Indeed, this king of arms is capable not only of lifting the burden of the earth, but also of bearing the burden of battle. (Acting out the affliction of cold) Ah! How is it that even amidst the oppression of such heat from suffering, the distress of cold manifests itself? (Looking ahead) What! Has the king of mountains arrived at the front? (Proudly) Come, come, O King of Mountains, father-in-law of Hara! Cool the host of gods who are scorched by the humiliation of Tripura! (Entering)
Himavat—(with remorse, shaking his head) O Lord of Sages! Alas!
What can we do here for the sake of the leader of the immortals?
Since we have had our wings shattered by the thunderbolt and have become laden with a heavy mass of water,
as we are being freely sprinkled [by clouds], why do we not pulverize the host of demons and the sky-dwellers? (35)
"Therefore, even though I am currently standing firm, I shall now fulfill the desire of the one who seeks it.
Nārada:

(With humility) O Three-eyed One, difficult to perceive! Who is being sought now? Neither the Lord of the Triple City nor the divine chariot have arrived here; only the two sages, Nandin and Masi, are present.
Nandī—(Looking around in all directions with great agitation) Ah! What is this?
The night-dwellers roam about even though it is not yet night; the sun has reached its zenith even though the dawn has not yet appeared.
Ah! What a marvelous occasion this is, which expands the darkness that clings to the lotus-feet of the Lord! 36.
(Offstage) To him whose power and prowess are the destroyers of the Daityas...
He who, without having his crown destroyed, slanders the lowly— this very Rāhu,
with fangs terrifying due to the heavy burden of his skull-bowl and lacking any covering, now strikes down the sun.
"Therefore, let whoever among the gods here is capable of rescuing him come forward!
Maheśa—(with agitation)—"Nandin, bring me my bow! Let the world of the sun be instantly freed from sorrow!"
Nandī:

Ah! Who is this wicked rogue who seeks to seize Rāhu, who has been captured and is now free from his body? Let the burning of Tripura be undertaken instead, by which the path of the sun—along with the Devayāna and Pitṛyāna paths—is utterly uprooted and destroyed.
(Offstage)
(With anger) Ah! Who is this that uproots Dharma?
Dharma is eternally powerful and the sole cause of victory;
Dharma protects others effortlessly through mere remembrance.
Tell me, who among those enemies of Dharma— Jambhaka, Kaiṭabha, Bhaṅga, Jandhaka, and Nāraka— ever attained prosperity?
Nārada— (With joy) How is it that my elder brother, Dharmas, the son of Brahmā, has already arrived?
Dharma—
(Entering) O Blessed One, support of the entire world! Here is Dharma bowing to you.
Maheśa:
Ah, Dharma! Why do you speak thus? Even for us, he who assumes the form of a bull is our own support. Please, be seated here.
Dharma:
O Maheśa! Since the world is obstructed by Tripura, my place is right here (and he sits down).
Nārada:
(Approaching suddenly with humility) Blessed Dharma! Here is your younger brother, Nārada, saluting you. (He bows down.
Dharma—(With joy) My child, beloved of Kali!
By favoring those who feed on nectar and by suppressing the intoxicated Dānavas,
I shall bring about a fierce conflict.
For your pleasure and for my own spiritual advancement. || 39 ||
Nārada—(With joy) O Blessed One! With you as their partisan, the Lord Nārāyaṇa will be the commander-in-chief of the gods; what doubt, then, can there be regarding victory?
For where there is Dharma, there is Kṛṣṇa; and where there is Kṛṣṇa, there is victory.
Kārttikeya—(With suppressed anger) How can Nārāyaṇa become the commander-in-chief of the gods, setting aside me as the general? (Aloud, with agitation) O Nārada!
Having abandoned the desire for manliness, shall I not fall into the state of a woman?
O Sage, having cast aside my pride fivefold, I shall not become small;
nor shall I experience the transformation into the forms of a tortoise, a boar, a fish, or the like.
The Supreme Person among men is worthy of the gods, not a person such as I. (40)
Nārada:

(With joy) By good fortune, the host of the gods prospers, since this son of Śambhu has become so impetuous. (Approaching with a laugh and smelling Kārttikeya on the head) May this youth, whose valor is no longer that of a child, rejoice as the delight of the Trident-bearer!
By his grace, may the gods, free from decay, attain old age. || 41 ||

Maheśa: O Kārttikeya! Why do you prattle like one ignorant of the truth? The enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is your maternal uncle. Kārttikeya: [Pauses]... Maheśa: O Kārttikeya! Why do you prattle like one ignorant of the truth? The enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is your maternal uncle. Kārttikeya: [Continues]... Maheśa: O Kārttikeya! Why do you prattle like one ignorant of the truth? The enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is your paternal uncle. Kārttikeya: [Continues]... Maheśa: O Kārttikeya! Why do you prattle like one ignorant of the truth? The enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is your grandfather. Kārttikeya: [Continues]... Maheśa: O Kārttikeya! Why do you prattle like one ignorant of the truth? The enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is your great-grandfather. Kārttikeya: [Continues]... Maheśa: O Kārttikeya! Why do you prattle like one ignorant of the truth? The enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is your father-in-law. Kārttikeya: [Continues]... Maheśa: O Kārttikeya! Why do you prattle like one ignorant of the truth? The enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is your brother-in-law. Kārttikeya: [Continues]... Maheśa: O Kārttikeya! Why do you prattle like one ignorant of the truth? The enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is your son-in-law. Kārttikeya: [Continues]... Maheśa: O Kārttikeya! Why do you prattle like one ignorant of the truth? The enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is your nephew. Kārttikeya: [Continues]... Maheśa: O Kārttikeya! Why do you prattle like one ignorant of the truth? The enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is your maternal cousin. Kārttikeya: [Continues]... Maheśa: O Kārttikeya! Why do you prattle like one ignorant of the truth? The enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is your maternal grandfather. Kārttikeya: [Continues]... Maheśa: O Kārttikeya! Why do you prattle like one ignorant of the truth? The enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is your maternal great-grandfather. Kārttikeya: [Continues]... Maheśa: O Kārttikeya! Why do you prattle like one ignorant of the truth? The enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is your maternal uncle’s son. Kārttikeya: [Continues]... Maheśa: O Kārttikeya! Why do you prattle like one ignorant of the truth? The enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is your maternal uncle’s grandson. Kārttikeya: [Continues]... Maheśa: O Kārttikeya! Why do you prattle like one ignorant of the truth? The enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is your maternal uncle’s great-grandson. Kārttikeya: [Continues]... Maheśa: O Kārttikeya! Why do you prattle like one ignorant of the truth? The enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is your maternal uncle’s wife’s brother. Kārttikeya: [Continues]... Maheśa: O Kārttikeya! Why do you prattle like one ignorant of the truth? The enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is your maternal uncle’s wife’s brother’s son. Kārttikeya: [Continues]... Maheśa: O Kārttikeya! Why do you prattle like one ignorant of the truth? The enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha is your maternal uncle’s wife’s brother’s grandson. Kārttikeya: [Continues]... Maheśa: O Kārttikeya! Why do you prattle like one ignorant of the
(With humility) If my uncle remains, will my father, my uncle, or even my grandfather have to undergo the hardships of battle?
Maheśa:

(Smiling) Oh, Nārada! Go and summon the Grandfather and Kṛṣṇa. Let it not happen that the Asuras of Tripura become arrogant due to the granting of boons by them; with their very permission, I shall consume them.
Nārada: As the Lord commands. (He exits.
Maheśa:—

"O great Indra and other gods! All of you prepare yourselves at your respective quarters. This burning of Tripura is already accomplished. However, the illusory manifestation (*māyā-prapañca*) of the Dānavas must here be guarded against, for it is difficult to perceive. Indra and the others—(with humility and joy): "As the Lord commands."
(Thus they all exit. End of the First Act.
(Then enters Allika.)

Alīka—(Looking ahead) What! Is this my dear friend walking backwards? How wonderful, how wonderful! If he is blind, how is it that he moves with such rapid steps? If he is not blind, why does he not see me? Very well, I shall call out to him. O you who are going backwards, backwards! Where are you heading? Viparīta—
(Looking suddenly, with joy) Dear friend Alīka! By good fortune I have been called by you. Otherwise, having gone without seeing you, I would have been grieving while searching for you.
Alīka: But why do you not see me?
Vipaśyāyan:
