Alas! My heart was so preoccupied with the burden of carrying the weight of the kingdom’s affairs that I did not notice you.
Alīka: [Laughs] No, no! You did not see me.
(With apprehension) Friend, what sort of state business is this?

Vipra: Having been humiliated by the lords of the gods, the demons met together, consulted, and dispatched Nārada to the presence of Hari and Viriñci; this has been reported to the lord of the Dānavas by his spies.
Alīka—
(With contempt) This is a gathering of dogs for the purpose of defiling the quarters; it is a meeting of immortals for the purpose of destroying the Lord of Tripura.

Vipa—(With indignation) Oh, friend! Since you have been raised in the royal court from childhood, you are indeed skilled in the ways of kings; why then do you speak thus? One must remain vigilant even toward an enemy as small as an atom.
Alīka:
Then tell me, what was commanded by the Lord of the Three Cities?
(He whispers the same words into his ear.)
Alīka:—(With joy) Excellent, excellent! This is truly heart-gladdening.
Vipa—

(With pride) Friend! In this matter, both you and I must say that the victory of the Asuras is reversed and the slaughter of the gods is false. Therefore, go and cause Viriñci to change his mind; Nārada remains in the presence of Viṣṇu. I, too, shall cause Hara to change his mind and cause the gods, headed by Purandara, to change theirs. (Exeunt both).
(End of the Interlude). (Then enter Nārāyaṇa and Nārada).
Nārāyaṇa:
(With apprehension) But why is Nārada today standing there as colorless and pale-bodied as an autumnal cloud? Even this lute, hanging from his shoulder, seems like a burden.
Nārada:—
(Sighing with distress) O Vaikuṇṭha! Are you manifesting a melody of the immortals that weaves together the indistinctness of piteous wailing and clearly displays its modulation?
O Enemy of the Asuras! This lute of suffering played by my emaciated body does not please you at all; therefore, I remain silent. || 1 ||

Nārāyaṇa—(With great agitation) A dire calamity! A dire calamity! O Nārada, you are an expert in the affairs of all the worlds; therefore, tell me, whose is this momentary rise after such a long period of decline? Nārada—
Oh! How auspicious is the fortune of those who bestow gifts, since for that purpose another is questioned by you, who pervade the entire universe! Therefore, what shall I not declare?
This entire triple world is scorched by the fire of its defeat at the hands of the Lord of Tripura;
it does not find even a moment’s peace before you, the sovereign of the three worlds. (2)
Moreover,
even for a moment, the sky does not provide space for the celestial damsels to sport,
whether in yoga or in battle; with their bodies disintegrated, they do not come into contact with the sun.
When the path of the gods is blocked by the expanding wheels of the vast army of Tripura, even one who has performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is unable to reach the city of Indra.
Nārāyaṇa said:

"O Nārada! You too speak thus. Do you not see that by propitiating the fierce [deity] with fierce austerities, the Dānavas become fierce? Am I dependent on others in what I must do? My mace is always the destroyer of Dānavas."
The sight of the Sudarśana alone is terrible;
this Nandaka of mine has no dull power, and I desire only to carry out the command of the Lord. || 4 ||

Nārada: (With derision) Oh, the power of those created by the Asura-maker, by whom even the omniscient have been rendered ignorant! Śambhu himself knows this: that the Asuras of Tripura, having received boons from Janārdana, do not fear the boon of Hara, and even toward them when they are hostile, he maintains no hostility. Thus did the Blessed Bharga say to me: "Murāri is indeed my second self, for Hara is half of his body; therefore, should he ever strike an Asura who has received a boon from him, he might become angry with me. Therefore, go and investigate!"
Nārāyaṇa:— (With humble courtesy) O Nārada!
By means of granting the boon of sharing half of his body...
May he himself, being pleased, cherish me;
and on occasions of service in battle, may Nandin not be superior to me in the presence of Śambhu.
(Then enters Nandin. Nandin:

Oh! What a mass of misfortune for the gods, that this creeper of mutual strife has sprouted among them! (Looking all around) How is it that I have already reached the world of Viṣṇu! So, where is Nārāyaṇa here? (Looking ahead) Why, here is Nārāyaṇa conversing confidentially with Nārada!

(With astonishment) Ah! What is this? For here he is, his eyes swollen from weeping, having recounted his humiliation before the Enemy of Kaiṭabha, and now departing in agitation. So how is it that he gazes here...? Or rather, the course of Nārada is difficult to fathom. Very well, I shall approach him. (Approaching) O Supreme Person! Why do you remain thus after mocking the Great Lord? Moreover, he who was honored by the water of your eyes made you the lord of the entire world.
O Śauri! He by whom you were held within half his body like Gaurī—Sthāṇu himself—is surely an object of laughter.
Nārada—(With anger) Ah, you liar! Why do you suddenly utter such a highly censurable thing? Nandin—

(With anger) Ah, Nārada! It is true that you are fond of quarrels; however, you should not act as an instigator of discord between Hari and Hara. You yourself have just addressed the Lord of Beings (Śiva) in such a manner. Indeed, the Enemy of Kaiṭabha (Viṣṇu) has spoken thus to me with reproach: "Am I a servant of the commands of that Sthāṇu (Śiva)? Do I raise up or humble the Dānavas according to my own will?
Nārada: (With astonishment and agitation) Ah! When did I ever turn back and go into the presence of the Lord of the Universe?

Nārāyaṇa:—(Acting out meditation, with a smile) O son of Śilāda! O Nārada! Enough, enough with this verbal dispute. Surely Hara has been deceived by some illusory Dānava, clever in assuming the form of Nārada. Therefore, let Nandin pay his respects to the Lord who bears the crescent moon on his crest before any great calamity befalls us. I too have come here bringing the Lord Viriñci. Nandin:—
(Aside) As the Lord of the Senses commands. (Exit) Nārada—Go, Nārada! Bring the Blessed One, the Lotus-Seated.
(Then enters Viriñci, followed by the disguised Nārada.
Viriñci—(with anger): Dear Nārada! You are not truly my son Nārada, since you have endured such an insult from the Wielder of the Discus!

Kapaṭanārada—(To himself, with apprehension) What have I heard? Or does he speak thus out of malice? Nevertheless, let it be so. (Aloud) Is it true, dear one, that you conduct yourself with humility toward the blessed Bharga and Govinda? Viriñci—

Excellent, excellent! (Looking all around) Ah! I have indeed arrived at the world of Viṣṇu. What shall I do? (To himself) Murāri is difficult to overcome in battle; it is better that I subdue him with the water of a curse alone. (Aloud) O Nārada! I cannot endure the waste of time with extensive combat; therefore, I shall render Keśava a corpse by means of a curse alone.
The False Nārada—(Remaining silent, to himself, with joy) By good fortune, I shall have accomplished my purpose.
Viriñci: (With a great roar:
That other Lord of the Ocean [is one who] easily leaps across [the world] at the play of the end of the age.

O Kṛṣṇa! That very ocean of curses, which was uplifted by you when you took refuge on the tip of a branch of the banyan tree, and which was embraced by the submarine fire of your wrath— this is some extraordinary Brahmanic power that now rises up as the handful of water offered for your funeral libation.
Kṛṣṇa—(Hearing this, with fear) Ah! What is this? What is this? (He rises.
Nārada—
(Approaching with haste, overcome by delusion) Father! Shame on you! Shame on you! Why do you engage in such improper conduct? Here comes Hari to meet you!
(The impostor Nārada vanishes.
Viriñci—

(Seeing Nārada) What, is this Nārada? (Looking to his side and not seeing the disguised Nārada, he stands with a face cast down in astonishment. Nārāyaṇa: (Smiling and with humility) Noble Grandfather! Cast off, cast off your embarrassment. Even though you are a Yakṣa and a god like me, some Dānava assuming the form of Nārada provoked Hari with a display of arrogance and anger, saying, "Hari mocks you," and sent the son of Śilāda here to insult me.
(Then enters Maheśa, followed by Nandin.
Maheśa— (with remorse:)
Alas! This cruel female black serpent has acted without reflection;
for some unknown being has bitten my heart incessantly, so that it now burns as if pierced by a dart within.
"O Nandin! Tell me, tell me! How did Kṛṣṇa become so provoked by the difficult examples you cited? What did he say? Nandin:

(With humility) O Lord of the fourteen worlds! Why do you speak thus to the Omniscient One? Kṛṣṇa, having already ascertained the wicked conduct of the Daitya, sent me here with a smile even before the invocation of the God of Gods.
Maheśa—(With eagerness) O Nandin! When will my peacock of a mind be freed from its torment by the sight of the dark cloud? Nandin—

(Smiling) Your Majesty is dejected; you do not realize that we have indeed arrived in the realm of Viṣṇu. Does Your Majesty not see Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa, together with Nārada, standing before you? Maheśa—(Approaching with joy and eagerness, and with a jest): Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Even the Creator himself has come here as a witness to our battle. Come, let us fight! (Thus he embraces him).
Kṛṣṇa:
(With humility) O God of gods! Why do you obstruct my devotion with such humility? (He bows.
Maheśa:
"O Blessed Grandfather! This Maheśa greets you.
(The Grandfather remains silent with shame.
Nārada—
"May these seats be graced by you.
Maheśa said:
"May the blessed Viriñci sit in front."
Viriñci—(With a sigh and with humility): O God of gods! Having been deceived by that vilest of Dānavas, I do not deserve such great honor as this.
Maheśa—
O Grandfather! Since this deficiency of ours is equal, please be seated.
(Everyone sits down accordingly.
Maheśa:
(With a smile) Oh, Grandfather! How could you have been deceived by that wretched Dānava?
Viriñci:

(With embarrassment) O Lord of the World! What can I say? I was addressed with lamentation and insulted by someone assuming the form of Nārada, shedding a flood of tears, who said: "The three cities of the Asuras, who were once drops of blood from the sacrifice of your father, now treat the three worlds with contempt. Therefore, uproot them along with him. Then, filled with rage, I went to the world of Viṣṇu. (Sighing) Have I perhaps commenced something improper?
"I have been protected by the Omniscient One, the foremost among the forgiving, Dāmodara. Maheśa:

(With a smile) "I too was approached and provoked by another Nārada, who said, 'Why does Hari mock you, saying, "What is he to me, a mere atom? Thereupon, I was enlightened by Nandin, who came into Keśava’s presence. Having quelled my anger, I have arrived here.
Kṛṣṇa:
(With a smile) Oh! How the one who loves strife manifests a multitude of bodies for the sake of watching a quarrel!
Nārada—(as if with anger, fixing his gaze upon the sky) Well done, O Dānavas! Well done! Mock the lotus-seated Father again and again; he will grant you boons.
Virinchi: O Nārada! Why do you become angry without understanding the situation?
At the conclusion of their sevenfold austerities, the Asuras have attained the difficult-to-attain status of noble Kāmas.
Even the immortals, having bathed and with their souls purified, grant appropriate boons;
yet those demons—who are repositories of sin and whose minds are intent on the destruction of the three worlds—are not slain. Whose tongue is there that can even speak such a thing?
And the boon was taken by them with a condition (*sopadhi*), namely that all three were to be slain as if pierced by a single arrow.
Nārada said:

"For this very reason they move about at a distance of a hundred *yojanas* from one another; thus, they have become truly unslayable. Where is such a bow? Where is such an arrow? And where is such an archer, by whom all three could be pierced with a single arrow?"
Kṛṣṇa:
(With anger) Not so, O Nārada! Will that fierce bow not become exceedingly hard?
Will the arrow not travel for a hundred *yojanas*?
When fate is adverse and obstacles are enraged, what is not unknowable? What is not difficult to endure? And will not even death itself draw near? (10)
Nārada—(With joy) O Kṛṣṇa! Even Fate is angry with you, and the Supreme Lord is angry! Nandin—
(With pride, looking toward the sky and the earth) Ah! Evil omens, foreboding the destruction of wicked Dānavas, are following Kṛṣṇa’s words! Behold, behold!

From the tail and the head, there arise waves of sound—twofold in intensity—produced by the bursting of vessels by the citizens, as the great and terrifying-headed [serpents] move with their bodies at evening.
In that city of the sky-dweller, meteors fall in all directions, creating the illusion of the southern quarter with their masses of thick, blazing sparks.
Nārada—(Looking upward accordingly, with joy): Truly, truly!
These meteors with blazing crests are manifesting in the sky above the city.
Like a lamp for Kāla as he searches for the wicked Daityas. || 12 ||

(Offstage) O you fickle demons! Stop, stop! What is this false display of agitation on your part? Surely these are the terrifying flames falling upon the wicked one as he flees. Indeed, by means of my disguise as Nārada, the guardians of the world, headed by Mahendra, have been thoroughly deceived by me. I truly lamented before them: "Alas, Father Kamalāsana! Alas, Maheśa! Alas, Keśava! How is it that you, who have put the demon Tāraka to rest, must now dwell at the bottom of the netherworld?"

"You too, all you gods headed by Mahendra, go there, go there! Pass the time there by looking at one another's faces. Then the gods, headed by Mahendra, departed immediately without hesitation. May the Lord quickly provide protection for the city and let the principal gods, led by Śakra, proceed as they wish. (Again, behind the scenes:)

"Excellent, O Viparīta, excellent! You are the crest-jewel of our servants. You have made the name 'Viparīta' (the Contrary) truly fruitful, in that the asuras have been made dwellers of heaven and the immortals have been brought to the depths of the netherworld.
Nārada—(With agitation and fear): "Have you heard this?"
Nandī: What is to be heard?
Nārada: Look, look! Immediately after hearing these contradictory words...
Making the sky resound with the dense rows of banners from the demon host, which is unrestrained by the excess of its joy and agitated by the waves of the great neighing of horses;
and turning the circle of the quarters into a mass of fresh clouds with the ichor flowing from his temples— this lord of the Dānavas has indeed set out for the city of Indra.
(Sighing with distress) When will the string of the Ajagava bow produce its twanging sound?
Alas, when will the mace be released, and when will that external weapon be cast forth?
Since those very lords of heaven, Indra and the others, have fled here and there, shame, shame on this long life of the gods! Alas! Heaven is being seized by the asuras! (14)
Kṛṣṇa:—(With great enthusiasm) But Nārada! Why are you so agitated? Even upon hearing the very name of heaven, the Dānavas are as if deaf. (He does not abandon his anxiety. Nandin:—

(Looking upward, with astonishment; to himself) Ah! What is this sudden, great darkness that spreads so abruptly? Surely this must be a magical illusion (*māyā*) employed by Kṛṣṇa, since it approaches the very army of the Daityas. (Aloud) A marvel, a marvel!
Behold, the elephants, having engaged in mutual combat, become agitated;
and the horses, becoming targets for the blows of the tusks of those very elephants, turn upon themselves.
Śakra’s city was far away, and even returning to one's own home became difficult;
behold, behold! In the army of the Asuras, darkness acted like the God of Death. 15.
Nārada:
(With joy) O enemy of the Dānavas! Salutations to you, salutations to you! If you are enraged, even the very name of the Dānavas shall no longer exist;
neither will there be elephants with auspicious temples, nor horses of fierce speed.
There are no noble men, nor stores of sharpened weapons, nor chariots with fierce illusions;
he neither leaps, nor advances, nor strikes, nor brandishes his arms, yet this hero, impelled by the darkness, destroys the host of Dānavas as if through sheer delusion. (16)

(Offstage) O heroic Dānavas! Why are you thus becoming agitated? This is surely darkness sent here by the immortals who have gone to Pātāla. Therefore, let certain Daitya warriors go down to Pātāla, uproot the gods, and obstruct the darkness! And this darkness shall be subdued by me through the illusion of the Kaumudī.
Nārada—(with haste) Oh father! Oh Devadeva! Oh Kṛṣṇa! I shall bring you all today, including Brahmā and the others. Brahmā and the others—
Excellent, excellent!
(Thus they all exit.
The Second Act.
(Then enters Viśadāśaya.
Viśadāśaya:
(Looking ahead) Why is this person seen as if with distinct syllables? (Examining closely) He appears indifferent to me as well; yet why does he seem agitated, as if perceived by rapid steps?

(Then enters Sphuṭākṣara as described. Sphuṭākṣara: Oh, it is the illustrious Viśvadāsa! Therefore, I shall bow to him. (Approaching with humility) Noble Viśvadāsa! I bow to you, who are the cause of the complete pacification of all doubts, out of respect for the King’s command regarding Vatsarāja.
(Thus he bows.
Viśadā—(With a smile) O Sphuṭākṣara! May you live long. Why do you appear so agitated?
Clearly—Noble sir, you who are pure in intent! Why this agitation?
Those who are deluded by rogues do not perceive the jewels that are the essence of truth.
Of those who are unbroken in their vows, yet masters of wealth and addicted to false speech. || 1 ||

Indeed, I have been sent by the Lord of the Dānavas, Sarvatāpana, to investigate the situation of the gods who have descended to the underworld. Having returned, I reported that the great sage Nārada has informed them of the deceptive illusions created by the wicked Dānavas; consequently, all the gods, overcome with grief and filled with rage, are threatening to destroy your cities. Therefore, let a counter-measure be taken. From that moment on, I have been anxious, and so I am going to my own abode.
I see that even the noble lady appears agitated today. So, what is this?

Viśvāmitra—(sighing deeply)—O you of clear speech! I am under the command of my venerable teacher, Bhūgugandana. What can I do? For I would never perform such an act—one that is contrary to family tradition, contrary to sacred knowledge, contrary to one's name, full of deceit, and devoid of merit.
Sphuṭā: (With a seventh confusion. But what has the Noble One undertaken that causes the Noble One to repent in this way? Viśākha:—

O Sphuṭākṣara! Thus have I been entreated for a different purpose by Sarvatāpana. Indeed, O Blessed One, O Lord of pure intent! The city of Indra, presided over by Bharga, Govinda, and Viriñci, is difficult to assail for us. Therefore, let some kind of illusion (*māyendrajāla*) be fashioned by your honor there, so that the gods, fearing its total destruction, might abandon it of their own accord in despair.
Sphuṭā:
Then what was done by my lord?
Enter— [for] even that which has been accomplished appears as if it were of contrary result in such [beings]; [therefore, employ] magic, sorcery, and the like, clearly.
(Samayam) Venerable sir! For their sake, let some other rite for peace and so forth be performed.
Viśvāmitra—(With agitation) O you of distinct syllables! Why this distress over a false ritual?
Other calamities of the minor gods and asuras can indeed be countered,
provided the trident-bearing destroyer of Andhaka remains not provoked.
What is the sequence for the rites of pacification and nourishment?
And I know one means of peace:
in this conflagration of calamity, which has blossomed through the fanning of the wind of misconduct, the service of the pair of Śiva’s feet is the supreme refuge, like the celestial river. (3)

"Having been summoned, all the gods have returned; enraged by the nature of Death (Kṛtānta), they are attacking your cities. Therefore, let some countermeasure be taken! Then, by my Lord Sarvatāpana—who knows what is beneficial and harmful through the heat of his own radiance—I was dismissed with reproach. Distressed by that, I am returning to my own realm. I see that the Noble One also appears as if distressed. What could this be? Clearly, Sarvatāpa, having abandoned false speech, will pursue the truth.

Enter—O Sphuṭākṣara! I have been appointed by the preceptor of the Dānavas to the office of both minister and priest for him; therefore, it is not fitting for me here to remain indifferent. You too are his well-wisher by hereditary right. So, let the distress of this humiliation be set aside. Come, let his welfare be pursued as far as possible.
(Thus, both walk about.)
Sphuṭā:

(Looking about) Noble sir, it is under your command. May the noble one inform you: this elephant of the Dānava king is stationed near Goñūra; and this army of Dānava heroes, led by Sugrahaṇa, is being deployed everywhere around the vicinity of Sarvapāra.
Viśvāvasu: ...
(Looking ahead, with contempt and a gesture of warding off) Is it you, O one of clear syllables?
You who are dark like a shimmering, massive bow-creeper, possessing a multitude of hard arrows,
and terrifying with the display of a lioness at play in the battle against Death?
Let this forest of Diti’s sons’ arms remain unassailed for now, lest the flame of Shiva’s wrathful fire, kindled by his arrow, should suddenly fall upon them here.
Clearly—Noble sir, you who are pure in intention! The lord of the Dānavas is close at hand; the forest fire of his anger is spreading.
(Then enters Sarvatāpa as described.)
Sarvatāpa:
How is it that Viśadāśaya has already arrived? Noble sir! I salute your holiness.
Viśa—
May the lord of the Dānavas, whose body is free from passion, become a vessel for supreme bliss;
may you grace every seat.

Viśa—(Pointing toward Paripārinīpanīta-prāptana, to himself with remorse) Ah! Who is this who has been fashioned as a black serpent, a manifestation of Rāhu that shall silence my throat? Let her go wherever she will, unknown to you. (Aloud) O Lord of the Dānavas! This one, whose syllables are distinct, is clearly distinct; he is supremely beneficial and deserves only the favor of the Lord of the Dānavas.
Sarvatāpa—
(Laughing with pride) "The angry one is speaking in clear syllables! What is to be done?
(Sphuṭākṣara bows and sits down.
Sarvatāpa—
(With longing) Noble Viśadāśaya! Has that been carried out by the noble one? Viśadāśaya:
The banner of Mahendra has been fashioned, its surface strewn with the feet of many-eyed [peacocks].

When I, having composed a hymn of praise to Your glory, was firmly bound with the noose of the Lord of Waters and stood before the rod of Death, I cast myself beneath the peacock of the youthful Śikhaṇḍin, who protects his own with joy, as I was placed upon the Kalpa-elephant. ||5||

And then, from here and there, there arose a tumultuous roar like a vast ocean of visible forces, consisting of illusions. Thereupon, those present there, being well-acquainted with the unfolding of the illusory events created by the gods above, broke into great laughter. And Śambhu, filled with fury, appointed the rending of Krauñca for the purpose of attacking your city. All—(angrily): O you of pure intent! This illusion was performed by me in the very presence of the Grandfather and the other gods, under the pretext that it was a matter of family custom.
Having cut down those banners and victory-flags of the intoxicated world-protectors with their own severed skins,
and having fashioned new ones, I, joined by my forces, shall once again march toward the capital city of the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Enter—(To himself, with dejection) Alas! What a mass of misfortune for the Dānavas, and what a hidden calamity! For this very reason, even the descendant of Bhṛgu does not look upon him.
(Offstage, with pride, in a loud voice)
This city of iron has been melted and reddened by the mass of the sun’s rays, which are made to blaze forth by the winds at the time of universal dissolution;
O heroes of the gods! with your arrows, darts, spears, and chisels, cut this [city] into pieces effortlessly and quickly, as if arranging a collection of *bandhūka* flowers. || 7 ||
Sarva—(Hearing this, with sarcasm and anger): Ah! How is it that this wretched Sūrya is burning Pāvakasahāpura with his solar heat? Stop, you! Stop!
That was another Sūrya; this battle lasts but a moment.
Having escaped from this calamity, may you rise up once more;
today itself, by means of my own radiance, I shall dispel the darkness and cause the world to be free from the sun's heat.
(He attempts to rise.
Viśa:

O King of the Daityas, great hero! Stay, stay! This is but false boasting born of pride on the part of one who has found an opening while having the fire as his ally. What is this excessive agitation?
(The universal heat remains just as it was.
Viśa—(To himself, with apprehension:
This solar heat is indeed burning; how the lunar heat exists is not known! (Aloud: O Sphuṭākṣara! Go and take care that the lunar heat does not [overcome us].
Sphuṭā:—
(With humility) As the noble sir commands.
(Exit.)

(Then, again behind the scenes, with pathos: While the sun scatters its garlands of rays like crests of flame over the world, and the city of the Asuras is being consumed like an iron frying pan in the fiery furnace;
Alas! Like moths drawn to a forest fire, the heroic Daityas, their passion flashing again and again, leap forth and fall repeatedly. || 9 ||

Sarva—(With fury and agitation) Ah! How is it that such an arrogant army of Daityas is actually being consumed by my brother Sūryatāpa? Enough, then, with this exertion of supporting the weight of my arms through anger! (He gesticulates with agitation.
Viśa—
O King of Daityas! It is not proper to remain so close. For those who stay at a distance, death remains far away.
(Sarvatāpana remains exactly as he was.
Viśa—

(With joy) O Lord of the Daityas! Look, look! This iron city of your brother-in-law, having attained the splendor of a flood of vermilion through its crashing impact, is pursuing you across the courtyard of the sky.
All—(with disdain, with joy)
Desiring to seize what is easily grasped, O Noble One, does he wish to burn what is distant?
Or rather, standing upon the deceptive things that lie above,
the Lord of the Daityas climbs toward the very pinnacle of space.
Like the submarine fire arisen from the ocean, having dried it up... || 10 ||
(Aside again:
This city of iron is being forcibly scorched by the flames of fire, which are expanded by the rays of the sun swollen with anger;
and it is filled with the crackling sounds of the burning citizens as they pass along the blazing paths.
This foul odor rises up, offending both the path of hearing and the sense of smell.

[Having heard all this, Patañjali becomes angry. Ah! Now that they have found their opportunity, these sky-dwellers are acting insolently. [Laughing with contempt] Oh, you fools! What is this joy at a time of calamity?
This city has become a mass of glowing coals through the burning heat of the sun; it is now free from the fear of death caused by the dense clouds.
May this [weapon], which was previously cherished for its lack of need for fuel, now consume the enemies by mere touch.
Enter—(with joy) O Lord of the Dānavas! By good fortune you prosper! Behold now what is above:
it bears a dark shadow and a mingling of its own flickering, ruddy luster.

Oh, this city is submerged to the very brim of the sky-stage by the vast quarters resounded with the crackling sounds of flickering flames, and made beautiful by the mass of shimmering smoke that seems to form a union with the Yamunā! 13.

Thus, his burning affliction has indeed been pacified. These Dānavas have become long-lived. All—(with joy): Oh! What heroism belongs to our brother Sūryatāpa, that having endured this calamity of burning, he has rendered this iron city free from danger by plunging into the waters of the Mandākinī! Now, however, it is only the fear of the moon’s heat that troubles me.
(Nepathya) Ah!

How is it that those very women—who once experienced trembling caused by the flower-arrowed god [Kāmadeva], who displayed gestures of contraction when touched by the limbs of their lovers during the preliminaries of love-making, and who uttered sounds of "sītkāra"—now remain motionless out of resentment toward the king of mountains as he hurls down a fierce, icy rain; yet, alas, they did not faint even under the heat of the moon in the city! 14.
Sarva—(Hearing this, with anger) O wicked ones! Why do you thus spread such rumors? For instance, this is like the extinguishing of fire by a moth.
This drying up of the ocean by a forest fire,
this destruction of the royal python by Garuḍa, and this waning of the moon’s heat by the moon itself— [all these are possible]. || 15 ||
(Once more, with pride: Where the submarine fire dwells, where the sun of the evening resides, and where the Halahala poison roams;
While I, the moon, am filled with wrath, you, having sought refuge, must provide protection for that ocean of my chest from the heat of the moon. 16.
O you of pure intention! This [creature] is to be eaten by my kinsman, Rāhu; therefore, there is no fault in me eating it. I shall devour him.
Viśa—

(With humility) O Lord of the Dānavas! May you devour him; or, at your command, let Rāhu himself certainly devour him for the sake of his non-rebirth. However, let Sphuṭākṣara, who was dispatched to the presence of the ascetic Candra, be awaited.
(Then enters Sphuṭākṣara. Sphuṭākṣara—

(With sorrow) Alas! By the perverse nature of fate, even prosperity results in misfortune. Thus, this silver rampart of the Candanavana grove and its silver ornaments have become a source of calamity due to the lack of snow in this snowy season.
All—(Looking with clear vision and recovering from their confusion): O gatekeepers! Is this some ghost approaching me?

Sphuṭā—(With agitation) Oh, my lord! No, no! I am neither a ghost nor a vampire. I am Sphuṭākṣara, the spy of Your Majesty, and I have come here to report the news of Candatāpa. However, in my current state, I can only say this much... [I have seen a battle with frost. Never before have I experienced such a phenomenon arising from the snow. Therefore, may the Lord of the Dānavas grant me some protection.
All—
(With anger) Here I shall consume both the moon and the snowy mountain! (He gesticulates fury.
Viśvāvasu—
(With humility) O Lord of the Dānavas! Enough, enough with this agitation!
Even the moon is subject to waning, and even the snowy mountain has its wings clipped by the Lord of the Universe.
Since you prepare yourself for battle against those two, how can this Salya be a burden of shame? || 17 ||
"Everyone—remaining right here, I shall employ the fire-weapon. (He does so with her.
(Behind the scenes:)

By him, through the fire-weapon (*pāvakāstra*), the distress of the cold was pacified and the lunar heat was, as it were, instantly steadied; alas! [he now sees] the city whose flow of rivers has been driven away by the intense summer heat.
With its powerful streams of silver mud, it quickly consumes those Daityas.
Sarva—(Hearing this, with anger) I shall now discharge the Āgneya weapon! (He does so with her.
Viśa—

Aha! This is a very great peril! By the discharge of the *āgneya* weapon, there will be an overwhelming of the cool-rayed [moon] through separation; moreover, the *āgneya* weapon melts silver. Therefore, go, Sphuṭākṣara! Tell Candratāpa that, having avoided the city of Rājata as the cause of misfortune, he should stay outside and fight outside. Sphuṭākṣara: As my lord commands. (Exit.)

Enter—(indicating the throbbing of his left eye) Ah! What does this throbbing of my left eye portend? May all suffering become the vessel for universal prosperity; and may the preceptor of the Daityas possess unimpeded splendor. (Looking toward the backstage)
O Asuras of Tripura! That power which conquered the three worlds has been woven by the Lotus-born [Brahmā] as a dense and excellent armor;
yet that fuel for the great fire of Kandarpa, bold enough to scorch the three worlds, shall be consumed at the time of destruction.
As long as the third eye on the forehead of the Three-Eyed One does not open even slightly with wrath. || 19 ||
Enter—(looking up with apprehension) What! How is it that Prince Ārū is approaching, accompanied by a vast retinue led by Nandi?
For indeed, the sky is filled with a great clamor, as if by Vetālas as tall as Śāla trees, their voices like the sound of intoxicated palm-clapping, resembling clouds flashing with lightning.
Even when the shouts of the great warriors are drowned out by the joyful cries of peacocks, the peacock of Kaubhara incessantly makes the circle of the quarters resound.
O Lord of the Dānavas! This prince approaches to engage you in combat; take up your bow. (Then enters the prince as described.
All—

(With contempt) Ah! Does this child Viśākha intend to fight Sarvatāpa? (Fixing his gaze upon the sky) Blessed, blessed is the Pināka bow; blessed are your weapons—the trident foremost among them—and your maces, whose handles are fashioned from the skin of a tiger; blessed is your eye, the sun, terrifying with its crest of blazing flames.
O Paśupati! Why have you sent this mere child, fit only for play, into the fray of battle?
(With a sneer) What order or transgression can there be in the death of heroes who treat the battle as a sport? || 21 ||
Kumāra—(With derision) Ah, this lowest of demons, eager for battle with my father! O hero!
Shall I suddenly reduce you to ashes like the God of Love? Or shall I, roaring in combat, swallow the pillar-like trunk of your arms, as I once did those of the enemy Jambha?
I shall now make your body appear like that of Andhaka, covered with the marks of spears and clubs;
O dear one, O best of Danujas, how can such a battle bring you joy? Let us arrange it otherwise.
Sarva:
Oh, prince! You are but a child; I have compassion for you. If you are truly unshaken in battle, then demonstrate your mastery of the bow.
I shall not strike you, O dull-witted son of Śikhivāhana.
"In this deep ocean of battle, I am no savior;
therefore, since your birth took place in that forest of reeds, seek your death in this very forest of battle."
Kumāra— (with agitation) O Dānava, your power has indeed departed; you are merely a possessor of power!
By my power, once I have released it into your heart,
this obsession with your body shall cease;
by my arrows, you will very soon become one who is as good as dead.
(Thus he mimes the showering of arrows.

All—(laughing with contempt): "O Viśākha! Your audacity in such indolence delights me, for I am filled with curiosity; therefore, I shall not string my bow against you. May you sport as you please within my army!"

Nandī—(Aside) Prince! By the boon of Viriñci, the Tripura Asuras are now exclusively immortal; therefore, enough of this fruitless exertion in battle against them. Shatter their strength alone with showers of arrows.
(The Prince does so.)
Nandī—(With joy and exultation) Victory to the Prince! Here, by you, the Dānavas have already been shattered with multitudes of arrows and by means of Vetālas. The Prince—

O son of Śilāda! How is it that those very Dānavas who were slain have returned to life with their weapons raised? What is this? Viśvāmitra: Ho there, heroes of the Daityas! Immerse the warriors who have ceased from battle in the pool of nectar, by which they shall be restored to life and fight with even greater vigor.
(Offstage) This is indeed being done. Does the minister not see that the strength remains undiminished? Prince—
(Soliloquizing) O Sarvatāpa! May that pool of nectar, by which the heroes slain in battle may live once again, ever increase, ever increase for you!
Since my desire for battle has been fulfilled by your warriors, who fight while having abandoned all fear of death, [I am satisfied]. || 25 ||
Nandī—(Aside) Oh, Prince! Fill the pool of nectar with fragments of the golden rampart pierced by the arrows of Agni’s son; otherwise, the Akṣauhiṇīs of the Dānavas will not be diminished.
(The Prince does so.)

(Offstage) With the fragments of the golden ramparts being shattered by the tips of the tridents of Śiva’s trident, the pool of nectar is filled with the sounds of the joyful children; and as they drink the floods of nectar, it suddenly resounds with their cries.
(Offstage) Alas, alas! How indeed can the Dānavas survive in battle,
now that this very onset of universal affliction has entered the army by force?

Enter—(Capable one! O timid ones! Why this agitation? When the delight of the Bhṛgus rejoices, what decline can there be for the Dānavas? O you who are tormented by the heat of the lord of the Dānavas! Reflect upon the venerable Bhārgava; I too shall reflect. (Both act out reflection. (Then Bhārgava enters.)
Bhārgava: (Proudly) I am unexhaustible, I am undrinkable, I am unseizable, and I am imperceptible.
And if there were no illusion (māyā), how could there be the overcoming of death by the Daityas? (27)
"Let the Dānavas, having been restored to life, destroy that army of the gods; this prince, my brother, must be protected above all else. For I have been designated as his son by the Lord Bharga.

Nandī—(With distress) Ah, it is the descendant of Bhrigu who has arrived! Indeed, he has obtained from the God of Gods the power to restore the dead to life. Therefore, his battles with the Danujas now result only in exhaustion. Moreover, it is not proper for me to withdraw the prince from battle without the command of Maheśa.
(Then Nārada enters.
Nārada:

(With pride) Ah, what a jest the Lord of the Universe, Śambhu, has played upon me! For, laughing, he sent me forth with the words: "O you who are fond of strife! Go and witness the tumultuous clash of battle between Kumāra and Sarvatāpa! Even for me, there is no such curiosity now to behold a quarrel. For, while I was only half-satisfied by witnessing the tumultuous battle at Lohapura, I have become utterly satiated by the sight of the slaughter at Rājatapura. Alas! What more can be said of the burning of Lohapura?

The prowess of the wind and fire, the snowfall from the moon and the Himalayas, and the filling of the city of Rājapura with a mass of frost—in all these cases, as well as in the slaughter of the hosts of Asuras who emerged [from it], the wielder of the noose possesses a lightness of hand. What need is there to describe my own martial skill in the taking of so many lives? Therefore, I shall now quickly withdraw Kārttikeya from the battle. (Looking ahead, with joy and wonder) How is it that this Kārttikeya is raining down a shower of arrows upon the station of Viṣṇu?
Ah!
This six-faced one is not superior to his father Maheśa only by virtue of his face;
he is worshipped even with clusters of mandāra garlands by the Siddhas, who have forgotten Śambhu’s valor! (28)

(Approaching him) I shall stop him. (Having approached) O Prince! O son of Śilāda! The Lord Bharga commands you: "This Bhārgava has indeed been accepted by me as a son; why then do you terrify me by afflicting this Dānava who has been taken under my protection? Nandin—(To himself) He has begun exactly what we intended. (Aloud) As the Lord of the Gods commands. (To Kārttikeya) Long-lived one, the father’s command is not to be transgressed; let it be so for now.

The Prince—(To himself, with distress) Alas, what ill fortune is mine, that an obstacle has arisen for this great festival of battle which I have finally attained after so long! (Aloud) (Sighing) As my venerable father commands. (Thus they exit with their retinue.
Śukra—

(With pride, to himself) Ah! Even though the Lord whose banner is the bull is enraged at the Dānavas, his honor toward me is ever-new and fresh. (Aloud) O Lord of the Dānavas, Sarvatāpa! And you, dear Viśadāśaya! Come this way; let us show our favor to the gods who have been oppressed in battle.
(Thus they all exit.
The Third Act.
(Offstage) The sun, whose peacock-feathered arrows have been forgotten, withdraws the mass of darkness;
for there is nothing, whether far or near, that can withstand his steady majesty.

Viśvāmitra:—(Hearing this and waking up) How has dawn arrived? Ah! Who has made me hear such an ill-omened sound so early in the morning? Or rather, it must be some person beginning a hymn of praise... [incomplete]. Therefore, I shall go and perform my salutation at the lotus-feet of my venerable preceptor, Bhārgava.

(Walking about and looking ahead) Here is the venerable Bhārgava... [I perceive him] as if he were a crystal filled with an internal substance that makes it difficult to behold, yet appearing as something turbid. (Approaching suddenly) Venerable Bhārgava! This one salutes you.
Śukra:
O gentle one! Live long!
Viśvāmitra— (with humble courtesy) But why do I perceive the Blessed One as if he were indifferent?
Śukra—
(With distress) O pure-hearted one! I have been defiled by the dejection brought about by the vision of an evil dream. Therefore, I shall now strive to perform some rite for pacification.
(Behind the scenes) By the excellence of our merit, all six have become one.
Now, these very people shall immediately go to their death.
Viśvāmitra:— (Listening) Who is this that has uttered such a riddle through the celestial voice?
Śukra:—

(Acting as if in meditation for a moment) Child Viśadāśaya! This is not the voice of the Sky-Sarasvatī speaking. These Citraśikhaṇḍins, tormented by the Asura Tripura, are striving for its destruction. I have discerned that Maheśa, the [other] gods of the directions, Hari, Viriñci, Krauñca, Arina, the Lord of Mountains, the Lord of Serpents, Candra, Sūrya, and Dharma—all sixteen of them—have girded their loins for the slaughter of the Asura Tripura and have attained unity.
Viśa:
(With distress) Alas! A great calamity, a dire disaster!
Śukra:
My child, Viśadāśaya! It is better not to speak of bad dreams; yet, by the word of the sage, I have been compelled to speak. Listen, sir:

he stands upon a camel, wearing a garment that imitates the young shoots of the *plakṣa* tree, with a garland of *bandhūka* flowers tied tightly upon his head, which serves as a crest for his entire body.
At the end of the night, as auspicious musical instruments resounded loudly, I saw that very same sinner going toward the south, bearing the entire bridal regalia of his marriage. (3)

Therefore, until I return after completing the rite for pacification and the methods for deceiving my enemies—[whispering into his ear]—you must remain here with full attention. Fearing that it might dampen their enthusiasm, I shall depart without informing any of the ascetics. Moreover, these men are not far away and are within range of my power; therefore, you need not fear.
Enter—(sighing sorrowfully).
Let them wander freely from afar; they are not far from death, for the Bull-bannered Lord is full of wrath toward those who are ripe with sin.
O Śukra, do not despair;
whatever is to be done, perform that with a virtuous mind whenever it arises.
O Vatsa, the course of destiny is inconceivable; who can comprehend it? (5)

I also behold the Blessed One, the bestower of boons and the Sustainer, whose fire of wrath was kindled by Nārada, with my eye of meditation. Therefore, go; remain attentive. I too shall accomplish what is desired. (Thus they both exit. Interlude.
(Then Viriñci and Indra enter.
Viriñci—(with despondency): My dear Nārada, why do you distress me?

How could that very river of my speech— which nourishes the trees of the Daityas with its shimmering, supreme nectar— ever burn them like a wave of fierce forest fire? O Lord of Amṛta, by whose compassion for the three worlds the wise [attain] liberation from the cycle of existence!
May that fierce god, with his own fierce instruments of restraint, crush the demons who have ripened for their end by Time.

Nārada: Father, enough with this trembling! This is the power of your venerable command, that these mere insects—the Asuras of Tripura—have reached such a vast multitude; and it is the Lord Bharga alone who deems their destruction difficult to accomplish. Therefore, enough now of this sluggishness born of false deliberation. Let my honored father behold: the earth may indeed serve as the chariot for the Lord, the Master of the Pramathas, when he is the warrior; but, Father, excluding you, who else there is capable of performing the duty of charioteer?
The bow is the king of mountains itself, its string is the serpent-king, and the fittingness of that very [bow] being drawn by him, whose body is like that of Trivikrama, would be truly appropriate.
(Offstage) Brother Nārada! Hurry, hurry to my father’s feet! This blessed Dhūrjaṭi, the driver of the chariot, has already mounted the earth-chariot. Nārada:

(With eager curiosity) Oh, father! Your eldest son Gharma speaks: behold, this most wonderful chariot of the earth has arrived, drawn by horses as swift as the wind; it is being joyfully occupied by the god who is the slayer of Andhaka, the foremost of chariot-warriors, as the spreading mass of rays from the moon and sun forms its wheels.
Simultaneously bearing both sleep and awakening within the lotuses of the celestial Gaṅgā.
And these sons of Aditi, headed by Mahendra, are pursuing them.
Brahmā—(looking with eagerness) Dear Nārada! Come, come! (The two [Umā and Śiva] approach and act out mounting the chariot).
Brahmā— (looking at Maheśa with humility) "Long-lived one"— (leaving this half-sentence, he smiles bashfully)— "O Blessed Bharga! This charioteer of yours bows before you."
Maheśa—(having uttered "Sūta" halfway, with embarrassment) Heaven forbid! I shall approach the Grandfather. Perform the role of charioteer.
(Brahmā assumes the position of charioteer through a gesture.)
Nārada— (With some confusion): He who, though released, does not abandon his target, the wielder of the bow Dhanurdhenu.
Therefore, O dear one, let this Viṣṇu, the wielder of the bow that destroys all afflictions, be saluted.
Brahmā—
(bowing with feigned confusion) My child Nārada! By this arrow of Viṣṇu, the entire world has indeed been pierced.
By his will, the one on the side of the same class either lives or dies. || 10 ||
Vāsudeva—(withdrawing slightly)—He greets the venerable teacher, sir! (They sit down as is appropriate. Maheśa—(looking ahead with astonishment)—Ah, look, look!
A golden city approaches nearby, its fierce rays [blinding us].
It rivals the courtyard of the sky and the foothills of Mount Meru.
Viṣṇu— (with wonder):
Behind that mass of luster, which creates the splendor of the Gaṅgā,
shines Brahmā— (with wonder).
Near him was an iron [object] that caused the illusion of a fresh mass of clouds.
Maheśa:
Oh, what a perversion of intellect among these Dānavas, deluded by the intoxication of their own valor, that they themselves become the targets for a single arrow!
Viṣṇu: [continues]...

(With deliberation) How is it that your ministers of pure intellect are so utterly deluded? Surely there exists elsewhere another true triad of cities; this one, however, is quite different. (Then enters Sarvatāpa, wandering with his retinue through a golden city.
Sarvatāpa:—

(With pride) Noble Viśadāśaya! Look, look at the misconduct of the gods, for another "Triad of Cities" has been fashioned as our rival! Go, you Sphuṭākṣara! Go! Bring back the heat of the sun and the heat of the moon along with their cities! Let this "Triad of Cities" created by the gods be destroyed! Sphuṭā—(Looking ahead) What? Have the heats of the sun and the moon already arrived? Let the noble one behold them!
Sarva—(looking with envy) Excellent, excellent! By these two as well, the illusory Tripurī has been seen.
Viśa—

(Smiling with a meaningful look) O Lord of the Daityas! Why are you so agitated? Turn back the three cities! All—(with anger): Oh, what kind of assistance you provide! A second triad of cities is advancing to fight, and yet you merely laugh!
(With a clear intention, rising with eagerness, he whispers into the ear, "It is exactly so.

All—(with anger): Ah! What is the use of this false whispering into the ear? Who would believe you, you twice-born ones born from a lineage of sages following the gods? If it were indeed so, why did Śukra depart without even speaking to me? By doing this, what benefit have you done us? On the contrary, you have only done us harm. For instance:
If that Śukra were created by Śiva out of Māyā and then had the three cities burnt by him,
then this burning of Tripura would become a supreme reproach against Hara. (12)

"Then, my lady! Please go as you please for now. Whatever is destined to happen among us will come to pass. Viśārada—(aside, with distress): "Surely some misfortune is approaching him. My mind is troubled; let it be exactly so. (Aloud) I shall now depart to the presence of my preceptor. (He exits.)
Maheśa—(Looking at the three cities that have fallen before him, with astonishment): The conjecture of Trivikrama has borne fruit; this other triad of cities has arrived.
Brahmā—
Furthermore, it is not known which of these two is the truth and which is composed of illusion.
Nārada—(with eagerness)—What is the use of this expansion of deliberation! Let her too, who has come within the range of my arrow, be slain.
Kṛṣṇa—(With a jest) It pleases one who delights in strife. However, wait a moment.
All—
(With a roar like the ocean: O heat of the sun! O heat of the moon! Haste! Hasten! Strike! Strike down this city-triad fashioned by the gods! (They act out the discharge of arrow-armour.
Maheśa—(Gazing with wonder) Ah! Behold, behold! (Reflecting)
Is this some darkness born from the birth of the enemy of the gods (Rāhu)?
Is it some canopy of smoke that cannot be dispelled by fire?
Or is it a mass of illusory figures arising from some inauspicious omen?
Is this a flood of arrows emerging from the army of the Asuras? || 13 ||

Kṛṣṇa—(With great astonishment): How is it that the first city-triad has already vanished? Oh, how immense is this delusion, that there is this second Tripurī which sides with the Daityas! Why then has it been driven away by the universal torments and the like? Surely this must be a secret creation of Śukra, undertaken by these arrogant ones who are ignorant of [the true power of] the [first] cities. Very well, let it be exactly as we desire.
All—

(Reflecting with pride) How is it that the illusory Tripurī created by the gods has already retreated? (Looking toward the sky with anger) You there, O gods! Being impotent in the face of the work of war, why indeed, alas, do you resort to deceit?
What are we, the sons of Diti, compared to those various manifestations of yours, whose primary nature is deceit, that have brought about our destruction? 14.
Nārada—(with eagerness)—Why is he waiting now? Let these men be slain while they are still close at hand!
Maheśa—
O Nārada! What occasion is this for valor?
For these [demons], deluded by the fever of pride, will themselves fall upon the path of the arrows; alas! Whose bow shall they seize to slay even them?
Fie on this wretched man who displays such vast ostentation for a trivial task! Fie on the bow, fie on the arrow, fie on this tumultuous battle, fie on the charioteer, and fie on the chariot! 15.
Kṛṣṇa:

(With a sneer) O Kali! Well said by the Supreme Lord. Wait; let the enemies for now remain as difficult to overcome as before. For valor attains its highest excellence when directed against an adversary who is difficult to assail.
Sphuṭā—

(With humility) My lord! This web of deception by our enemy has been utterly shattered. Therefore, let the sun and moon now move about in their respective places as they truly ought. Such is not the way of things that one should remain in a single spot.
All—(With irony) O you of clear speech! You are indeed wrathful. Who is capable of transgressing your word? Do what is appropriate.
"Clearly—
whatever my lord commands. (Having departed, she acts accordingly.)

Kṛṣṇa—(observing with agitation and confusion): O Maheśa! Look, look! Now they have become very far apart; I do not know whether they will remain within the range of the Creator's power or not. Maheśa—
(Exclaiming with joy and rising suddenly) They are already slain! What doubt can there be now? Let the venerable Viriñci drive the chariot with speed.
(Viriñci does so.
Nārada:

(Acting out confusion and expressing bewilderment) Ah! How is it that I do not even recognize myself by this shower of chariot-arrows? Where are my powers of sight and hearing? O Supreme Lord! Then I shall mount Kailāsa and behold the circle of sages, who are jewels among men, as they gaze on with curiosity. (He does so, moving through the air.
Nārada—(Looking ahead with wonder):
The arrow of Hari, the destroyer of Andhaka, triumphs;
its splendor of velocity does not fall within the range of words.
As if reaching some other target altogether, it becomes the mark itself.
Furthermore, his path was obstructed by those three cities. || 16 ||
Noble Dharma! Look, look! Your eyes have been opened to the noble truth! Indeed, this triad of cities is burning simultaneously by the fire of Śaṅkara’s arrow.
Dharma—(looking with satisfaction): Excellent, excellent!
This fire of the Tretā age, its vast enmity toward the obstacles of the former sacrifice well-known, having found its opportunity,
devours by force the triad of cities, formidable with its blazing flames, through the power of Śambhu.

(Offstage) Causing the touch of the untouchable, forcibly overturning the established order of castes, making the world boundless in its grief, turning it into a scene of weeping and wailing, and leaving it bewildered and fleeing in all directions—
Obstructing the path of the virtuous and acting without hesitation toward the destruction of children, young women, and elders—alas, what a calamity!
Like a wicked master, this fire swiftly brings about the dissolution of the cities; fie upon them! 18.
Moreover, he resorts to his bed like one who is weary; he occupies the auspicious throne like a king;
he enters the inner chamber like a lover; and he obstructs the quarters of the sky like an enemy.

"O Hero, this one who, consisting of fire, devours at will multitudes of horses and elephants—'Who is this? Who is this?'—Alas, fie upon you, O Lord! For the sake of the three cities, such a one has been created by you! (19)
The Sages:
(Hearing this, with joy) By good fortune, we have heard what was to be heard.
Nārada: —
(Looking around with joy) Noble sirs, I am distraught; I do not see the gods!
Sages—(With apprehension) Dear Nārada! Look around, look around!
Nārada—(Acting out distress) Noble sirs! What am I to discern?
These smokeless peaks are clad in armor.
A vast expanse of flames rises as high as the peak of the golden mountain;
sparks, tawny like the beaks of very young parrots, [fly] in the sky.
I perceive nothing else at all in the fourth state. 20.
The Sages:
(Looking ahead with joy) Ah! You are agitated by fear. Do you not see the Destroyer of Tripura approaching, mounted upon his chariot and surrounded by all his attendants?
(Then enters Maheśa as previously described. Maheśa:
O Blessed One, Eldest of the Gods! Halt the chariot! Let us stay right here on this very spot of Kailāsa, which is graced by the presence of the sage Nārada.
(Brāhmā does so. Nārada and the others approach with humility and bow.
Maheśa:
O gods! All of you, descend from your aerial chariots and sit according to your rank. And may the venerable sages also be seated.
(All the Kṣatriyas do so; at that moment, Maheśa remains bashful.
Nārada—(with pride)—O Lord of the World! What reward do the gods consider appropriate for you here for this marvelous deed?
O you who are crowned with the new moon, if you were worshipped with freshly severed lotuses from one's own head, it might be considered appropriate;
yet, alas, even that does not please you, O Śiva!
What can we do here for one who is solely intent on protecting the three worlds? || 21 ||
Maheśa—(with a bashful smile): O Nārada!
Vaikuṇṭha, Padmajanman, the leader of the gods, the protector, and the lord of the departed spirits—
Rākṣasa, Varuṇa, Kubera, Vāyu, Sūrya, Candra, Kumāra, Dharma, Śeṣa, and the King of Mountains—even I am fickle as the sixteenth;
O Nārada, why do you thus boast of me alone in the matter of destroying Tripura? (22)
Indra:—
(With humility) O gods, you employ your own limbs as you please.
You alone are the Puruṣa worthy of praise; what is the use here of calculating distinctions?

Maheśa—(To himself) Ah, this shame makes me shrink; therefore, I shall dismiss the gods. (Aloud) O venerable deities! Please remain as you wish and as is comfortable to you, and command what I should do now.
Indra—
(With humility: Even these Daityas have been cast aside by you like defects;
the worlds shall remain imperishable—what more, then, could possibly be requested now? (24)
Nevertheless, let this be:
may the hearts of the virtuous have the darkness of delusion dispelled by you, through the radiance of the eye on your forehead, which flashes with the brilliance of the crescent moon.
(Thus they all exit.
The Fourth Act.
Thus ends the work titled *Tripuradāha*, composed by the great poet Vatsarāja.
The *Hima* is concluded.

May the crest-moons of the Lord, whose rays spread across the expanse of his broad mass of matted hair and imitate the streams of the celestial river (Ganges) upon his head, bestow auspiciousness upon you— these rays being the crest-jewels of comedy, a farce (*prahasana*).
Seeing whom, Hara broke into a radiant smile as he incessantly and in vain brandished his trunk before Heramba, who was distressed by the heavy burden of rut-heat. || 1 ||
Moreover,
your arms are most numerous for the sport of embraces, your eyes are full of longing for gazing, and your faces are many for the act of kissing.

"Who am I to you, who are ever engaged in the playful dalliances of many earthly wives?"—may Hara, smiling as he was thus addressed by Śivā with words that were contrary to his own anger, protect you. || 2 ||

(At the end of the *nāndī*, the Stage Manager—looking toward the sky) Ah! The night has truly dawned. (Looking toward the western quarter) Oh! Indeed, everything is beautiful at this very hour. For instance:
Those who at that time filled this entire universe with the abundance of fresh *vikaṅkata* garlands made of passion—
even now, they remain settled upon the peak of the western mountain.
The rays of the moon bear the appearance of a mass of grey hair.
Ah! Even for me, who am subject to the offense of old age, this application to acting is truly a cause for laughter.
(Entering) The Assistant:

Sir, this is indeed a source of laughter, for our lord, surrounded by a circle of learned ministers as if they were gathered for the great festival of the Nīlakaṇṭha pilgrimage, is having the farce named *Hāsyacūḍāmaṇi*, composed by his own minister Kavirāja Vatsarāja, performed before him.
Sūtradhāra:
(With feigned indignation) Ah! I am truly favored. This very lord is the sole vessel for the skill of discerning dramatic works. (Shaking his head in astonishment)
In the houses of the learned, he has always forcibly made the daughter of the ocean his slave through the constant sport of giving, out of a deep-seated enmity toward her rival wives;
this King Paramardideva is truly a boundless treasury of knowledge, and the divine Goddess of Speech herself has surely assumed a male form.

Mārpa! Therefore, go and have the musicians prepare themselves. My heart's desires are now fulfilled, for in this assembly there are those blessed with noble wisdom and goodness, and the King of Vatsa, who is fond of speech that delights in aesthetic flavor.
This actor too is proficient in the gestures of drama; surely some mass of my own past merit has come to fruition for me.
(From behind the scenes, a song is sung:
Having been shaken by the thief of uneven darkness, the Fortune of the Sky,
seeking her own protection, follows the Blessed Sun.

Sūtradhāra—(Hearing this, with joy) My dear friend! These actors are indeed skilled, since this introductory song of the deceitful harlot is being sung. Come, let us two perform what must be done next. (They both exit.
(End of Prologue)

(Then enters Kapaṭakeli, who has risen from sleep. Kapaṭakeli—(Reflecting) Oh, it has become dawn! Indeed, the young rays of the sun, dripping with the nectar-streams of the eastern river, have already passed through the lattice-windows. How is it that for me, languid from the weight of drinking wine and lying in a single deep sleep, the night has slipped away? (Acting as if remembering, with joy and longing) Ah, the sweetness of the wine of the evening twilight! Therefore, I shall fetch it this very moment. For a delightful thing, once experienced, is never forgotten.

The serpent is enamored [of her]. Because of this theft, a quarrel has been provoked in our house. (Aloud) Kusumikā! Therefore, I shall reveal this through the mouth of some wise man. There is here, in the old garden temple, a holy man named Jñānarāśi, who is skilled in the knowledge of a Kevalin. I shall go to question him, so that when the watchmen strike their mallets, he too may become an accomplice. Kusumikā—

Moggallāna! Moggallāna! Wake up, wake up! (The servant lies there just so. Truly, he is fast asleep; even the peacock would have to wake him. Kapaṭa: I know the secret charm for this purpose. Moggallāna! Moggallāna! Wake up, wake up! Bring that well-prepared bitter liquor!
Servant:
Kṛṣṇamiśra! Take the vessels, take them!
Kapaṭa—
Vatsa Mūrkharaka! Come, let us both go until Kusṛmikā returns with the vessels washed. (He walks around.
Servant:
Mother, why have you moved away from here to somewhere else?

Kapaṭa—(With distress) Muggara! Have you not heard the news concerning your own household? That house, which has long been a treasury overflowing with wealth, has today been plundered by thieves. Therefore, I shall go to ask the venerable Nāṇarāsi, who dwells in the garden grove and possesses the knowledge of a Kevalin.
Ceṭa:—

(To himself, with pride) Live on, you thieves! Live on! May this deed of yours result in a happy rebirth. Indeed, this woman does not deserve even a mere touch from a libertine like me when he is impassioned! This quarrel has been provoked by this harlot against my very eyes. Kusumikā! I shall reveal this to the mouth of some wise man! There is here, in the old garden monastery, a venerable one named Jñānarāśi, who is skilled in the knowledge of a Kevalin.

I shall go to ask him about it. Wake up Mudrāraka so that he too may become an attendant. She is setting in motion a succession of calamities for the master of the house. (Aloud, as if with distress) Alas, alas! Mother, what has happened? The loss of wealth does not afflict me as much as the reproach that my wife has been stolen. Indeed, it is heard that fire is consumed by something; or rather, the loss of wealth is due to fate, not a reproach.
For thus, in the presence of the citizens who do not know [the truth], she steals away all his property.
"In jest, our mother said, 'How can a thief be like a father? (8)
Kapaṭa:
Mudgaraka! When everything has been destroyed, what time is this for speaking words? Let some remedy be applied now.
Mudgaraka: [He acts.]

I shall perform the funeral rites. (Looking toward the sky) Ho there, citizens! You shall not, you shall not disregard the death that has been brought about by your own mother, who is devoted to righteousness!
Kapaṭa—Boy, boy! Why do you speak such nonsense?
Servant:
I think it is well. By good fortune, this mother of hers, who has deceived the entire world with her magic, has been plundered by thieves.
Kapaṭa—
(With anger) Moggallāna! You do not restrain your own mouth, which is a gateway for excrement!
(He strikes him with a slap.
Servant:—
(Stepping back with embarrassment) Mother, you are angry whether there is a connection [to my fault] or not. I will not go with you.

Alas for my hopes! Even for a mere moment, this hellish household ceases its succession of misfortunes for people like us—thus she speaks, provoking me. Woe, woe, Mother! What is this that has happened? The loss of wealth does not afflict me as much as this humiliation that even my noble mother has been robbed. Indeed, it is never heard that fire has been quenched by foam. Or rather, the loss of wealth is subject to fate; it is not a matter of humiliation. And so it is said:
"Right before my eyes, he has plundered the entire wealth of the worlds of men;
tell me, who is this thief like our mother who steals with such ease?"

Kapaṭha—(As if with compassion) Moggallāna! Moggallāna! Come here, come here for a moment; now that the entire year has been obtained, the festival of wine must be celebrated. (Taking him by the hand, he walks about.
Servant—
(Looking all around) Oh, behold the splendor of this garden adorned by the onset of spring! Mother, look at this!
Like a drunken serpent, this bee is crawling step by step;
for that very reason, these vine-dancers laugh with their blossoming mouths. (9)
Moreover,
the intoxicated Rolamba female bees sing the song of the God of Love;
yet even they, stirred by the wind of their own minds, dance along with the creepers in the manner of a king's court.
Kapaṭa—(Reflecting) Muggaraka! To my heart, which is heavy with grief, spring does not seem right.
Servant—
It belongs not only to you, (pointing with his finger) but to her as well. For thus she remains silent due to the emptiness of her arms, having cast off her floral ornaments;
she appears like a jasmine creeper being plundered by the thief Spring. 10.
Kapaṭamugara:
Go now, disguised as yourself; what is that venerable man doing while staying in this temple? As for me, I shall remain right here.
(The servant does so and approaches.)
Servant:
Master, there are two or three shaven-headed fellows here who engage in verbal sparring; whatever one says, the other immediately retorts to him.
Kapaṭa—

Muggeraka! That blessed one is staying there, teaching his disciples. Therefore, let us stay right here until his lesson is finished. (They do so. (Then enters the Blessed Kauṇḍinya, teaching his disciples.
Jñānarāśi:
"Ah! Are these two verses of yours already committed to memory?
Disciple:
"O Nāṇarāsa! They have now entered into my stomach."
Jñānarāśi:
(With anger) You fool! You address me by my name!
Disciple: [He speaks.]
"But does sin accrue from uttering your name?
Jñāna:
"Fie on you, fool! One does not utter the names of one's gurus."
The disciple:
How can he take the name of the mountains?
Jñāna: [He does.]
The teachers are not to be saluted with prostrations and the like, but rather as "the venerable Upādhyāya-pāda"; thus you should address me.
Disciple: O Teacher!
These two verses have both entered into my heart.
Having gazed upon you, who are so beautiful, and having reflected again and again upon all your limbs, this one thing alone has been established:
that women are always to be meditated upon. (11)
Jñāna—(With anger) Fie on you, fool! You have confounded me by reversing the order of the syllables.
Disciple—
"O Uañjhāa! Why are you angry? Just as the verse was written by you in white pigment, so has it been read by me. (He shows the surface of the leaf.
Jñāna—(Laughing) "Fool! You have misread the letters; read that second line again!"
The disciple said:
Homage to you, O pale one-eyed one! Homage to you, O scorcher of the universe!
Homage be to you, O treasury of falsehood, the sole creator of great beings! || 12 ||
Jñāna—(With anger) Ah, you wretch! You mock me, whose eyes are as pale as flowers! (He prepares to strike.
Disciple—

(Stepping back in agitation) Why do you strike me? These teachers, the masters of laughter, cannot tolerate their own disciples possessing a superior excellence of intellect. Therefore, I shall depart for now!
Jñāna—(to himself) This man knows my weak point; it is better that I win him over. (Aloud) Dear Kauṇḍinya! Come here, come here!
Disciple:
(With agitation) Sir, I shall come. You are indeed of a fierce disposition.
Jñāna:—
"Kaṭha-iṇḍinya! Enough of this agitation regarding my fierce nature. Behold: the king, having taken up the rod of punishment, protects all people;
like the sun, he brings happiness to the world by assuming his scorching form."
Even a teacher may act harshly when instructing his disciples; for those who possess hearts that have reached maturity, such a turn of events is indeed appropriate.
"Come, I shall teach you again once you are purified. (Having thus comforted him, he makes him recite:
"Having surveyed all the scriptures and having reflected upon them again and again, this one conclusion alone has been reached: Mārāyaṇa is to be meditated upon at all times. (14)
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one! Salutations to you, O creator of the universe!
May there be salutations to you, O Lord of the heart-lake, O primordial ancestor of the Great Puruṣa! || 15 ||
(Śiṣya likewise recites. Jñāna—(with anger) You fool! Recite thus!

The Disciple—(reading again with purity and with despondency): O Teacher! This meditation of yours is composed of very harsh syllables. Nothing at all is accomplished by this. Therefore, teach me the Kevalī-vidyā, so that wealth may come under my own control from the people.
Jñāna—
(With disgust) You fool! Shame on you, shame on you! You are tormented by a craving for enjoyment. Oh, what delusion!
A deer generally avoids snares with great effort, yet through its own negligence, it becomes suddenly entangled and overwhelmed with grief.
Alas, the world is deluded; it rejoices all the more as it fastens the nooses of sense-objects, which are inherently treacherous, around its own neck.
The disciple:
The Arhats speak thus; yet you do not know the *kevalī-vidyā*.
Jñāna—
"Be silent! I alone know the absolute truth, but it brings no good," she said, and thus she was disregarded.
For instance, although she had performed purification through divine means, her father was killed by a thief because of her false speech.
My brother, while digging for a treasure trove, was bitten by a black cobra and perished;
furthermore, due to his failure in the science of warfare, he was sought to be slain by the king.
Thus I have become a venerable one, yet this Kevalī is indeed our family enemy and a source of ruin.
Śeṣya:
(Laughing) I have already recognized the extent of your threefold prowess and the majesty of your knowledge. Therefore, let me know that secret which is as dear to you as your own life.
Jñāna:
(With a smile) You fool! You are talkative; you do not deserve to be a disciple of Kevalin.
Disciple—(Laughing with intent) Preceptor! What have I done to offend you by my talkativeness?
Jñāna:

Kauṇḍinya! You are indeed our very self. Therefore, listen to the conduct of the foremost among those who possess exclusive knowledge (*kevalin*). For what would be the use of words? "Our fruit is [already] manifest"—such would be the grasp of hidden pride.
When questioned, one should utter indistinct and faltering words and not declare a definitive conclusion.
Having observed that the matter is already accomplished, one should say repeatedly, "This was certainly decided by me previously," and one should approach some deceitful witness to assist.
Moreover,
with a mind agitated by anxiety, you surely did not compose a worthy question; at that time, you did not correctly grasp the meaning of what was heard from me.

"By your lamp, this delusion regarding the fruit has arisen; for our knowledge is indeed absolute, and it does not waver even at the end of an aeon"—thus might one who is truly wise convince a person who is wavering. (19)
Disciple:
O Teacher, something is certainly becoming clear.
Jñāna—
(Looking toward the tiring-room with apprehension) You fool! Stop, stop! Some woman accompanied by a single man is approaching from this direction.
(Then enter Kapaṭakeli and Mudgaraka. Mudgaraka:—
Attā! This vessel is indeed well-suited for a drinking party. Kapaṭa—(angrily) Come now, keep quiet!
Let it be; let us proceed with confidence for now. (Aloud) Kauṇḍinya!
Like Brahmā, I know the death or the life of a living being;
like Śiva, I shall lift up from the surface of the earth this world whose heavy burden has been stolen away.
I know all the deeds of the world as its inner self; and I cause you to attain that which has been stolen by thieves, as if it were clarified butter held in my own hand.
Kapaṭa—(Spitting with joy) Muggara! Listen, listen to the nectar-like words of the venerable one! Come quickly! (Thus they both approach.
Kapaṭa—
"Venerable sir! I bow to you.
Mudgaraka:
"I too bow to you."
Jñāna:
May there be prosperity for both of you. Please be seated.
(Both sit down.)
Kapaṭa—(With humility) Venerable sir! May you restore to me all my property that was stolen during this night.
Disciple:
(With agitation) Ah! What is being suggested? Today the teacher did not go anywhere after leaving the palace at night.
Kapaṭa—(Covering his ears with agitation) Heaven forbid! I suggested that he should have the thief apprehended by means of his power of supernatural knowledge.
Jñāna—(With a smile) Kauṇḍinya! Stop, stop! (To Kapaṭakeli) Noble lady! Such knowledge as this is unbecoming of us. Kapaṭa—

(With humility: "O Blessed One, ocean of the essence of compassion, who else but you is the refuge for a destitute person like me? And that accumulation of wealth has been obtained; it shall indeed become yours alone. Jñānagāśin:—(To himself, with pity: "My desire has already been accepted by her. Nevertheless, I shall merely act out the state of being indifferent."
"I do not know, I do not grasp; what use have I for this anxiety?
This very non-acceptance is the great fruit for those who are hypocritical. (21)
(Aloud) O auspicious lady! I have accomplished all that was to be done simply by your desire. Kauṇḍinya! Hand over the book of Kevalin; I shall determine whether there will be gain or loss.
Disciple—(Bringing forward the book) Let the offering of cakes for the Kevalin’s book be made first.
Muṭūraka:—
(Rising suddenly) I shall bring flowers!
Disciple:—
"O blessed one! With gold or jewels, a *kevalī* becomes a *pūjā* of cloth.
(Kapaṭakeli looks at the face of Jñānarāśi.
Jñāna—
(To himself, with satisfaction: Kauṇḍinya deserves to be a disciple of the Kevalin’s secret doctrine. (Aloud: Noble lady! It is exactly so.
One who possesses faith should determine gain from gain by means of gains.
Having honored the Kevalin, who shines like gold and jewels, Manu declared this. (22)
"If there are no [real] flowers, let these [artificial] ones suffice.
Kapaṭa:
"Noble sir! Let the side of the foolish be adopted! (He worships the book with his ring.)

Jñāna: Kauṇḍinya, take this; you shall distribute it among the monks. Disciple: [Asks: "How so? Jñāna: "Take this; you shall distribute it among the monks. Disciple: [Asks: "How so? (To herself) Ha! I know you; you speak with your lips, not with your heart. (Aloud) As the teacher commands. (She takes the ring.
Jñāna—(Opening the book) Ah! I shall now draw the planetary diagram (*grahakuṇḍalī*). (Gestures as if writing.)
If the son of the Sun (Saturn) sees Vyatīpāta situated in the twelfth house,
and if Rāhu is the "breaker of the cart" (occupying the seventh house) and Ketu is situated in Aries, [the result is as follows].
When the Sun is in the ascendant with Mars and is aspected by malefic planets,
one should certainly declare in the inquiry the loss of wealth and the body.
And this is not the right occasion for it. At any rate, there is the recovery of a lost object.
Kapaṭa—(with joy) By the favor of my noble sir!
Disciple:
(With astonishment) Oh! How great is the power of the teacher’s knowledge! All the verses of Śālihotra have been placed upon his throat.
Jñāna—
"Kauṇḍinya! Go from here and bring Upaśruti.
Disciple—(Exiting and re-entering): "Go away yourself, you slave! Go away yourself!"
Muhūraka—(Rising with agitation) Ah! You rogue of a mendicant, why do you revile me? Wait, wait! With your own shaven head, I shall perform the worship of the Jina’s image!
Disciple:
(Frightened) O Brahmin, O Brahmin! This woman has indeed been brought here by me. Truly, truly, I am not reviling you.
Kapaṭa—O Muggaraṇā! You do not restrain your own mouth, which is a gateway to evil.
Jñāna:
O gentle one! Stop, stop! This is not an insult; it is a salutation. Now, having accepted this salutation, please come here.
Mudgaraka:
"You are deceiving me! You are indeed deceiving me! Jñāna—(as if with apprehension)—Ah! What are you prattling?
Mudrāraka:
Noble sir! This is what I have heard.
Jñāna—
(Miming the sound of a lisp) Kauṇḍinya! This letter *gha* belongs to the *ya*-group.
Disciple:
But I know it as belonging to the *sa*-group.
[The Teacher asks: "Regarding that knowledge—how many measures (mātrās) does it have?
The disciple [replies]:
Five. As for knowledge— how many [instances] of the *anusvāra* are there?
Disciple:
As much as you are able to write.
Jñāna: [writes].
First, thirteen; then, with thirteen and five, it becomes twenty-two.
The pupil:
No, no, it becomes twenty-six.
Kṛpaṭa:
Indeed, there are eighteen. Let the noble sir inform [the King].
Jñāna:—

(Reflecting to himself) Ah, this woman is clever at calculation; well then, I shall finish it however it may be. (Aloud) My good lady! Our tradition of calculation is quite different. Therefore, first provide the names of the members of your household.
(Mudgaraka writes down names such as Kapaṭakeli, Madanasundarī, Udbhaṭakroḍa, Chapparāvat, and Kusumikā.
Jñāna—

(Writing it down, to himself) Since this "Deceitful Play" (*kapaṭakeli*) must be suspected as being well-suited for theft, it was brought here first by Īyer. Therefore, I shall have it performed right now. (Gesturing as if counting, aloud) This "Deceitful Play" appears to have been stolen.
Mudgaraka:
(Laughing loudly with joy) Well done, noble sir! You have recognized her very self; she is indeed the one who steals our house!

(Kapaṭakeli stops him with a smile and a sidelong glance. Jñāna—(Reflecting; to himself, with apprehension): By this mutual display of laughter, it is determined that this is indeed Kapaṭakeli. This is not good. (Reflecting and acting out a memory): Her daughter is the courtesan Madanasundarī, whose heart is solely devoted to the casket of the arts. These two, Kokila and Pārāpata, are her servants and practitioners of theft and gambling. So be it, for now.

(Aloud, with a feigned air of playfulness: "My dear lady! The thief has been identified, and your name was mentioned merely for the sake of concealment. You may now depart for your home. You must request the cuckoo and the pigeon with great secrecy.
Kapaṭa—(Aloud, with pride: "May my noble lord grant me leave."
Jñānabhadrā: "My dear lady, please go ahead. For one must not become angry over that which is destined to be obtained. (Kapaṭakeli exits with Mudrāraka.)
The Disciple:—
(Offering the ring) May your honor adorn yourself with this.
Jñāna:—
(As if with agitation) Kauṇḍinya! What is this delusion? Look, look!
Time, whose heart is solely intent on the conjunction of old age, death, disease, and calamity, brings about its perversion at every moment.
On her stainless body, the application of ornaments is superfluous;
in her house, where the great drum resounds, the lutes produce only discordant notes. || 25 ||
