The Disciple: (Laughing) Teacher! I am indeed your disciple. Why do you deny me? Here, take it.
(He puts on the ring from Jñānaśirī’s finger.)
The Disciple—(smiling significantly and joining his palms in reverence)—O Blessed Ring! Homage to you! May you remain right here, in the hand of the Teacher.
Jñāna—

(With feigned anger) Ah, you villain! You who are loquacious with false chatter! Have my misfortunes truly been forgotten? (Acting out the recollection, with a start) Kauṇḍinya! Your words have reminded me of my request for the *kalākaraṇḍaka* charm. For that gambler, whose entire wealth has been lost, desires to win back his fortune through the power of my mantra. He has great confidence in us. Therefore, come, let us go to a secluded spot suitable for the recitation of the mantra.
This garden is a place where one might easily escape the pursuit of the relentless courtesans.
Disciple: ... [The disciple speaks].
Therefore, come this way, come this way, Preceptor! (Thus they both exit.
End of Act One.

(Then enters Jñānarāśi, intent on the recitation of mantras, and his disciple. Disciple: O Teacher! Much time has been spent in the recitation of mantras. I think that even the Lord of the Kalāpakhaṇḍa, the breaker of the game of dice, would not have delayed the power of this mantra so long. Therefore, come, let us go to the garden itself; my limbs are burning from the intense heat of the midday sun.
Jñāna—(pausing his recitation): This is indeed so.
This flood of light is truly fierce and formidable, like a cruel demon.
It can be countered by those who are deeply affectionate, learned in the scriptures, and possessed of excellent wisdom. || 1 ||
"Come, let us go. (They both exit.
Disciple:
"This is the garden. May you enter, sir. (He acts out entering.)

The Disciple—(having walked a few steps and looking before him, not yet having reached him): "O Teacher! Look, look! Here in the Mādhava pavilion, some woman stands absorbed in meditation just like the Teacher. Another also stands by her side, carrying sandalwood and flowers for the purpose of worshipping the deity.
Jñāna—
"Kauṇḍinya! Let us sit right here by this red-ashoka tree. What is the use of the mādhavī bower?
(The disciple sits down—[reflecting, to himself with wonder and derision]: "Oh, the teacher! Oh, the teacher! Indeed, he is being watched very well by one standing right here!")
(Then Madanasundarī and a maidservant enter as previously described.
Jñāna—(Looking, to herself) Oh! The perfection of her beauty! For instance:
Washing away the harsh words of cruel discernment with the waves of her loveliness, this long-eyed maiden suddenly reveals the deity Kandarpa even within the heart of me, a man of self-restraint.
Maid: Mistress!

This yellow sandalwood paste, which was handed over by the artisan, seems to be yearning for contact with your limbs. And this jasmine creeper, which has long been united with you and whose fragrance is not to be found elsewhere, is clinging to you as if it were its divine support. Furthermore, this betel-roll, held in your lotus-like hand, is languishing as if exhausted, as if distressed by the turning over of your lips. So, what is this distress of your heart at a time when joy should be the occasion for allaying your fever?
Madanasundarī— (not hearing him, sighing long and hot, and resorting to Sanskrit): Feeding upon the poison of mango buds, the bees continue to live.
The throats of female cuckoos are scorched by the fire of the thundering sound of the clouds;
these creepers do not faint from the sandalwood breezes or the winds of the Kālakūṭa poison.
Fie upon the incompetence of my servant’s heart! Though pierced by the arrows of Love, I still live. (3)
Jñāna:
Kauṇḍinya! What is there for us here, who are without support? Come, let us go. Kauṇḍinya: [responds].
"O Teacher! Stop, stop! Your ears, scorched by difficult study, find relief in their sweet conversations.
Jñāna—(To himself) Mine as well. (Aloud) Kauṇḍinya! You who long for the chatter of courtesans dressed as painters are weary of your studies.
(The maid recites "O Mistress Maṭṭinī," and so forth. Madanasundarī likewise acts out her anxiety.
Maid—(Taking her by the hand): Mistress Madanasundarī! Why do you utter such inauspicious words? Do you not accept the gift of ornaments? Will you see only such a performance as this?
Madana—(With wonder and joy) Friend! Where is that gambler?
Maid—

"Madam! He, who has indeed conquered the pride of the Samalajūtaka gamblers, will celebrate with you the festival of the drinking party in the Madana garden. Furthermore, it was reported by my keeper of the Madana garden that the casket of ornaments sent by you has been placed in the hands of his mother as a pretext for a private meeting.

Therefore, Navamālikā, even this betel-roll held in your lotus-like hand seems to languish, as if distressed by the kisses upon your face; it is fainting away. So why is there such agitation in your heart at this very hour of the onset of spring? Madana—
(Rising with longing) Dear friend! Come, come, embrace me! (The servant girl embraces her.
Disciple: O Preceptor!
May this fire burn us! Look, look at the good fortune of this woman, that she is being embraced by Madanasundarī!

Jñāna—(To himself, with longing) Kauṇḍinya has spoken rightly. (Aloud, as if in anger) Hey there! What are you prattling? Ah, you wretch! I shall extinguish the fire of your insolence with the water of a curse! (He reaches for the water in his water-pot.
Disciple—
"Why do you pour out the water from your water-pot? You will suffer from the thirst of midday. I know your power.
Jñāna:
"Fool! Though you have perceived the dissolution at the end of the dense play of deception, you do not believe it."
Disciple:
By your very first word, "I am stolen by Kavaḍakeli," I have been captivated.
Madana—
(With impatience) Come, let us go right there and wait for the gambler.
(Rising and taking the handmaiden by the hand, he walks about.
Disciple:
"Cease this quarrel over the forest fire! Look, look, she is going away!
Jñāna—(looking, to himself, with longing and regret): "How is it that she is actually departing?"
Just as this fickle-eyed woman, like a shadow of the tree of passion, departs far away after having released [her hold],
so too does this [fever] forcibly seize my limbs in that very same manner.
Alas! He embraces [the world]; how difficult his majesty is to withstand! || 4 ||
Disciple: O Teacher!
You are like the sun, whose fierce heat is difficult to endure. Therefore, come, let us enter this very Mādhavī bower. Here alone, meditation, concentration, and the rest will be possible.
Jñāna—

(To himself, with joy and longing) May my dear child live long! Kauṇḍinya has expressed what was in his heart. (Aloud) As it pleases my child. (Both act entering. (Reflecting to himself with pride) Ah, this is that very altar, honored by the embrace of Madanasundarī. Therefore, I shall recline upon it for now. (He acts out lying down with effort. Disciple:—
"Let the teacher here perform as he wishes the meditations, dhāraṇās, and so forth.
Jñāna—(with inner distress, to himself): Whence has this come to me now? For instance:

My sighs have become choked; where indeed is that speech which was the obstacle to the restraint of my breath? That name itself now touches me only occasionally; where is that constant muttering of prayers?
My mind has been seized by her and has gone elsewhere; the Lord who slew Kaiṭabha has bestowed another initiation upon me today—the God whose bow is made of flowers.
"And this all-pervading fever of mine grows more intense; therefore, I shall honor this very cool altar with my writhings. (She does so.
Disciple—(As if with agitation) Why does the Teacher roll about in this manner?
Jñāna—(with a shudder) My dear Kauṇḍinya! My limbs are tormented by a terrible fever.
Disciple: [He listens.]
(Miming a touch) Oh, what a terrible fever this is! Surely you yourself know the mantra for curing fever; so why do you suffer?

Jñāna—(Reflecting to himself) Ah! For one afflicted by the fever of separation from Madanasundarī, the employment of the mantra for her subjugation is my only refuge. But for one seized by the demon of a talkative disciple, where is there any means such as a female messenger? Therefore, let it be thus. (Aloud) Dear Kauṇḍinya! I have been perfectly reminded. Fetch the writing materials, so that I may compose the seed-mantra capable of conquering the fever.
Disciple:—(Having gone out and re-entering) Here are the offerings; let the teacher paint.
Jñāna:—

(Taking a birch-bark leaf, writing the subjugation mantra upon it, and rolling it up) My dear Kauṇḍinya! Take this, having made it into a ball with sandalwood paste like a seed, and bring it here so that, having worn it, I may become free from fever.
Disciple:

(Taking the written leaf, walking around, and looking at it) Ah, let me see what is written here. (Unrolling it and reading it, with a smile) Ah! Following the mantra, it is written: "May Madanasundarī be brought under my control. I shall not tolerate this. I too sustain my life only through the hope of union with Mānasundarī. Therefore, let it be thus for now.

(Wiping it off, [thinking] "May he fall under my power through this deceptive play," she draws [the figure], covers it in the same way, and having made it like a seed with sandalwood paste, enters again. "Let the Teacher plant this. (Jñānarāśi takes the seed and, with a gesture, plants it.
Disciple:—
(Saharṣāścaryamitra) How is it that in just a moment the teacher appears as if liberated from fever?

Jñāna—(To himself) This mantra has yielded its immediate fruit many times. And this disciple here is one whose nature is as treacherous as poison; therefore, let us proceed with that first. (Aloud) Dear Kauṇḍinya, the application of the mantra has been performed. Now I wish to perform the worship of the Blessed One, the conqueror of fever. Therefore, let various flowers of diverse colors and fragrances be brought.
Disciple:

As the Preceptor commands. (Exit; then, to himself) I have already recognized the Preceptor; what need have I for flowers? I shall climb this very tree with trembling branches and observe everything from there. (He does so.
Jñāna—

(Looking ahead, with a smile) Ahaha! The power of my mantra has borne fruit, for here comes Kapaṭakeli, bearing an offering of flowers, betel, and other gifts, having arrived here on a mission as a messenger for Madanasundarī.
(Then enters Kapaṭakeli as described. Kapaṭakeli presents the gift before Jñānarāśi, and laughing with a puff of her breath, she sits down bashfully.
Jñāna—
(With pride and joy) Oh, noble lady! Have you obtained that object?
Kapaṭa—(Longingly) O fortunate one! That has been obtained and lost; but my heart has been carried away by you, so you alone are my refuge.

Jñāna—(To himself) Ah, what is this! Is she one whose passion has been awakened by the intoxicating flavor of wine? What, then, should be the response here? For now, I shall employ her according to my desire. (Aloud) My good lady, is your daughter Madanasundarī well?
Kapaṭa—

(Reflecting) No, indeed, no; I have heard it. She is truly my elder sister. But I, through the favor of a playful person like you, having become happy and attained fullness, am perceived as a younger sister of a different sort.
Jñāna—(To himself, with a mocking smile) Oh! What audacity this old woman possesses! Or rather, this is quite appropriate.
The eyes, blooming with wind, repeatedly bring about an appearance of evenness as the cheeks sink; the chest, by its heaving, assumes the semblance of high breasts;
and by concealing their white hair, they manifest a state younger than even their daughters—such is this strange, difficult-to-comprehend assumption of youth in old age.
Kapaṭa—(longingly) O handsome one! Release the whip for a moment; I shall adorn my limbs with yellow sandalwood paste.
Jñāna—

(To himself) Oh! What an excess of transformation in this old woman! Or rather, perhaps love does not abandon old women, as if out of courtesy, for it was served with great longing by her in the prime of her youth long ago. (7)
(Aloud) Desist, desist!

I bow from afar to that [state] which falls inevitably into an infinite mass of mud, though it delights in the playful display of various aesthetic flavors. O Mother! I remain here in happiness, having abandoned all fear of falling.
I wander upon a path devoid of flavor, for those intent on their own self-aggrandizement.
Kapaṭa—(With a laugh) My dear! You are a man of the city; you know how to joke when you address me as "Mother. But you do not know the secret of the venerable ones. Have you not heard this verse?
"The Blessed One always performs the service of Kāmadeva."
Hari, the progenitor of Kandarpa, is exceedingly pleased with him.
"But I am not a Jaina! How many times have I offered my own head, severed by my sword, at the feet of the Blessed Ones?
Jñāna—(angrily)—"Ah, you sinner! You shall fall into the mire that defiles the vision of the Blessed Ones!"
Kapaṭa—(Laughing) O handsome one! I shall not fall. Here is my support: your staff. (She touches the staff.
Jñāna—
O sinner! Do not touch me! Do not touch me! This rod is the rod of Yama for you!
(Having snatched the rod, he begins to strike.
Kapaṭa—
(Stepping back quickly) Hey, you luckless fellow! There are no cuckoos or pigeons here; that is why you strike me, who am defenseless!
(Then enter the enraged cuckoo and pigeon. Pigeon:—
Kokilaka! Has that divine dancer ever been seen here in this garden, he who caused our quarrel over the theft?
Jñāna—(looking ahead with fear) Mother! You alone are my refuge here.
Kapaṭa—
(With anger) Even now do you address me as "Mother"?
Jñāna—
(With humility) O beautiful one! You shall grant me protection for my life; I am at your disposal.
Kapaṭa:
Therefore, let the venerable one remain composed.
(The Heap of Knowledge acts accordingly.
The Cuckoo—(looking ahead with pride): O Pigeon! Look, look! There he stands, being embraced by his own mother standing near him. Come, let us approach.
Both—(Approaching with agitation and shouting loudly) "Hey! What are you doing here?
Kapaṭa—
(Stopping him with a sign of her hand, in a voice as if fainting) Kokila! Be silent! Let there be no interruption of the Blessed One’s concentration.
Kokila: Mother!

He indeed appears to me like one distressed by the intense sweetness of the sound, since he whirls about with his eyes closed. (Looking at the pigeon with a sidelong glance) Or do you think it is you?
Pārāvata:
Cuckoo! It is even so. Come, let us bathe in the water of this lake. (They both proceed accordingly.
Kapaṭa:—
(With agitation) Ah! What is this? Stop, stop, you there! Stop! Do not be consumed in the fire!
Cokila: Mother!
If this is fire, why then are you not constantly burning while holding it in your lap? (They both hold her down with force.)
(Jñānarāśi, with a roar of defiance, wrings his head.
Pārāvata:
O Kokila! This Picchilavāla cannot be kept here.
Kokila:
Pigeon! I shall hold you by the hands and I by the feet! (Thus they begin to strike each other.
Pigeon:
(Chopping off the seed from his arm and seizing the ring from his hand, he recognizes it. Kokilaka: Recognize this ring, Kokilaka; it was given to him by his mother, Mādhavasena Śiviṣaṇā. Kokila:
(Mockingly) Well done, Mother! Well done! You hand over his entire fortune, yet in our opinion, you only transfer upon him the stigma of being a thief. (Both shake [the ring]).
Jñāna—(With a cry) Kauṇḍinya! Kauṇḍinya! Where are you? Where are you? Here I go, leaving you behind, to attain the world of Viṣṇu. Kokila—
"Tell him it is at the foot of the tree.
The Pārāvata:
"O Kokilaka! This noble sir is leaning against this very nearby *vichudaivada* tree with its trembling leaves. Let him enjoy the success of a sky-traveler for a moment."
(The cuckoo; looking at the branch above. Kauṇḍinya:

(To himself, with fear) Here he is, burning and scorching, driving even another back! So, first of all—(Aloud) Save him! Save him! Seize him! Seize this wretched ascetic, before I am destroyed! For he constantly plucks the sprouts from my mango tree. Standing right here, I shall watch him through my spyglass. (Acting out the descent, he prepares to kill him.)
Jñāna:
Oh, what extraordinary devotion there is toward the Guru! Very well; let this low-born fellow live for now.
(Kapaṭakeli smiles and looks at the face of Jñānarāśi.)
Pārāvata: Hey, are you the park-keeper?
Kauṇḍinya: [He speaks.]
Agha-iṃ?
Kokila: O pigeon!
Since my mother looks at my face with fear, having hidden [me] quietly, therefore this very one is his second Koṇḍinna. (Having approached suddenly, she seizes him as well.)
Pārāvata:
This one is also [the work] of that Blessed One. Let there be success for both of us here at the same time!
(Thus, he binds the necks of both with the two yoga-bands.)
Kauṇḍinya:—(Sighing deeply with distress) Let treasures remain in their respective places; let the world, scorched by poverty, suffer; let the multitude of sciences flourish. Kokila:—
(With envy) Hey! Do you know how to extract treasures?
Kauṇḍinya:
Who here has not been reduced to ashes by him?
Cuckoo—(Approaching with a cry) Venerable Jñānarāśi! Have mercy on us!
Jñāna—

(To himself) Well done, Kauṇḍinya! Well done! Let it be so for now. (Aloud) Child! This distressed man is prattling; let us do what is desired by him. (Having cast off their yogapaṭṭas as cuckoos and pigeons, they both prostrate at his feet. Both:—
Be gracious, be gracious, noble sir! May you prosper, O wealthy one!
Jñāna—O children! I have forgiven you; for those like me are rich in forgiveness. It is my duty to assist others.
Since it is our supreme duty, as those of the highest compassion, that these two children must certainly be favored, therefore let us rise!
Both—(rising)—Long live the noble sir! Long live the noble sir!
Jñāna— (with pride) This Kumbhadāsī has been commanded by my mere glance.
To whose house would it not resort, bringing with it a collection of calamities? (10)
Kauṇḍinya: "Bring the juice of the lāṅgalī plant.
Kauṇḍinya:
"What is the use of that?"
Knowledge—
have you not heard this?
With eyes anointed by the juice of the lāṅgalī plant together with the mantra, [one beholds the truth].
Or the wise man attains that which is a treasure or a storehouse. || 11 ||
Cuckoo:
Venerable sir! Is destruction more grievous than the loss of a treasure?
Jñāna—
Even if it lacks the proper measure, that which pacifies all suffering is better than a treasure-house of wealth.
The Cuckoo:
Let that very thing be ours.
Jñāna: And what next? Hasten, Kauṇḍinya! Hasten!
Kauṇḍinya:
"Sir, you are a knower. (Having exited and re-entering) "Let the Teacher take this; let him give it.
Jñāna—(Taking it) "Upon whose eyes shall the collyrium be applied first?"
Kokilī: Great joy!
Pārāvata:—
(Approaching) Great One!
O Illusionist—Venerable Sir! This woman also is worthy of your compassion.
Jñāna:
Ah! Why such eagerness? Death is near for everyone.
Pārā: [She speaks.]
Therefore, first attend to the cuckoo.
Jñāna—(having done so): Child! Fix your gaze upon this foot of the tree.
(The cuckoo does so.
Pārā—Cuckoo! Do you see anything?
Cuckoo: Nothing at all.
Jñāna—

(Aside) Dear Pārāvata! True indeed is this popular saying: "To those distressed by wealth, there is neither friend nor kinsman," since he does not speak even though he sees [us]. That at every step there are treasures—is that the prattle of a madman? Therefore, I shall show you something else entirely.
(He acts accordingly, showing the eyes of the pigeon.
Deceit—
"Venerable sir! For me as well! (The heap of bones makes a gesture with her hand.
Kokila—(Aside) Pārāvata! Do you see anything?
Pārā:
Nothing at all.
Kokila: [Silence]
Alas! Do you see anything?
Kapaṭa:
No, no; my eyes are becoming swollen.
Kokila—(Aside) Pārāvata! My mother does not see you; you do not see her; and I do not see her. So, what is to be done here? (Having taken it away and returning) Therefore, take this (aloud):
O Teacher! This collyrium is indeed small. Therefore, with another preparation, may you and my younger brother, Pārāvata, anoint our eyes so that we may see the treasure simultaneously.
(Both do so; the Kaukila and the Pārāvata press both [Kṛṣṇa’s] eyes firmly and rub them intensely with their own eyes.
Jñānarāśi and Kauṇḍinya—(acting out the pain)—Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! Your eyes are bursting!
Cuckoo and Pārāvata:
O Haāsā! Seize him, seize him! Kill him!
Jñāna—
"Āḥ, Kauṇḍinya! Have you even brought this *upavipañci* [eye-salve] now? That eye-salve was quite another!
Kauṇḍinya:
"O Teacher! Do you wish to kill me? My eyes are already ruined just like this."
Pārā—(Acting out extreme pain) Alas, alas! I am deceived in this wrong place.
Kokila—
O pigeon! Why do you fly away? Or have you perhaps seen some woman here who was never before seen by you? Or is it that no woman at all exists within me?
The day has passed in vain; what opportunity for sorrow is there for us in this world? || 12 ||
Jñāna—(aside, with a smile): This is indeed true.
Having accomplished all that was to be done, they await death as if it were a beloved guest.
(Aloud) Dear Kokila and Pārāyata! Is there any body of water nearby here? This untimely death is pacified merely by washing one's eyes.
Kokila:
There is the Madanodyāna garden nearby, where our lord Kalākaraṇḍaka enjoys his social gatherings.
Pārāvatī:
Then how shall we look for the path?
Kokila:
"Let us go, even though we are weary.
(They all walk about slowly. Kauṇḍinya acts out flying onto a cuckoo. Cuckoo:
(Pushing her away with his foot, angrily) Ha! What treasure is here? I am but a cuckoo! So go elsewhere!
Kapaṭa—(Acting as if falling) Child cuckoo! Support me, support me!
Kokila: Oh!
Stay right where you have fallen. Who is capable of lifting you up? You have become as heavy as an elephant!
(Kapaṭakeli somehow rises and acts out falling again and again.)
Pārā—
(With derision) Let the lady first find treasures at every step!
Kokila—
(Acting out extreme anguish) Alas, alas! This is a calamity for the city, that the touch of the lord Kalakaṇṭha’s feet was not obtained at the moment of death.
Kapaṭa—(Crying out with joy while beating her breast): Daughter Madanasundarī! Where are you? Give me an answer! For I am helpless and must wander about, unable to behold the lotus-eyes of your face.
(Then enters Madanasundarī, accompanied by her retinue, agitated, along with Kalā, Karaṇḍaka, and Drā.
Madanasundarī: Mother! What is this?
(Feigning a fit, she clutches his neck and weeps.
Kalākaraṇḍaka: (Looking on, approaching with agitation) Venerable Jñānarāśi! What is this?
Jñāna—(recognizing him by his voice): Dear Kalākaraṇḍaka! I have been struck down by ill fate; what shall I say?
Kokila and Pārāvata—
(With anger) Master Kalākaraṇḍaka! Behold this world, entirely deceived by illusion, ruined!
Kalākaraṇḍaka (with anger): Ah, you wicked ones! Enough, enough of this rashness! (To Jñānarāśi) Venerable sir! Tell me, what is this? This servant of yours is ready. Jñāna—
Child, bring some water meanwhile so that the eyes of everyone may be washed.
Kalākaraṇḍaka:
Kusumikā! Mudgaraka! Surely the pond is quite nearby; let the water be brought then.
Both:
"As the Master commands. (Exiting and re-entering) "The casket of arts has been brought.
Kalākaraṇḍaka:
"Let the eyes of everyone be washed! (They do so).
Jñāna—(washing his face and opening his eyes): "Dear Kalākaraṇḍaka! By good fortune you are seen; by good fortune your calamity has been pacified."
Kapaṭa—(With joy) By good fortune, I have beheld the moon of your face! (He kisses Madanasundarī.
Kokila and Pārāvata—
(Taking the casket of the arts from their feet) "By good fortune, you have become guests to us while we are still alive!
Kalākaraṇḍaka:
"Children! Let this Blessed One, the teacher of the world, be saluted for a moment."

(Both do so. Jñāna—May you all rejoice, rejoice together with Kalākaraṇḍaka! Dear Kalākaraṇḍaka, no one here has committed any offense. For the sake of these two who were eager to see the treasure, the eye-salve that was brought has, through its fumes, turned into something else entirely and intensely powerful.
Kālakaraṇḍaka:
(With humility) What is being said? Indeed, even through negligence, calamities do not overcome the Teacher of the World.
Jñāna—
"My child Kalākaraṇḍaka! Have the waves of dust been conquered? Are your heart's desires fulfilled?
Kalākaraṇḍaka:
(With joy and humility) "O Blessed One! What more can be said? For one who is protected by your compassion, there is nothing whatsoever in this world that remains unattainable."
Mudrāraka—(With pride and eagerness) My lord Kalākaraṇṭaka! This is your mother, this is your teacher, this is your retinue; since you have become free from debt, let us now celebrate this festival.
Jñāna—
"My child, Kalākaraṇḍaka! Tell me, what further favor can I do for you?
Kalākaraṇḍaka:
(With joy and humility)
Were those invincible dice, which brought about the loss of my kingdom, not conquered?
Was she, the beloved who was the very breath of my life, not won back? Did the moon-faced woman not unite with me? And has my retinue not crossed to the further shore of the ocean of calamity?
"O Blessed One, having already performed half the task for me, why do you wish to give me something else? (13)
Nevertheless, let this be:
may the rulers of the earth protect the world; may the clouds, bestowing joy, grant auspicious rain at their pleasure.
Let it be, let it be! Let this fool, whose very soul is swollen with pride, be the wretch who has mounted the vehicle of the Lord of the Night’s beloved. 14.
The farce entitled *Hāsyacūḍāmaṇi*, composed by the great poet Śrī Vammarāja, the minister of the Great King Śrī Parameśvaradeva, is completed. Gaṅgadhara— delightful as the beautiful moon,
bearing the submarine fire within the fire of his forehead-eye— ...
May Bharga, who bears an exceedingly uneven island yet is delightful with the jewels of his qualities, increase your prosperity like the ocean. || 1 ||
Moreover:
May those vomits of the ocean protect you— vomits resulting from the churning of Mount Mandara, jagged with its peaks,
by which the ocean’s reproach was cast off through the agitation caused by their force.
Śrī obtained the constant embrace of the Enemy of Madhu.
(At the end of the *nāndī*, the Stage Manager enters.
Stage Manager:
(Looking toward the east, with pride) Ah, the hour of dawn has attained boldness!
For thus it is:
the Goddess of Fortune has arisen from the ocean, whose lotus-beds are shimmering, and approaches the orb of the thousand-rayed sun;
she seems as if filled with eager longing for the festival of beholding the lotus-face of her beloved, who dwells within that orb.

I have awakened at the very hour sacred to Brahmā, yet I have not reflected upon anything for my own welfare. Indeed, it is heard from the Smṛtis: "Having risen during the hour sacred to Brahmā, one should contemplate what is beneficial for oneself. Therefore, I shall now reflect upon that as well. (Looking toward the backstage) Who is here of our company?
(Entering) The Stage Manager: *Please note: The original text contains a stage direction (*nepathyābhimukham avalokya*) which has been translated as "(Looking toward the backstage).
The Sanskrit term *sthāpakaḥ* refers to the Stage Manager.*
(With humility) Here I am. May your honor command me.
Sūtra—(With joy) By good fortune you have arrived! You alone are our greatest benefactor; therefore, please consider this: how might all twelve of us brothers simultaneously fulfill our duty?

The Director—(Shaking his head with joy) Oh, what noble brotherly affection! This desire, so difficult to attain, is fulfilled for Bhāva solely through the abundance of his good fortune. Even the twelve Ādityas, after revolving before him for twelve months, become recipients of supreme sovereignty. Therefore, having reflected, I shall inform you. (Reflecting for a moment, then with joy)
For the simultaneous fulfillment of all your desires, you must resort either to King Paramardin or to the ocean. (4)
Sūtradhāra:

(With joy) Well observed! Well reminded! By the performance of the *samavakāra* *Samudramathana*, composed by the poet Vatsarāja, our very own Paramardideva shall become an ocean that fulfills all our desires.
(Offstage)
Thus it is. From the ocean, all desires are fulfilled.

Sūtra—(Acting out the recognition of the voice): Ah! This is Padmaka, the confidant of the goddess, the daughter of the ocean. Therefore, let us two now go and accomplish what must be done next. (They both exit.)
(Prologue) (Then enters Padmaka. Padmaka:—

It is not so. All those desires will be fulfilled by that giver of boons. Indeed, it was told to you by Gaṅgādharī how all the gods and asuras, having consulted together with Viṣṇu, the slayer of Mahiṣa, and the son of Jamadagni, were united in their desire to churn the ocean using Mount Mandara as the churning stick. Therefore, there the blossoming fruit of Lakṣmī’s love for Viṣṇu will bear fruit; even though Viṣṇu has departed, the image of Lakṣmī drawn by Viṣṇu himself was shown to him by Vindhyavāsī.

The obstacle has been thoroughly cleared away. Therefore, even though my knowledge is limited, there is this possibility that my desire for Lakṣmī will bear fruit. Indeed, the blessed Goddess Gaṅgā, beloved of the Ocean, the crest-jewel of the holy, who dwells upon the head of Lord Śambhu—the source of all majesty—overshadows everything by her power. (With distress) But how, then, can there be the sustenance of life for Lakṣmī?

Ah! It was not well done by the great queen Gaṅgā, the daughter of the ocean, that she described the virtues of Viṣṇu in such a manner before Lakṣmī; thus, her bond of affection for him has been strengthened. Or rather, enough of my grief! Who could have any doubt regarding the success of this undertaking, when even the mind of the goddess Gaṅgā is convinced?

So here in the Velāvana forest, having rested for a moment... (pausing and acting out a recollection) Ah! I shall go and show Lakṣmī even this *viṣṇucittavaṭa* tree entrusted to me by the goddess Gaṅgā, before that Celāvalī arrives. For at the time of my departure, she was asking her father for permission to come to Velāvana. As for me, longing for the pleasure of my own sleep, I have departed as if with a heartless resolve.
(Offstage, with anger)
"Āḥ! Who is this fool speaking so harshly as if he were censured? Look, you sinner! Look and see whether or not there is a tongue belonging to you who speak thus!
The Hunter—(fearfully): "Āḥ! Who is this that scolds me without cause? (He looks here and there.)
(Then enters the venerable Niṣṭhuraka, enraged.
(Niṣṭhuraka, full of anger, reads aloud the passage beginning with "Look again," etc. Pajjhaka:

(To himself) Ah, the venerable one is angry! Surely he is angry because of the identity of his name with "Niṣṭhura" (the Cruel). (Aloud, with humility) Venerable sir! I bow to you. Where shall my tongue, which practices wicked conduct, go? Indeed, I reproach myself for being devoid of compassion and calling myself "Niṣṭhura. Niṣṭhuraka:—(To himself, with embarrassment) Ah, he reproaches himself for his cruelty. (Aloud) Good sir, why do you reproach yourself in this manner?

Aha! O Lord of the Ocean, it was not well done by the Great Goddess Gaṅgā that she described [Viṣṇu’s] virtues before Lakṣmī in such a manner and instilled in him a bond of love for Him. Or rather, enough of my grief; who could have any doubt regarding the success of this undertaking, when even the mind of Goddess Gaṅgā herself is convinced? Therefore, I shall go after resting here in the coastal forest for a moment. Ah!

I shall show this painted cloth of Viṣṇu, offered by the goddess Gaṅgā, to Lakṣmī before that lady Velāvalī arrives. For at the time of my departure, she was indeed questioning her father, the Ocean, regarding the coming of the forest on the shore. As for me, longing for the pleasure of rest from my journey, I have become as if censured by one who is cruel.
Niṣṭhuraka:
But where is your mistress?
Padmaka:— Noble sir! My lady is greatly distressed by the heat. Padma:—
She remains in the midst of the ocean.
Niṣṭhura—(with derision): If she who undergoes penance in the middle of the ocean were to become free from suffering upon reaching the [royal] circle, [then what of it]?

Padma—(With affection: Venerable sir! You speak in a manner worthy of your name, but not worthy of your appearance. For venerable ones, overcome by compassion, bring about even the desires of those who lust through their mantras, tantras, and acts of mediation.
Niṣṭhura—
(Sighing) Ah, you villain! What are you prattling? How could I, having abandoned the mantra for the grace of Puṇḍarīkākṣa, ever seek to propitiate the mantra of the ocean of love for your mistress?

Padmā—(With humility) Noble sir, do not be angry! Indeed, by your mantras, the Blessed One with lotus-eyes will become gracious toward you in another birth. But as for the Queen, the daughter of the Ocean, since you have acted as her messenger, she will grant your desire immediately.
Niṣṭhu:

(With derision) Hey, you fool! Is there no shame in you for speaking thus, nor in me for listening? How could the Lord of the entire universe, the Blessed One, whose abode is Vaikuṇṭha, feel such longing for the company of a mere human woman? This is a great mockery even for your master’s daughter, that she should fix her attachment upon him; for the swan of Brahmā cannot possibly be the object of love for a water-crow.
Pajha:
(With bashfulness) Noble sir! Do not say so.
The elephant possesses all-seeing vision and the charm that deludes;
yet Govinda excels in good fortune through his love for Lakṣmī in the midst of the ocean.

Niṣṭhu—(With derision) If that is so, then Nārāyaṇa’s taking of a wife is already as good as over. Why do you boast in this way? Oh, how truly wonderful, how truly marvelous! What connection can there be with one who does not even enter the path of vision? Hey, you fool! Even our own teachers instruct us thus:
"He is difficult to behold, devoid of qualities, subtle, absolute, and the size of a thumb."
He is free from passion, the master of great illusion, Kṛṣṇa, the enchanter of the three worlds. || 5 ||

Padma—(With anger) Those who think thus do not know your teachers, nor do those like you listen [to them]. This is like a display of forms before the blind in their misfortunes. Look, look! The glory of the blessed Kṛṣṇa! (Thus he shows the painted cloth.
Niṣṭhura—

(Looking with astonishment) Hey there! Where did you find this? I have indeed painted the form of Madhusūdana here for the sake of meditation. While dwelling here in the Velāvana hermitage, I meditate upon this form of Kṛṣṇa day after day. Once, it was carried away by the current of the swelling Gaṅgā.
Pajha:

Venerable sir! This is indeed a picture-scroll bearing the likeness of Madhumathana, sent by Lakṣmī—the daughter of the Ocean and wife of the Ocean—who was distressed by separation from Madhumathana. Niṣṭhu:
"Give me back my own [painting]!

Paddā—(With anger and mockery) Even though it was given, it does not remain in your hand! Is there something in your power such that even by painting it, the god Kṛṣṇa cannot be shown? For this very reason, under the pretext of being swept away by the waves, the picture-board slipped from your hand.

Niṣṭhu—(With anger) Ah, you villain! Not even a trace of sin exists in me. Now, it will be enough with your conversation, you who are of such defiled character. Therefore, withdraw from here, you face of fear; go away from this place!
Pajh—

(With pride) Ho there, O Blessed One! While I was performing difficult penance, why was I placed in the presence of Lakṣmī, who is solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa, and why was the fulfillment of Lakṣmī’s desires frustrated? Furthermore, the ocean—filled with the flood of the waters of the celestial river—constantly laps against my waist.
While being served by one who is difficult to endure and whose speech is harsh. || 6 ||
She worships Hari in her heart with a lotus garland placed upon the surface of her chest;
intent on the practice of meditation, she disregards the conversation of her attendants.
How could the Goddess of Fortune not bear fruit for her who desires to wash away the mire of sins through meritorious deeds, yet remains abstinent from food? (8)
Now, however, right here in the waters of the ocean, the princess honors the Blessed Goddess with hundreds of thousands of flowers from the coastal forest.
Niṣṭhu—
Will your princess come here?
Pajha:
What then?
Niṣṭhu:
Therefore, this present situation is inappropriate here, given the proximity of those possessed by passion.
Pajha—
(angrily) By you, this sacred grove shall be abandoned!
Niṣṭhu—(With anger) Ah, you villain! What are you prattling? (Raising his staff, he wishes to strike him.
Pajha—
(With anger) Wait, you! While I summon some aquatic creature, however difficult it may be to capture, for your sake. And furthermore—[Niṣṭhuraka...]
(Looking ahead with fear) Oh, you villain! This wicked water-elephant, merely remembered by you, is emerging right here! Therefore, I shall go wherever I can. (He flees.
Padma—(Observing) Surely this is Lakṣmī approaching on an elephant, for on both sides of her are seen her two friends, Lajjā and Dhṛti. Therefore, I will wait right here.
(Then enters Lakṣmī as described.
Lakṣmī:

Friends! This [garland] of mine is already filled to the brim with a profusion of fragrant flowers. Therefore, right here, I shall honor the Blessed Lord Rudrāṇī with flowers gathered by my own hands.
Dhṛti:
As it pleases the noble lady. Lajjā: [She speaks.]
"O leader of elephants! May you remain steady here. (The elephant stands thus.
Padmā—
(To herself) I shall watch from some hidden spot here. (She does so. (Lakṣmī acts out crossing over.
Dhūtī—
Dear friend! O Modesty! Grant some thinness to the princess. Modesty:
She is indeed very frail, yet she does not appear so because of her abundance of loveliness.
Likewise, through the excellence of her beauty, she possesses a resemblance to the moon, the foremost rival of the sun;
yet, for one whose longing is difficult to endure, this becomes even more truly marvelous. (9)
Lakṣmī:
Come, young women, come! The flowers are being gathered.
(All act out the gathering of flowers.)
Lakṣmī— (With joy and wonder) Someone has fashioned creepers out of pearls six months old!
Why is such great length seen here in these words of yours? || 10 ||
(Dhṛti and Lajjā mime looking at each other's faces and smiling.
Lakṣmī—(With apprehension) Sahasrārjuna! Why is there laughter here?

Lajjā: Dear friend! You are indeed laughing at one who is unfamiliar [with these things]. These are not strings of pearls, but blossoms of the *vicaillaka* tree; these are sprouts of the *kaṅkelli* tree, not petals of the *vibhūta* flower.
Lakṣmī:
(Smiling with embarrassment) "So, let us gather these very ones.
(They do so.
Lakṣmī—
(Acting out the harassment by bees, with agitation) Friend! Who are these small, restless birds flying up?
Dhṛti—(Laughing) Dear friend Lakṣmī!
Behold, the bees, intoxicated by the fragrance of your face, do not delight in flowers; scorched by the waves of your hot sighs, they appear as if they were being tormented. 11.
"It is a marvel that there is no fear for one so weakened by longing. Lakṣmī—(With bashfulness and a smile):
"Friend! I shall not ask you. Dear friend Lajjā! Drive away these bees of yours who are said to subsist on nectar!
Lajjā—
Agha? [What?
Dhṛti: My dear friend! I have gathered these mountain flowers. Now let the blessed Bhavānī be worshipped. Lakṣmī:—
"Let the marriage-offerings be brought from the attendants. (Dhṛti does so.
(Lakṣmī enacts the worship of Pārvatī.
Lajjā—
(With a prayer:
O ascetic, may you be honored with various flower garlands by Lakṣmī, just as Kṛṣṇa is honored by your lotus-eyes through your grace. 12.
Dhṛti—(With pride) Dear friend Lakṣmī! By good fortune you have appeared. I see your left arm throbbing; it portends the imminent sight of my beloved. Lakṣmī—
(The opinion of Salañjari. Begone, begone! (Thus she strikes her with a flower.
Padmā—(To herself) On this occasion, I shall show her this black canvas. (Rising quickly) O Queen! Let this image of Kṛṣṇa be honored even with these flowers by means of the flowers of your eyes.
(Thus she offers the painted cloth.
Lajjā—(Looking with amusement) Well said, well said! What can be said of Pomañca? Just as Pomañca is a treasury of material goods, so are you a treasury of pleasures.

Lakṣmī—(Looking at the lotus with a gracious smile, and gazing at the portrait of Viṣṇu with joy, wonder, and pride) Oh, what beauty! Oh, what beauty! It is truly fitting that the Great Sage calls this Supreme Man "uncreated" (*anirmita*); indeed, no one could ever create such a form. (With longing) My heart! By good fortune you have increased. The tree of grace from the Goddess Kātyāyanī has indeed blossomed; now, through the very fulfillment of my desire by beholding this painting, it shall bear fruit. Padma—

Goddess Lakṣmī! Why do you delay? This very picture-scroll has been sent by the Goddess Gaṅgā; let it be worshipped. Through the worship of Janārdana, Janārdana himself is obtained. Are you empty-hearted? Indeed, I too have been sent by the Goddess Gaṅgā to perform obeisance at her feet.
Lūjjā:
Dear friend! Poma speaks well: "Let the painted Madhumathana be worshipped."
Lakṣmī—(Looking at Dhṛti’s face with trembling, stammering) Enough with these preliminary offerings!
(Dhṛti does so; Lakṣmī mimes the act of worship.)
Lajjā—
(with a mocking smile) How indeed can the gathering of handfuls of flowers succeed for one whose hands are trembling?
How can one whose speech is faltering and who lacks self-control possess a complete assembly? || 13 ||
O lotus-eyed one! Your mind is agitated by the snares of false views; therefore, meditate with perfect composure upon the lotus that is pure in its very nature. 14.
(Lakṣmī, with a bashful smile, wishes to decline the worship.
Dhṛti—(With agitation and entreaty: Do not do this!
O friend! May your nature, which consists of the essence of desire, prevail over the Moon; yet, do not suddenly assume a form that is difficult for those free from passion to endure. 15.
(Lakṣmī offers a handful of flowers with a smile.

Lajjā—(Quickly binding the target in her upper garment with bashfulness and entreaty): O fortunate one, best of men! Look, look at the husband of the princess! You are indeed to be won over by devotion; therefore, draw near.
(Offstage) Ah, what is this!
Trees with bodies eager to fly up, having uprooted themselves, are filling the sky with their dense masses like winged trees, by means of the waves of their expansive trunks.
By this [wind], which is difficult to withstand and exceedingly swift, all the trembling world is suddenly shattered by a continuous gale like that at the end of an eon.
Pajha—(To himself) Surely Murāri is approaching, accompanied by a retinue of gods and demons; surely Mount Mandara follows him, since this terrifying tempest of wind arises.
Lakṣmī—

(Acting out the force of her falling sin): Alas, alas, my friends! Lead me to the lap of my father, the great ocean! Indeed, having repeatedly performed various jewel-offerings to the Blessed Goddess Kaccāyanī, I requested my father for the sake of an offering of seasonal forest flowers and came here. And this is the fruit that has resulted from it!
Lajjā—(With agitation) O King! Come, come! (The elephant hastens toward the sound.)
(All of them act out the entry into the ocean.

Pajha—(To himself) Ah! I shall not yet report the account of the slaying of the great ocean as told by the goddess Gaṅgā; the princess will become utterly distressed. It would be better for me to remain right here, describing this very event. (He stands thus.)
(Offstage) Here is the enemy of Mura, his great desire manifesting, having approached the ocean together with the gods and demons!
Mount Mandara, the king of mountains, approaches with its mass of lofty peaks touching the sky for the purpose of the churning effort. (17)

Pajha—(With joy) Even though it is undesirable, today Bhartṛdārikā will have a vision of Govinda. Therefore, I shall approach the ocean and enter its depths. (Having thus enacted the entry into the ocean, he exits.
(Then enters Vāsudeva in a celestial chariot, accompanied by a retinue of gods and asuras, headed by Mahendra.)

Vāsudeva—(With joy and curiosity): O Lord of the Gods! Behold, as they descend from the courtyard of the sky, the waters are churned by the crocodiles who seek to seize the shadows of the hosts of gods and demons.
Even here, on Mount Mandara situated at a great distance, the king of oceans shines as if being churned. || 18 ||

"Having descended from that mountain, let us wait in the Velāvana forest until all the gods, including Brahmā and Maheśa, as well as all the Asuras, and that Mount Mandara, arrive. (He sits down in the middle of the Velāvana forest.
Vṛhaspati—(looking all around with wonder and fear):
"Alas! This increase in the ocean's size agitates my heart intensely;
this churning will surely end in disaster and lead to our mockery. O gods, perform your ablutions here immediately and depart with your hearts heavy."
Joy arises from the creatures, provided that no adversity occurs. || 19 ||

Indra—(To himself) Ah! the timidity of Bṛhaspati, whose intellect is rendered solely blind by his constant preoccupation with mantras. So be it. (Aloud, with pride) How vast is the ocean, that lake conditioned by the river of heaven whose waters begin as streams flowing from the hollows of the pitchers held by the lotus-born Brahmā?
This resolve of the host of Daityas and gods to churn [the ocean]—how indeed does it not become an object of laughter for them? (20)
(With a smile of praise) O Bṛhaspati,
wielder of the thunderbolt and crusher of Bala!
You are the most excellent of ministers.
Therefore, in this lake whose waters are milk, what cause for discouragement could there possibly be for you? || 21 ||
Bṛhaspati—(smiling with disdain): O Lord, Master Purandara!
The submarine fire is the master of the conflagration of the three worlds.
What is not his? What is not his? That Kālakūṭa [is his].
In this world, when one is agitated by anger, there can be no means of protection for the enemy of Vṛtra, such as armor and the like. || 22 ||
Dhanada—
(With pride and disdain) Live! Whether you cause the churning of the ocean or prevent it, do as you please!
What valor is there in drinking the milk spoken of by the submarine fire? || 23 ||

Vṛṣabha—(With contemptuous laughter): Let alone his valor! By the mere greatness of this [hero], let Mount Mandara here become as restless with flickering flames as the submarine fire, and remain fixed in its whirling motion.
May you all become like insects, circling at his sides in a state of broken agitation. || 24 ||

Vasu—(To himself) Ah! The host of gods is intent on churning the ocean, yet I am enslaved by the noose of love for their daughter. Should I therefore abandon the effort to churn the ocean in accordance with the counsel of the divine minister [Bṛhaspati] and begin the marriage in another manner? Or, having been brought here at the request of all the gods and asuras, how can I cause them to suffer such disappointment and shatter their hopes? Let it be so for now. (Aloud) O Vācaspati!
Your thunderbolt is not dull, nor is your intellect faltering.
Everything that occurs will have auspicious results, with Hari as my companion and me as his follower.
Vṛṣākapi—(To himself, with pride) Ah! By my very lack of resolve, the task of the gods has become firmly established for me, since the Blessed Mukunda has made such a vow. So be it, then.
(Aloud) May the Ocean fulfill all our desires.
Those [words] of the gods who have been liberated by Madhusūdana are proven;
having now obtained these words of yours, which are difficult to attain, they have indeed drunk the nectar itself, though not in bulk.
Indra:
(With humility) O Janārdana, the water from your feet is the Gaṅgā.
How small is the churning of the ocean filled with water by those who carry out his commands—by the gods, Dānava, Mandara, and others! Oh, what a diversion is this tumultuous upheaval! 27.
Vasu—(Looking upward) O Thousand-eyed One! Behold, here indeed approaches the Lotus-seated Lord;
for he is like one thirsty for the milk of the Ocean of Milk.
This swan,
the grandson of Brahmā, though not being pursued by his grandfather, approaches even closer than the king of birds.

Indra—(looking upward with joy and wonder): How is it that even this Lord Maheśa is approaching with such speed! This is a great marvel never seen before; even the God of gods is moving so swiftly! Kṛṣṇa—
O Mahendra! Do not act thus; let the inhabitants of heaven, who possess delicate prowess and enjoy the full exercise of their desires under the lord of the well-pleased [Indra], sport instead.
When a great calamity descends through the power of fate, this very god who wears an elephant-hide is one's sole refuge. || 29 ||
(Then Maheśa and Brahmā enter. Brahmā— (Approaching with haste:)
Exert yourself, O Govinda! Before long, may your desires be fulfilled!
For those whose weariness from exertion has borne fruit, rest serves as an ornament. (30)
Maheśa—(with a joyful smile) Kṛṣṇa! Let the command of the Eldest of the Gods be carried out.
Vāsudeva—
(With humility) O Ugra! In your presence, we all exert ourselves with great intensity;
for some extraordinary power awakens in servants when they stand before their lord. (31)
"Then let Mount Mandara come!
Indra—(looking into the sky)—"Kṛṣṇadeva! Look, look! Having descended from the sky, Mount Mandara has appeared, plunging into the great ocean."
Out of respect for him, Maināka rose up as if to welcome a guest,
under the pretext that his reflection had been transferred into the middle of the ocean.
Vāsuki— (smiling with sixfold grace, looking at Śeṣa upon the neck of Hara):
He who supports the earth like a sloughed-off skin.
O Mandara mountain! It is you alone who possess the authority to serve as the churning rod for the Lord of the World; this task cannot be accomplished by the kings of serpents.
Śeṣa:
(Humbly) How could such power belong to me, who am but a biting insect?
May the Lord do whatever He wishes, having bestowed His own majesty upon me. || 34 ||

Maheśa—(With a smile) O King of Serpents! Deliver the message of Mukunda without delay. (Śeṣa suddenly descends from Śiva’s neck, rises up with a dramatic gesture, and encircles Mount Mandara situated in the midst of the Ocean of Milk.)
Mahendra—(With pride) Oh, gods! Oh, gods! As before, support the eyes of the king of serpents on both sides! (All do so and act out the churning; Mount Mandara stands thus.
Maheśa—
(Viddhasya) O Kṛṣṇa! All the crooked ones—the gods and asuras alike—bow before you; you alone are their irresistible four-armed arm, free from all obstacles. 35.
Therefore, let your honor decide this; let there be no mockery of the gods and demons.
Kṛṣṇa—(approaching suddenly and turning Mount Mandara, to himself with longing):

Having contemplated that Lakṣmī here in the ocean, my sighing has become agitated and long; yet, though it is capable of churning the Gaṅgā with its sound, it restrains itself out of great compassion.
Therefore, I shall now turn it with feigned indifference. (He turns Mount Mandara.
Brahmā—(looking on with curiosity) Maheśa! Behold!

Dancing like Mount Mandara with its hosts of gods and asuras, he plays with the bees-like [serpents] through the charming pastimes of swift coming and going performed by the pair of arms and the mouth at the tip of Śeṣa's tail.
Maheśa—(With joy and wonder): Oh, what a great marvel is occurring! For instance:
the crests of lofty waves are surging due to the intensity of the force of the swelling current.
Like hands, they fell upon the summit of Mount Mandara from the ocean whose waters were churned by the serpent’s coils. || 38 ||
Vāsu—(Gesturing as if listening) Wait, wait a moment! Something seems to be emerging.
(All become motionless.)
Vasu—
(With joy and curiosity): At the conclusion of the thundering of vast clouds, which were flashing with the ill-omened signs of the falling of the thunderbolt...
Like the sweet sound of a young peacock, this slow-moving vehicle brings delight.
(Then the Vedas enter.
Vāsu—(Recognizing them through his knowledge; to himself, with joy): By good fortune, these Vedas have indeed arrived!
Vāli:

(With humility) Blessed Lord, Master of the World! You are the common master of both gods and asuras. It must be considered that masters bestow their grace equally upon their attendants when those attendants possess equal devotion and effort.
Maheśa:—

(To himself) Ah, Dānavāri is eager for a division! And that is unpleasant; yet, it must be granted for now. (Aloud) O Lord of the Dānavas! Enough of this impatience. What propriety is being transgressed by Acyuta? Therefore, he alone is the authority. Kṛṣṇa—

(To himself) Excellent, O Omniscient One! Excellent, for you have instructed nothing that is not already distinguished. So be it. (Aloud) O Lords of the Dānavas! Let it be considered that whatever emerges from the ocean remains, even now, within the very womb of the ocean. And let the Guardians of the Quarters, whose power is like fire, protect the multitude of objects on the shore-forest. Once the undertaking of churning the ocean is accomplished, let there be a distribution according to the command of the Lord. Bali: As it pleases Acyuta.
Kṛṣṇa:
O venerable Vedas! Let this labor of churning be abandoned for now in this appropriate forest at the edge of the ocean, out of deference to the guardians of the quarters.
The guardians of the quarters, Agni and the others: [speak].
(With humility) This way, this way, venerable Vedas!
(Having circumambulated, they all stand accordingly.
Kṛṣṇa:
(With joy) Ah, O gods and asuras! Churn it vigorously once more! (They all do so.
Kṛṣṇa:
Wait, wait a moment!
(All remain standing.
Kṛṣṇa:
(Acting out the observation, with astonishment) Some venerable person is approaching now.
This fresh river, noble with its rising spray, leaps forward with the rhythmic cadence of thundering waves,
surging from the vast expanse of its mass of froth bursting forth from the rows of ripples.
(Then Airāvata enters.
Indra —
(looking on with astonishment):
This very Maināka mountain, who formerly hid himself secretly in a corner of the ocean's depths out of fear of the thunderbolt’s blow,
now emerges once more from his deep exhaustion, his lofty peaks glistening white. (41)
Kṛṣṇa:—(To himself) By good fortune, this elephant is surely no mere Mairāvata. (Aloud) O Supreme Lord! This lordly elephant has emerged; let him be beheld.
Maheśa:—
(With a joyful smile) This distinguished elephant deserves the status of a king. Let him occupy the shade of the trees on the shore, which is cool even in the cool season.
(Airāvata does so.
Vāsuki—
Moreover, churn the Mandara mountain again!
(Everyone does so.
Vāsuki—
"Wait, wait! Something more is coming. (Everyone becomes still.
Bāli—

(Looking) Oh, Vāsudeva! Now the churning of Mount Mandara has become futile, since something that seems to be insubstantial is emerging. Vāsudeva—(To himself: Your churning of Mount Mandara is indeed in vain; everything for you will turn out to be insubstantial.
Indra: Well said by the King of the Dānavas! For indeed:
"The shower of spray from the upward-streaming milk, tossed up by the force of the vital breath, falls in profusion."
From the peak of the mountain situated in the midst of the ocean, Hayāsya clearly emerges, causing great agitation. || 42 ||
This is indeed already accomplished;
Vāsudeva—
let it depart entirely for now.
(Then enters Uccaiḥśravas.

Vāsava—(Looking at him, to himself) Ah! This is King Uccaiḥśravas, the king of horses, who is heard to be endowed with all auspicious marks. Let it be so then. (Aloud, with a jest) O Lord Śambhu! May this horse, endowed with all auspicious marks and fit for the horse-sacrifice, be granted to the Blessed Hiraṇyagarbha.
Brahmā—(with a smile) Oh! You intend to have us accept the gift of Hari’s horse!
Maheśa—
(With joy, pointing him out) Oh Kṛṣṇa! Since he is a member of the army, let even this horse remain near the elephant.
(Uccaiḥśravas does so.
Kṛṣṇa:—
(With joy) Ah! Let the gods and asuras churn Mount Mandara once again! (The gods and asuras do so.
Dhanada—
(With wonder and reflection) Ah! Let the churning be slowed for a moment;
behold, some substance that gladdens the heart arises, its form and configuration barely discernible, like an ocean by the surging flood of its own tranquility.
As if enraged by the churning, he ascends toward the heavens.
(Then Candra enters. Indra — (With joy and reflection:)

Is this a jar of nectar? Or is it perhaps a mass of the essence of milk from the ocean, churned and agitated by Mount Mandara? Is it some unprecedented, delightful being? Or is it not rather that nothing at all would be so wondrous in an ocean already full of wonders? (44)
Kṛṣṇa:— (Acting out remembrance; to himself,
with longing) Is that face, seen in the painting, now appearing before me— the face of the daughter of the Ocean?
Have you heard how [the God of Love], because he was the death-knell for the Kṣatriyas, conquered the nectar of immortality? (45)

(Examining closely) Ah! This is something else entirely, defiled by a stain; it is not that same face. (Sighing with sorrow) My gaze, running here in the hope of seeing my beloved’s face, now turns away instantly, seized by the hand of this blemish. (46)
(Examining him) This must surely be the one with rays like nectar. (Aloud) O Lord Śaṅkara! Here is the moon, the maker of nectar, who has arrived.

Candra—(Looking at my side, joyfully, to himself) By good fortune, my father, the ocean, has been churned, since this Blessed Lord of the Pramathas, whose sight is difficult even for great sages to obtain, has come within the range of my vision.
Maheśa—(Gazing at the moon, to himself) Ah! The labor of churning the ocean has now borne great fruit, since this lord of sacrifices has been obtained. (Aloud) O Kṛṣṇa!
Moving from cloud to cloud, you drink the waters of the Ganges which are cool within.
May this leader of the twice-born, being delighted, dwell for a moment upon the forest grove at the edge of the ocean, thoroughly dispelling the exhaustion born of churning. (47)
(Candrarati acts it out.
Kṛṣṇa—(With pride and excitement): Oh! How wonderful are the fruits of churning the ocean! Therefore, let Mount Mandara be raised up once more.
(The gods and demons act accordingly.
Varuṇa—(Looking ahead with distress) Ah! Why do these creeping vines of the Śeṣa serpent spring up, having spread from the very foundations of the ocean?
Indra:
(With indignation) Those who, like aquatic creatures, meet their destruction through such wicked and evil-minded men as Mandara...
They breathe forth as soon as they behold [him], their streams of tears stirred by the leap of joy. || 48 ||
All the gods and asuras exclaimed:
"Aha! How wonderful, how wonderful! We rejoice;
it increases with respect to every single limb."
Such is the rise of power;
that very same fierce exhaustion from the labor of turning Mount Mandara subsides in an instant. (49)
What can it be?
Vāsava— (feeling it) Surely these are great medicinal herbs, not mossy creepers.
(Then the great physicians enter.
Kṛṣṇa:
(With respect)
O Śiva, you who destroy the suffering of the earth! Here come those of virtuous character, bearing a profusion of unfading flowers and worthy of being worshipped;
O Śiva, grant them the hope that their great afflictions may be destroyed by the fire of your radiant laughter. (50)
Maheśa—
(addressing the serpent):
O you who are being born from the womb of Aditi, I shall consume both [your] birth and your mother.
Through the grace of these noble ones, may even those who are hostile toward us become filled with supreme joy. (51)
Kṛṣṇa: Let the command of Maheśa be carried out.
(The medicinal herbs remain as they were.)

Vāyu—(With enthusiasm) O gods and dānavas! Turn back the Mandara mountain! I too shall multiply its speed a thousandfold by the power of my own velocity. Let the Ocean of Jewels bestow objects difficult to obtain!
(The gods and dānavas do so).
Kuvera—(With astonishment) Enough, enough! Behold, behold the manifold colors of the great ocean!
Kṛṣṇa—
(Reflecting) Are these many flames of the fire of the Tuṣita heaven flickering?
Or is it the ocean displaying its spray, or perhaps a bow that rivals the rainbow of Indra?
Is this some other wondrous substance arising here, or is it a mass of light so densely armored that the ocean itself acts as a shield for the eyes? || 52 ||
(Then various colored jewels enter.
Kṛṣṇa—(Observing them with joy) Ah! The jewels have arrived. Among these, there is a certain particularly lustrous and curved preeminent jewel. (With longing)

This heart-stealing [moon], which causes the waters of the entire ocean to surge with longing, does not please me by its mere luster; rather, it seems to melt my heart even from within, as if stirred by the memory of kinsmen acquired in previous births. (53)
I shall announce this to the God of gods, O Kṣīrakaṇṭha: "Examine, examine the jewels that have arrived.
Maheśa—(with pride)—"Today the earth has achieved its purpose! Indeed, it must be said: the treasures have arrived; Lakṣmī has arrived; the nectar has arrived. Therefore, now—"
May these jewels, the crest-gems of purifiers, for a moment assume the role of ornaments for the Velāvana forest,
as if seeking an embrace from the ocean until the end of time with their long-reaching arms of rays. 54.
(The jewels remain with her.

Vāsu—(To himself, joyfully) O heart, O heart! By good fortune you prosper through this proximity to the sight of Kamalā. No, no, the arrangements ordained by Maheśa do not come to naught. (Aloud, with eagerness) Hasten, hasten, O gods and demons! Let the Mandara mountain be whirled about!
(All do so.
Indra—(with wonder and confusion): Let it cease, let it cease! That churning-whirlpool; this is some other, most gentle substance.
(All observe with wonder. Vāsava— (looking on with reflection:)
Could this one, with waves of splendor arising from his gentle luster, be a brother to the moon—
yet not a fulfiller of the great festival for the eyes?
In the middle, however, it is not like that; there is no blackness. || 55 ||
Indra—(observing with wonder): Oh! This female form has suddenly emerged and become manifest!
Vāsuki—
(Reflecting with noble intent) Ah! What beauty she possesses!
Surely some ocean of loveliness dwells within the depths of the great ocean; her mother must have been born from that very source.
For how else could there be such a worthy match for this ocean, from whom flows forth the stream of nectar-like ambrosia?
Moreover,
when her slender body was tossed upon the waves by the flood of her shimmering splendor, her limbs were made to sway like the motion of a swing.
As she was filling [the vessel], her bracelets struck against her armlets with a clanging sound.
(Recognizing her, to herself, with a sigh of joy: Surely this is that very girl whom I embraced at Gadgā; may she not become a widow.
For: "The familiarity I have long cherished for her, upon seeing her in this painting, suddenly bursts forth like a sprout and attains the brilliance of a thousand suns. (58)

(Then enters Lakṣmī. Lakṣmī: Alas! Alas! Oh, the wretchedness of my life that even in such a perilous situation it does not emerge! (Looking ahead at Kṛṣṇa, as if with recognition) How is it that this abundance of beauty resembles that dear friend seen in a painting? (Sighing) Or rather, who has ever seen such things shattered? What shall I do? Yet, he delights my sight here. (She gazes upward.)
Vāsava—(To himself, with tears) O heart! You are fortunate to prosper! Even amidst such great agitation, her glance was as if full of intent. For indeed:
[Her eyes] were scorched by the mass of waves from the ocean of milk, heated by the exhaustion resulting from the churning of its full and surging force.
My limbs are chilled by the side-long glances of her whose eyes are filled with horripilation— glances that grant the pleasure of effortless, innocent waves.

Maheśa—(Seeing Lakṣmī, to himself) Surely she is the destined beloved of Puruṣottama; such indeed is Lakṣmī. (Aloud, with intent: O Puruṣottama! Deliver this peerless, helpless woman by taking her hand in marriage.
Lakṣmī—
(To himself, as a serpent: What, is this the Supreme Person? This is some other high-souled being who gives the command! So, will he perhaps take pity on me?
Vāsuki: Here, I shall carry out the command of Śiva. (Extending his hand, he brings forth Lakṣmī.)
Lakṣmī—(To herself, with longing, leaning upon Vaikuṇṭha): Wonderful, wonderful! Even in his great suffering and separation, he is like the moon to its circle of kinsmen.
"O Ukkala, what is this great joy that has arisen among living beings?"
(Aloud, turning and looking at the ocean, with distress) Oh, the agitation of my father due to the great pain!
Vāsava—
(With joy)
"O fair-faced one! Cast off this fear; your father, the ocean, is being entreated, yet he truly does not heed us.
To him who spoke thus, Mandara replied with harsh contempt regarding the gods and demons who had arrived: 60.

(To himself) This much is my happiness; any bodily exertion for the sake of another is something else entirely. (Thus, with bashfulness, he somehow lowers it from his neck. Lakṣmī—(Proudly, to herself) Nectar has been tasted by me, and the moon has been seen; yet never before have I experienced such sweetness of speech. Therefore, this must surely be that very same beloved. The virtues heard of from Gaṅgādvāra correspond exactly to those in him.
Vasu—(humbly) O Supreme Lord! Here comes Lakṣmī.
Maheśa—

Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! I knew from the very beginning what was being whispered by this mother of mine, the wife of the Ocean, the Mandākinī upon my crown. (To Gaṅgā) O Gaṅgā, you who can take any form at will! Rest Kabhalālayā in the forest on the shore.
(Gaṅgā rises suddenly and does so with her).
Bali:—

(To himself, with distress) Alas! I perceive that even Maheśa, Keśava, and the others possess a truly wicked intent; for though they hold their positions, they do not share the treasures obtained from the churning of the ocean. (With contempt) Very well. Even later, the other objects will be easily obtained by the strength of my arms alone, provided the gods do not become immortals by drinking the nectar. Therefore, I must remain vigilant at the moment the nectar appears. For now, then. (Aloud) Friend Kujambha! Come, come!
Kujambha:—
(Entering) What are you commanded to do? (Bali whispers thus into his ear.
Kujambha—
(With joyful exultation) This is accomplished!
Indra:
O venerable Nārāyaṇa! This resolve is centered entirely upon you. Why do you now merely praise it?
Vāsuki—
(Whirling Mount Mandara, to himself with longing):
As long as there was the enjoyment of the pleasure of a bold embrace from that girl with eyes like those of a young deer, during which she was overcome by fear...
Having utterly stripped away the strength of my arms and the power of my intellect, Kāma thus mocks me; what can I do in this matter? (51)
(Aloud, with feigned indifference) O gods! O demons! Whirl the Mandara mountain once more with all your might!
(They all do so). Dhanada:

"Look, look! Their faces are tossing about like jars! Indra—(with agitation): "Let it be, let it be for now regarding the churning of Mount Mandara! How is it that all the jars are floating up together? (Reflecting) Are these [jars] distinct because they have burst open? Otherwise, how could they float with their mouths turned upward?"
Dhanada:
(Reflecting) What is this vessel, its mouth turned upward, in the ocean—a mine of wonders?
Vāsuki: ...
(Reflecting, along with his companions:
Surely this boat, constructed with jars containing treasures, is approaching us.
Whose eloquent speech is renowned even throughout the three worlds for crossing the ocean of poverty.
Indra—(with wonder):
Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Look, look! Something else is emerging from the heap of treasure-pots. (Observing for a moment, with joy and wonder):
This is a most marvelous jar that has arisen from the midst of the flood of the ocean!
That which, though previously unknown, arises and brings supreme joy to those who are bound by delusion. (63)
Kṛṣṇa—(To himself, with pride):

Surely this must be a jar of nectar, since at the mere sight of it, even my inner soul becomes overwhelmed with joy. (Aloud, with pride) O Maheśa! O Maheśa! By good fortune you prosper through the arrival of the nectar; the jars of the treasure-trove have arrived.
Maheśa—

(Sadly and with agitation) Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! You must remain vigilant here. Let the jars of nectar themselves protect the Velāvana forest; summon and deliver the jar of nectar to the consumer of oblations.
Kṛṣṇa — (With pride and a loud laugh) O Agni, crest-jewel of the Pāyanas! Come, come hither!
Vāli—(With agitation) Friend Kujambha! Janārdana, the God of gods himself, is calling for Pārava. Therefore, go and bring Pārava from the Velāvana forest. (He looks with a sidelong glance.
Kujambha—
(Exiting from the word "Saddasā," Pāvapacepa enters and says with humility: "What does the venerable Keśava command? Kṛṣṇa:
(With pride) Friend Śociḥkeśa! You are the foremost among all; you are the most excellent among all. Therefore, take this nectar-jar. (He hands the jar to him.)
Kṛṣṇa—(With derision) O friend Śiṣpin! Why have you become so feeble and despondent?
Kujambha—
(Humbly) Does such radiance emanate even from those like us when they are near you? (He steps aside.
Bali—(To himself, with pride) Well done, well done! Kubera has been thoroughly subdued.
Vasu—(To Mahārṣabha) O givers! We have accomplished our task and are now conversing; therefore, let us now, with unrestrained impetuosity, shake Mount Mandara by the power of a thousand arms.
(They all move accordingly.)
Vāyu:
(With fear) Alas! I now behold the ocean turning pale as if it were enraged; and from here, some wicked aquatic creature is emerging.
Indra:
(One must discern correctly: This is not a water-dwelling creature;
it is terrifying, exceedingly crooked, hard-hearted, and possesses a curved mouth expert at cutting through the vital organs.
Like a goad for the ocean, this one approaches the storehouse of wicked deeds.
Dhanada—
(with astonishment) Behold, behold! From this direction comes this unbearable rod, like that of the Lord of the Gods.
This cruel rod of punishment approaches,
out of fear of which the multitude of aquatic creatures flees far away into some part of the ocean.
Vāyu:
(Aside) A certain fish, its body visible through the rays of its shimmering luster, is approaching from this direction.
Indra:
(Observing) Do not speak thus;
if this were merely darkness, why would the fish perish upon its touch, their bodies torn asunder?
With his limbs covered by a mass of horripilation delightful from attachment, this Maṇḍalāgra rises from that ocean.
Vasu:
O Supreme Lord! Look, look! The ocean is greatly agitated. Maheśa:—

(With discernment) Have his soldiers gone forth armed, or is this Udayugha himself advancing with valor? This great soul from a foreign land is profound in his modes of wrath. The weapons of the high-souled one issue forth spontaneously, stirred by the effort of churning. Therefore, having paid homage to these [weapons] along with their presiding deities, settle them in the coastal forest. These will be easily obtained even by the gods and will lead to great fruit.
(Kṛṣṇa, having done so, again sets the churning process in motion as before.
Mahendra:
(Looking with astonishment) Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Look, look! A certain marvelous emerald of immense size is gleaming here. Vāsudeva—(Examining it closely)
This vessel of wine has arisen from the power that is the cause of the mass of bliss; therefore, hold it firmly with intense devotion.
The emerald shines with swarms of bees.
Dhanada:—
(With agitation) A great danger, a great danger! Look here at those birds wheeling about up above.
Struck by the wind of the great waves, they fall;
these enemies become whales, and milk instantly turns into the nature of fire.
Indra—(Reflecting) Look, look! A certain creeper has indeed emerged here.
Kṛṣṇa—
(Examining it) This must be poison! Alas! A great calamity has befallen us! Śiva! Śiva! The gods have arrived, and the poison has also arrived!
Maheśa—(With agitation) Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! You must arrange these two substances, along with their presiding deities, and deposit them in the Velāvana forest!
(Kṛṣṇa does so.
Mahendra—(Impetuously):
O gods and asuras! Now, exert yourselves with even greater force in this churning, so that once we have obtained the marvelous objects, we shall have no further desire for churning. (They all do so.)
(A confused clamor behind the scenes) Vāsuki—(listening, with agitation): Ah! Who is this whose terrifying clamor spreads on the western side of Mount Mandara, frightening both gods and demons?
(To himself again: Smoke rises from somewhere, defiling the eyes with its impurity;
these flames, longing for the destruction of the nectar of immortality, flicker about.

Is this the Ocean of Milk, noisy with the uneven sounds of its churning-sticks as they are parched by the heat of the milk and rendered rough by pride, returning once more with a dark-blue luster; or is it some other cloud above? (69)
Vāsudeva—(Looking all around with fear and wonder) How strange! Alas! In a mere moment, I see nothing at all.
Where has the great ocean vanished? And where has that Mount Mandara gone?
Where has the lord of serpents fled, and alas, where have those gods and asuras gone?

What manner of thing has occurred, wherein the entire circle of the quarters is set ablaze by waves of terrible darkness that meet together, making the very expanse of heaven and earth appear like the underworld? (70)

Maheśa:—(With agitation) O Kṛṣṇa! Your duty lies in protection; therefore, take now the objects obtained from the churning of the ocean along with the gods and asuras, and protect them somewhere. I shall pacify this calamity.
(Thus they all exit.)
Act One.
(Then enter Caikuntha in the guise of a deceptive lover and Vainateya in the guise of a female companion.
Vainateya:

(With joy) O Janārdana! What is this boast regarding your skill in creating a form so much swifter than your own universal form, which possesses the nature of the entire world? Furthermore, this female form manifested by you today has certainly never been experienced even by you before. Why, moreover, is this display—by which you have rendered fruitful the ripening of your past merits and the god of Love—extended in vain in this bower of the coastal forest devoid of men?
For indeed, a pair of eyes plays languidly and listlessly near the ears; the creeper-like brow dances, and it fans the flower-arrowed god of Love.
This lotus-face of yours intoxicates with its constant, radiant smile; you too experience agitation within yourself when you behold the mirror.
Vaikuṇṭha:

Friend Vainateya! This extraordinary erotic sentiment (*arthakṛṅgāra*) is conducive to a great purpose. And here, I shall expand upon the display of coquetry out of fear of the sudden arrival of some person.
Vaina—
(With agitation) What? A sound as if of someone here is heard! Surely someone is approaching.

Vaikuṇṭha—(With apprehension) Friend Vainateya! Therefore, from this point forward, for the purpose of enacting the state of a woman, let us two engage in a conversation in the vernacular language, acting out the role of one who has made the god of love his ally.
Vaina—
(looking through the gaps between the leaves, aside) A certain great-souled and distinguished person has indeed arrived with his attendants.
(Then enter Bali and Kujambha.)

Vāli—(With satisfaction) Friend Kujambha! Well done, well done by you; with great skill, you have drunk the very essence of nectar. Yet, what is this "nectar" that, though obtained, is as if unobtained, since I have not secured some maiden whose beauty rivals that of the daughter of the ocean?
Kujambha—

(To himself, with loathing) Alas! This delusion of passion; for now he perceives nectar in the lower lip of a woman through her embrace. (Aloud, with humility) Yet, I consider that even this is not difficult to attain for one of your powerful fortune.
Vaikuṇṭha—(To himself, with derision) Both things shall become difficult to attain.
Vāli:
Friend Kujambha! Why does this fragrance of musk waft forth from here? Kujambha:
(Gesticulating as if smelling, with astonishment) Oh, Lord of the Dānavas!
This fragrance is certainly not familiar from thousands of forest creepers;
rather, this wave of musk-scent betokens some unknown source.

Therefore, rising, I shall first examine it. (Having done so, with joy and wonder) O Lord of the Dānavas! Come, come; gratify your eyes! From this day forward, your birth shall be fruitful. Behold this jewel of a maiden, never seen before!
(Vāli rises with longing.
Vainya—
(Aside) Vaikuṇṭha! Let the external manifestations of the pangs of separation be enacted.
Vaikuṇṭha—(To himself)

That very separation which I intended to represent through various means such as sighing, paleness, and emaciation—now, kindled by the sorrow of being separated from the Daughter of the Ocean, it has become truly real. (3)
Vainayikī:
Dear friend Mohanikā! Why do you thus distress yourself without even considering your own self? Tell me, where is that charming youth who was seen by Śivāvinādinī?
Mohanikā:
"O clever girl! Enough with this consolation. Indeed, indeed, there is no one at all in the three worlds who possesses such a resemblance to him.
Vālī—(Listening with longing): But why, then, by this wonderful expectation, is that virtuous man being made successful by this beautiful-eyed woman?
Kujambha:
Come, let us reveal ourselves for a moment. (The two approach Uma.)
Nipuṇikā—(Rising with joy and modesty) O Great Lord! A salutation from the princess!
Bali—
(Aside) May your ladyship’s daughter obtain what she has requested.
Vaikuṇṭha—
(To himself) Although her syllables are faltering due to her agitation, this whispered message will be complete.
Kujambha:— (Arranging his upper garment as a seat) Let the Lord of the Dānavas grace this seat. Bali:—
(Sitting down with a sudden start, to himself, in wonder:
Never before has such a jewel among women been seen in the craftsmanship of the Creator;
could she perhaps be composed of the very power of Madana, the world-conqueror?

(Aloud, to Vainateya in the guise of a female friend: "Noble lady, who is this daughter of your master? For what reason is she so distressed? Vainateya, disguised as Nipuṇikā: "O noble one! She is indeed the younger sister of Kamalā, the daughter of the Ocean. Ever since she beheld a certain youth of extraordinary beauty in a dream, she has been languishing, her body tightly veiled by women due to an internal, burgeoning, and most violent agony. Yet, out of extreme courage, she does not even fear death."
Who utters the cry of supreme compassion? Who [dwells] upon the Malaya breeze?
Who, with longing for life, listens to the warbling of the kalakaṇṭha cuckoo? (4)

(With a meaningful gesture, expressing her own thought: "But now, ever since the moment I beheld you, I feel as if I am experiencing some inexplicable longing. Who knows whether there is a resemblance between you and one seen in a dream?
