(She stands with her face cast down in modesty, casting sidelong glances as if threatening Vainateya while assuming the demeanor of Nipuṇikā.
Bali:

(With longing and yearning) O innocent one! Favor me with glances that are intoxicated by the potency of nectar. O fair-browed one, my life, which is now as if lifeless, is entirely dependent upon you.
(Paikuṇṭha looks at him with a smile, his face turned downward.
Vali— (with longing:)
This wondrous garland of her lotus-eyes, strung together with the thread of love,
has fortunately become a veil for me, O fair-limbed one.

(Aloud) Friend Kujambha! I have been honored by the favor of Sudṛśā. But why does our venerable preceptor Bhārgava delay? For he was summoned by me to take the seat of honor at the great festival of the consumption of nectar, after I had sent Sandhānaka [to fetch him]. Is the preceptor perhaps lame, or occupied with some other task?
(Then enters Bhārgava, followed by Sandhānaka. Sandhānaka: —
(With a bow) O Dānava! Here has arrived our preceptor Bhārgava.
(Vāli, rising with haste and approaching him in the proper manner, bows down.
Śukra:

(With pride) "May Kali increase as he prospers! (To himself, with embarrassment) Ah! How is it that while I intended to say "Vāli," being overwhelmed by a surge of joy, the word "Kali" has escaped my lips? Very well; let this remain unknown for now.
Sandhānaka—(Bringing forward a seat) May the noble sir grace this with his presence.
Śuka:

(Sitting down, gazing at Vaikuṇṭha in the form of a maiden, to himself with wonder) Oh, what an unprecedented marvel is this female form in the creation of the Lord of Creatures! Is she perhaps composed of the very essence of beauty? (Vaikuṇṭha, in the form of a woman, sits there likewise, bashful.)
Vāli—(With pride) O venerable Bhārgava! This daughter of the ocean, who mocks the abode of Lakṣmī with her beauty, is full of passion for me; beyond this, the venerable one is the authority.
Śukra—

(Sadly) What is there to deliberate upon here? Be free from obstacles; you are the vessel for a succession of all prosperity. (Behind the scenes) One does not consider this fate to be very cruel, since the Dānavas—having abandoned the field of battle and having seized all the wealth acquired from the entire ocean by those gods who mocked them—have now arrived undaunted.
Vali—(Rising in anger) Ah! Has Vali become so weak that such a thing will happen?
Kujambha—
"Prepare, prepare the armies!

Śukra—(indicating the throbbing of his left eye, to himself, with distress): Ah! How is it that this ill omen, which portends my own misfortune, follows even after another ill omen? Therefore, for now: (Aloud) O King of the Dānavas, this great festival of battle is not appropriate. At present, the gods are exultant.

Vāli—(With derision) O Preceptor Bhārgava! You surely know the strength of Vālin; why then is this being said? (With agitation) By that very mountain used as a churning-stick, which was violently whirled by the pillar-like strength of my arms...
The ocean was churned by him in such a manner that it yielded the poison born from it;

having crushed those who were restless with the heat of their arms due to that very [poison], I shall now swiftly make the father of this [Goddess Lakṣmī]— the enemy of the Daityas— once again fierce with irrepressible pride.
Śukra:

O Lord of the Daityas! For you, who have consumed the nectar and are thus a conqueror of death, the commencement of battle brings only happiness. Bali (with pride): O Preceptor! This nectar is merely medicine; what is the use of it?
Having fashioned this exceedingly wonderful nectar, born from the ocean,
with my two arms,
I have brought about the destruction of the race of my enemies.
It suddenly bears my immortality. || 8 ||
This was vowed by me in the presence of the Blessed One, my Guru:

"Having made those who have reached the end of their lives at the holy ford on the riverbank into rivals on the field of battle, I shall abandon the journey through saṃsāra, satisfied with a joy exceeding that of nectar."
When you, the family preceptor, are honored with the seat of honor along with your friends and kinsmen, shall I, together with my beloved Mohinī, swiftly attain nectar or not? (9)

Mohinicepo Vaikuṇṭha: (To himself, with joy) By good fortune, the counsel of Bhārgava has been frustrated; by good fortune, Bali has mounted the swing of Death as if upon a difficult vow. Śuka: *Note: The provided text contains a fragment of a dialogue from a Sanskrit drama. The names "Mohinicepo Vaikuṇṭha" and "Śuka" appear to be specific characters or titles within that context.*

(With anger) O fool! Since the lineage of Dānava has fallen into ruin because you are thus possessed by an evil obsession, I shall nevertheless instruct you: Those great Daityas—Madhu, Mura, and the one named Hiraṇyākṣa—soon met their end in the flames of the sword-like fire of Viṣṇu’s discus.
Now that Hari has gone to Vaikuṇṭha, how is it that this audacity, born of the pride of your arms, manifests itself against women?
(Vaikuṇṭha and Vainateya look at each other with mutual pride and act out a concealment.
Bali:
(With anger) O Preceptor Bhārgava! What are you prattling? Vaikuṇṭha stands right before me! This alone I request of my Lord.
Protect this maiden, who possesses manifold beauty and is free from attachment to passion; she is peerless and was created by Himself for great happiness.
"Let this effort of mine not be in vain. || 11 ||
"Friend Kujambha! Bring me the vessel of nectar.
(Kujambha brings it). Bali—
(Taking the nectar and assuming the form of a maiden, she enters Vaikuṇṭha: "O Lord!
Take this nectar yourself; this nectar is useless to me.
O beloved, may your desires be fulfilled within a few moments; I am going to the festival of battle. (12)
(Thus he holds a vessel of nectar before him.

Vaikuṇṭha in the form of a maiden—(with compassion, as if with a faltering voice): "For the sake of victory in battle, [I shall wait] for two or three muhūrtas" (when this was said regarding the *arghya*, she speaks with apparent shame and a faltering voice): "I will wait for two or three muhūrtas. Then, at the meeting with the Pāpaka, I shall abandon this body which has been without purpose."
Vāli—(With agitation.
O fair-browed one! What occasion for swelling now is there? I have almost arrived. (He exits with hurried steps.)

Vaikuṇṭha in the form of a woman—(aside, with joy) My desire is accomplished, as if by the removal of a great obstacle. Therefore, enough of staying here. So be it for now. (Aloud, as if bashfully) Dear friend! Place this vessel of nectar in your hand. You are indeed clever; surely this will not be lost from your hands at all. You have brought it back once again. (She does so with a graceful gesture.)

Śukra—(To himself, with apprehension): Ah! Nectar has fallen into the hands of another, and my soul is filled with doubt; what, then, shall I do here? Very well; let this be merely the wicked sport of Bali. Vaikuṇṭha—
(To himself) Enough of this delay! (Recalling something) I shall bring fire for the purpose of incineration. (He mimes the recollection of fire.
Śukra—(Looking all around with agitation) Ah! What is this?

With its vast flames it soon armor-clads the circle of the quarters, and with masses of great smoke it makes the sky exceedingly thick; and due to its extreme boiling, it causes even the Ocean of Milk to surge upward. What is this fire that spreads so intensely without the destruction of a kalpa? || 13 ||
Moreover, having dispelled the mass of smoke and other obstructions by means of its fierce radiance, the sun performs its function there; indeed, it is perpetually self-luminous.
Furthermore, through the succession of its clusters of flames, shaken by the wind, this entire world repeatedly appears like a great golden vessel of the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa).
So, what is appropriate here?
Vaikuṇṭha:
Dear friend Nipuṇikā! There is no hope for that fortunate one. Therefore, come; let us make ourselves meaningful by resorting to fire. (Both rise.)

Śukra—(To himself, with apprehension) Oh, her love born of former passion is indeed a devotion that ends only in death! Having taken up the nectar as it were, she begins to enter the fire. Thus, both have failed to be protected by me. Very well, I shall stop her. (Aloud) O auspicious lady! Why is this inauspicious act being undertaken so suddenly? Wait for a few moments. Vaikuṇṭha—
(With distress and indignation) Alas! Why do you speak such improper words? It would indeed be appropriate for me, who am so deeply attached to that disciple of yours, to act in this very manner.
Śukra:

O simple girl! For the protection of both you and the nectar, I have been entreated by the Lord of the Danavas in your very presence. Therefore, if you do not desist even when being restrained, I shall create a pillar of fire.
Vaikuṇṭha:—(To himself) The nectar has now come into my hand. Therefore, I shall now witness his curiosity as well. (Aloud) Let him do what is appropriate for one who is ignorant. Śukra:—

(Performing a gesture with the *agnistambha* mantra, with astonishment) Ah! With its broad flames spreading violently forward, this fire of intense brilliance does not heed the ritual application consisting of mantras, as if possessed by the vow of a hero. (14)
(Reflecting) Could the power of the mantras of Bhārgavī fail when directed toward the sacrificial fire kindled at the time of the rite? No, no, it could not turn away.
He whose constant attention is fixed on the destruction of the race of Asuras—where indeed is that wealthy Enemy of Kaiṭabha here? || 15 ||

I shall discern this through meditation. (Acting out meditation; to himself) Ah! This Murāri has taken the form of a woman; thus, this calamity has begun. Why still fear? (Aloud, with derisive laughter) Vaikuṇṭha! Vaikuṇṭha!
Shame, shame on the nectar produced by wallowing in the ocean! And shame, shame on that collection of rare objects!
O Vaikuṇṭha, what indeed have the foremost of the Danujas not obtained, such that you have been turned into a woman? || 16 ||
Vaikuṇṭha:
(Casting aside his form as Mardila with a sneer) O Bhārgava! Those who are experts in the path of policy would never act thus; why do you speak in this manner?
Vainateya:

(Casting off her form as Śrī, with a mocking laugh) O Preceptor of the Daityas! Let us depart. You too, having gone with the Daityas, take your place at the head of the assembly during the great festival of partaking the nectar.
(Thus they all exit.
The Second Act.
(Then Kṛṣṇa and Lakṣmī enter.
Kṛṣṇa—(Observing Lakṣmī, to himself with joy and boldness: Surely the Creator was a complete stranger to the craft of fashioning such a creation; for instance:
The digits of the moon, the sprouts of the celestial tree, the nectar, the brilliant lights, and those various jewels—
such is the wondrous array of resources belonging to him.
He alone becomes the one who releases; he is the lord who has let her loose.

(With distress) Why do I contemplate her thus, as one overcome by despair? (Reflecting) Surely, having heard that the time for her marriage is approaching, this despondency—so natural to a maiden—is arising within her. Very well; I shall console her. (Aloud) Release me, my beloved! Why do you bind my fingers with your feet, agitated as you are by the fear of separation from your father?
O fair-browed one! Gathering together the happiness of your affection, I shall remain like a water-creature within the ocean of your embrace.

Lakṣmī—(To herself, with pride) Even so it may be; or does my beloved console me? (Aloud, with a voice choked with tears) How could this be? Since the time of the pain of the churning, even a mere sight of him has been difficult for me to obtain; yet here, in the very form of my father, who is like a divine tree, I behold your form revealed.
Kṛṣṇa—

O slender-limbed one! Your meeting with your father is indeed imminent. Surely the Lord Śiva, along with the gods headed by Prajāpati, fearing that he might commit some impropriety under the sway of greed, has dispatched Varuṇa to bring the Blessed Ocean here. And as for the depth of your father’s nature, what pain could there be from a mere Mandara-whirlpool? Whatever of the multitude of treasures acquired through churning the ocean he grants to anyone, that shall belong to him.
Therefore, may you take heart.
Kṛṣṇa:—
(Reflecting, to herself) Alas, what a perilous situation for young maidens!
(Lakṣmī, consoling [him], looks toward the ocean with compassionate affection:
"Because of the distress caused by separation from kinsmen, and because of the great festival of obtaining a beloved..."
The minds of young maidens flare up in passion for a moment and are filled with love for another moment. || 3 ||
So, this much for now. (Aloud) My dear, my dear!
Here is one whose many wave-arms rise up eager to seize [us], and who has fashioned a graceful seat from the whistling of the *kāraṇḍava* birds.
O tremulous-eyed one! This mass of shimmering darkness, its luster gathered as if eager to behold you, shines forth. || 4 ||
(Lakṣmī remains with joy.
Kṛṣṇa—(indicating the throbbing of his left eye, to himself, with dejection) Ah! Is there still some obstacle remaining even now? (Offstage) Alas! Alas!
As if snatching away all the worlds in an instant, covering the sky, the quarters, and the earth, a certain actor—darkness—unfolds himself, more skillful than the fire at the end of an aeon. (5)
Moreover,
these supreme objects— the moon and others— which were acquired through the exhaustion of churning the ocean,
being distressed by the blows of ill fortune, now forcibly desire to return once more to the midst of the sea.
Kṛṣṇa:

(Hearing this, with agitation and crying out loudly) Oh, Guardians of the Quarters! Protect, protect me for a moment... [hears a cry] ...messengers have been sent to obtain news. And I am here protecting the nectar and Lakṣmī. Indeed, there is a swarm of wicked Daityas here, eager and longing. (With dejection and distress) Ah! How is it that even he, Śiva—who experiences such terrible calamity from the mere drawing of his bowstring—has become "Un-auspicious" (A-śiva)?
(Then enters Bhārgava, wearing a skull-garland and carrying a shield.)
Bhārgava:—(With agitation and alarm) Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! My limbs are dissolving from the heat of the poison.
"Give, give this nectar to me! Why do you delay? ||7||
Kṛṣṇa—(To himself, with distress) Ah! Alas, alas! I behold what has never been seen before. Oh!

This very thing is an ill omen: that this terrible darkness and this fierce wind! Therefore, I shall drink nectar; I will not look at Vainateya in his presence. Oh, what a great cause for reflection this is!
For instance:
"Let the terrible Kālakūṭa poison burn Śaṅkara; let it burn—no, no, even that would not cause such extreme agitation."
For he, being an embodiment of supreme splendor and invincible, was indeed incapable of even enacting a divine dramatic performance.

"I shall discern him through meditation. (Performs a gesture of meditation; then, with anger: "Ah, Śukra! In this crooked battle, what have you done? Though you have committed an offense—being both a bearer of Śiva’s disguise and a twice-born—you are not to be slain by me. Therefore, depart before you fall within the range of Śiva’s eyes!
(Śukra vanishes in fear.
(Then enters Śaṅkara, followed by Vainateya.)
Kṛṣṇa:—(Looking at him, rising with courtesy, and blowing a kiss with a smile) Salutations, salutations to the guileless Śaṅkara! Please, sit here. Śaṅkara:—
(Taking his seat upon the throne brought by Vainateya, with a smile: Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇā! What is this extraordinary display of devotion toward you today? Kṛṣṇa:
(With a smile) Why should anything be reported to one who is all-knowing?
Śaṅkara:

(With a smile of approval) Bhārgava has begun a fitting retaliation for what was done [to him]. For you, having assumed the form of a beautiful woman, deceived the Daityas; the nectar was recovered—what more need be said? This wondrous form of yours is being elevated to the pinnacle of accomplishing the tasks of the gods. So why does Varuṇa, who was sent to bring the ocean, delay?
Kṛṣṇa:

"O Vainateya! You too, having gone by the command of Maheśa, bring the Ocean here quickly. Vainateya—(having walked a few steps and turning back): "Behold, Brahmā and the other gods are approaching; and here comes the Ocean, the repository of jewels, followed by Varuṇa. Why, then, have these [gods] gone forward to rise in greeting him?"
Kṛṣṇa:

O Vainateya! No, no! These are surely the gods, beginning with Candra, who—distressed by the destruction of their splendor caused by the darkness of the illusion produced by Bhārgava—and being pursued by his wicked conduct, have gathered together on the shore and are now approaching. (Then enter Brahmā and the other gods as described, followed by Varuṇa and the Ocean.)
Maheśa and Kṛṣṇa:
(With great joy) We salute your holiness, the eldest in the world. Please be seated here with Mahendra and the others, each according to your rank.
Sāgara:
(Humbly) Here is the Ocean bowing to you all.
Kṛṣṇa—
(With courtesy and respect) May your honor, who are so near, please sit down here.
(Sagara does so with her.
Lakṣmī—(Piteously, with tears): Father! What is this that has happened? (She clings to his neck.)
Samudra:—(With compassion) Daughter, daughter! Do not despair. Through the grace of Rudra, the conclusion will be auspicious.
Maheśa:—
(Aside) Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! I cannot bear to show him my face.
(Thus he stands with his head bowed down in distress.
Samudra—
(With humility) O Lord of the three worlds, you of the South! Why are you troubled? Look, raising your face with a serene gaze!
"You are the best for me—no, no! You are merely my servant; out of fear, I mistake even this contempt for honor. (9)

Moreover: I am neither a coward nor have I been defeated by anyone else that I should thus despair; for indeed, when I was about to protect Maināka from the thunderbolt of the enraged Śakra, I was seen by the Daityas with their faces struck by the blows of leaping waves.

By the grace of Śambhu, I have become awakened; though I am one who would burn the three worlds with the fire from my eye, my greatness remains unimpaired even at the time of creation and even at the time of dissolution.
Śaṅkara:
(With joy and reverence) What more need be said?
The very essence of creation has found its birth in you.
The Creator fashioned even the seven worlds;
you are the sustainer of all, yet the King of Sindhu is not your sustainer— there is no one at all who is so.
"Therefore, take this collection of goods; forgive our indiscretion.
Samudra—(with pride and humility): "O Lord Bharga! This is a favor bestowed upon me as well. Why now, by returning it, do you instead inflict a punishment?"
Śaṅkara:
Therefore, may you yourself, having distinguished them, honor the gods with your own mouth.
Samudra: [So be it.]

I shall carry out this command of the God. (Looking all around) Let the Vedas, like sweet-sounding bees in the forest of the lotus-face of Brahmā, dispel the pain of separation from their own source by resting upon my lap.
(The Vedas approach.
Samudra:—
"May my noble son, the Moon, fulfill my purpose by attaining the status of being the ornament upon the head of the Lord of the Pramathas.
(The Moon does so with her.
Lakṣmī:—
(To himself, with dejection: My life is fixed in my throat; I do not know what my father will say.
Kṛṣṇa: (To himself, with longing: Now is the moment for the fruit of the ripening of my good deeds.

Samudra:—(With joy) May Govinda, who is ever intent on bestowing grace upon his devotees, cause my lineage to blaze forth by accepting this lotus from the Lotus-Pond (Lakṣmī). (Thus he places Lakṣmī’s hand into Kṛṣṇa’s hand. And let this Kaustubha gem be the sacrificial fee for the great gift of my daughter. (Thus he offers the Kaustubha.
Kṛṣṇa:—
(Visioning Lakṣmī, to herself with longing:
Those sprouts of Kāma’s arrows that have sunk into the body of the fair-limbed one—
these very ones have been drawn out by my hand under the guise of her horripilation.
The Ocean:

And let this lordly elephant, the companion of the king of steeds Uccaiḥśravas, who is strengthened by his residence upon the throne of the King of Gods, uproot the forest of the lotuses of the Durdharṣa dynasty.
(Airāvata, together with Uccaiḥśravas, takes refuge with Indra.)

May these mountains, such as Meru and Mandara, be even more fortunate by serving as the repositories for great medicinal herbs and jewels dedicated to the welfare of the entire world. (The medicinal herbs and jewels take refuge in Meru, Mandara, and the others. May the Ocean accept the treasures that have brought an end to poverty, O Lord of Wealth!
(The treasures likewise submit to him.)
The Ocean:
Let Varuṇa accept the wine that brings delight to the entire world and the noose that destroys those who have done harm. (Varuṇa does so.
The Ocean: [Accepts.]
Taking up his great weapon, the hook, the wind-god acts with such audacity in the slaughter of the enemy lineage that he is unrestrained.
The ocean—let the leader of the goblins take up his sword, which is devoted to the protection of the world. (The one devoid of thirst acts accordingly.)
Samudra:
Let it be; though he is the Śamana who pacifies the breath of the entire world, let him be even more fierce by means of this staff.
(Yama rises joyfully and takes up his staff.)
The Ocean:
Accepting the poison, let the great serpents, headed by Vāsuki, become even more difficult to restrain; and this [poison] is most formidable. (Vāsuki rises joyfully and takes the poison.)
The Ocean:
May the nectar preside over the mouth of all the gods, which is the source of light. By partaking of this, may the gods become free from decay and immortal. (The nectar takes refuge in the Fire).
The Ocean:
(With joyful exultation) O Lord, whose crest is the moon of nectar!
O Lord of the Pramathas, today I consider myself to have achieved my life's purpose through this festival of churning and crushing, brought about by you.
Since I have attained the state of a donor by bestowing these substances upon the multitude of gods and supplicants, what else do I desire? (13)
Nevertheless, let this be so:
may ornaments that delight in the flavors of magnanimity and heroism bring happiness; may people whose minds are perfumed by the true path flourish.
May the clouds rain down as they are filled with the weight of their joy, and may the poets become embodiments of the festival of Sarasvatī. 14.
(Thus they all exit.
The third act.
Thus ends the *samavakāra* titled *Samudramathana*, composed by the great poet Vatsarāja.
